##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> अयमग्निः सद्यस्तदानीमेव जातो जायमान एव यज्ञं व्यमिमात ।
> विशेषेण निर्मिमाते । उत्पादयति ॥ माज् माने शब्दे च चौहोत्यादिकः ॥ अत
> एवायमग्निर्देवानां पुरोगाः प्रथमगामि मुख्योऽभवत् ॥ गमेर्विट्प्रत्यय आत्वे च कृते रूपं ॥ ततः प्रदिशि प्रकृष्टायां दिशि प्राच्यामृतस्याहवनीयात्मनागतस्यास्य होतुर्होमनिष्पादकस्याग्नेर्वाचि । अत्र वागाश्रय आस्यं
> लक्ष्यते । वाच्यास्यॆ स्वाहाकृतं स्वाहाकारेण प्रक्षिप्तं हविः सर्वॆ देवा अदंतु ।
> भक्षयंतु । इदं सूक्तं यास्केन सम्यगभ्यधायि । नि. ८.५-२१ । तदत्रानुसंधीयतां ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

This Agni, born at that very moment, as soon as he is born, व्यमिमात (*vyamimāta*) the sacrifice: he specially makes, produces it (the root माज् (*māj*), of the Cauhotyādi class, in the sense of measuring and of sound). For that very reason this Agni became पुरोगाः (*purogāḥ*), the first-goer, the chief of the gods (the form arises when the affix विट् (*viṭ*) is added to गम् (*gam*) and ā is substituted). Then, in प्रदिशि (*pradiśi*), the excellent eastern quarter, in the voice (वाचि (*vāci*)) of this Hotṛ, the accomplisher of the offering, Agni, who has come in the form of the Āhavanīya: here "voice" as the seat of speech denotes the mouth. Let all the gods eat the oblation cast with the cry स्वाहा (*svāhā*) into that mouth. Sāyaṇa adds that this sūkta was well explained by Yāska (Ni. 8.5-21), and that it should be consulted here.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- सद्यः (*sadyaḥ*)—at once
- जातः (*jātaḥ*)—Agni, having been born
- यज्ञं (*yajñaṃ*)—the sacrifice
- व्यमिमीत (*vyamimīta*)—produces
- अग्निः (*agniḥ*)—that same Agni
- देवानां (*devānāṃ*)—for the gods
- पुरोगाः (*purogāḥ*)—as chief

### Printed p. 367

- अभवत् (*abhavat*)—has become
- प्रदिशि (*pradiśi*)—in the excellent eastern quarter
- ऋतस्य (*ṛtasya*)—who is in the form of the Āhavanīya
- होतुः (*hotuḥ*)—the accomplisher of the offering
- अस्य (*asya*)—of this Agni
- वाचि (*vāci*)—in the mouth
- स्वाहाकृतं (*svāhākṛtaṃ*)—offered with the cry svāhā
- हविः (*haviḥ*)—the oblation
- देवाः (*devāḥ*)—the gods
- अदंतु (*adaṃtu*)—eat

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

As soon as Agni is born he produces the sacrifice. That same Agni is the chief of the gods. The gods eat the oblation offered with the cry svāhā into the mouth of Agni, who is in the form of the Āhavanīya in the excellent eastern quarter and is the accomplisher of the offering.

##### English translation
As soon as he was born, Agni constructed a sacrifice, he was the preceder of the gods; may the gods partake of the oblation presented with the swaha through the voice of him the hotri of the sacrifice at the eastern station.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

Yāska's explanation of the word स्वाहा (*svāhā*):

स्वाहाकृतयः । स्वाहाकृतयः स्वाहेत्येतत् सु आहेति वा । स्वा नागहेति वा । स्वं प्राहेति वा । स्वाहुतं हुविर्जहोतीति वा ॥ (*svāhākṛtayaḥ | svāhākṛtayaḥ svāhetyetat su āheti vā | svā nāgaheti vā | svaṃ prāheti vā | svāhutaṃ huvirjahotīti vā ‖*) (Ni. 8-21)

The word स्वाहा (*svāhā*) has four analytical meanings.
(1) सु आहेति वा (*su āheti vā*): सु (*su*) = well, आह (*āha*) = says. Because it is uttered well or clearly, it is called स्वाहा (*svāhā*).
(2) स्वा वागहेति वा (*svā vāgaheti vā*): स्वा (*svā*) = one's own speech (वाक् (*vāk*)). There is a Śruti sentence (Brāhmaṇa): तं स्वा वागभ्यवदज्जुहुधीति तत्स्वाहाकारस्य जन्म (*taṃ svā vāgabhyavadajjuhudhīti tatsvāhākārasya janma*). That is, when making the offering, the offerer himself adds and says the word स्वाहा (*svāhā*) at the end of the Ṛk, the Vedic mantra; hence the name स्वाहा (*svāhā*).
(3) स्व प्राहेति वा (*sva prāheti vā*): here स्व (*sva*) = his own oblation, आह (*āha*) = he says that he offers. Hence the name स्वाहा (*svāhā*).

### Printed p. 368
(4) "Or because he offers the oblation well offered (*svāhutam*)": the oblation which he offers in homa is offered by uttering the word svāhā, that is, by presenting the oblation in Agni; hence the name svāhā.
For the meaning of svāhākāra Yāska has given the following passage as an illustration:
सद्यो जातो व्यमिमित यज्ञमग्निर्देवानामभवत्पुरोगाः । अस्य होतुः प्रदिश्यतस्य वाचि स्वाहाकृतं हविरदंतु देवाः ॥ (*sadyo jāto vyamimita yajñamagnirdevānāmabhavatpurogāḥ | asya hotuḥ pradiśyatasya vāci svāhākṛtaṃ haviradaṃtu devāḥ ‖*)
सद्यो जायमानो निरमिमित यज्ञमग्निर्देवानामभवत्पुरोगाम्यस्य होतुः प्रदिश्यतस्य वाच्या स्वाहाकृतं हविरदंतु देवाः ॥ (*sadyo jāyamāno niramimita yajñamagnirdevānāmabhavatpurogāmyasya hotuḥ pradiśyatasya vācyā svāhākṛtaṃ haviradaṃtu devāḥ ‖*)
(Ni. 8-21)
Its main sense: Agni, who has just been born (that is, has just been established in the sacrifice), sits before the gods and, performing the duty of the hotṛ, that is, the work of inviting the gods, carries the sacrifice through. May the gods eat the oblation which this hotṛ, stationed in the east, offers, offered in homa with the utterance of the word svāhākāra. The idea is therefore that svāhā is the name of the word uttered at the end of the mantra when the oblation is offered, according to rule, in the duly established Agni for the sacrifice, to please the gods.
In some Āprī-sūktas the plural *svāhākṛtayaḥ* is used. Since the word svāhākāra is added and recited also with the eleven Prayāja mantras used when offering to the eleven deities of this sūkta, the plural *svāhākṛtayaḥ* is employed.
In the Prāṇas and the like the word svāhā is used in another sense. The Mahābhārata calls the daughter of Bṛhaspati, son of Andhakāyi, Svāhā; in the Purāṇas the goddess Svāhā is said to be the daughter of Dakṣa Prajāpati and the wife of Agni.
On the nature of svāhākṛti the opinions of the learned are not of one kind. Yet all the entities indicated by this word are directed to the terrestrial Agni alone. Because this Agni is the maker of svāhā and also its product, the terrestrial Agni is so called; so the author of the Nirukta and the author of the Bṛhaddevatā state their view: अग्नेया इति तु स्थितिः (*agneyā iti tu sthitiḥ*) (Ni. 8-22). In the last Ṛk of some svāhākāra Āprī-sūktas, deities such as Pūṣan, the Maruts, Vāyu, Sūrya, Indra and Varuṇa are all praised. Since the gods are gladdened by mantras ending in the word svāhā, the word svāhā holds an important place in the sacrifice.

### Printed p. 369
## Sūkta 111 (Maṇḍala 10)
Introduction.
In the Ṛgveda no other deity has the prominence that Agni and Indra have. Considered by the number of sūktas and Ṛks, the first place goes to Indra. About a quarter of all the mantras in the Ṛgveda-Saṃhitā praise Indra alone. Since it is necessary to know about Indra fully and critically, we shall set it out here. To the question who Indra is, the seer Gṛtsamada has given the proper answer earlier in Ṛ. Saṃ. 2.12. Stating that briefly here, the matters found in the Ṛgveda about Indra are told.
O people, he who, as soon as born, became the foremost of the gods, firm of mind, radiant, who by deeds such as the slaying of Vṛtra honoured and protected all the gods, and through the strength of whose body heaven and earth both were afraid, joined with the greatness of his army-like might: he is Indra.
O people, he who made the trembling earth stand firm, who made the mountains that roamed everywhere with wings bend to his control and stay fixed, who fashioned the wide atmosphere, who held up and propped the heavens: he is Indra.
O people, he who, having slain the cloud, made the seven flowing rivers such as the Gaṅgā flow, who freed the cows caught in the confinement of the asura Vala, who created the fire in the form of lightning in the midst of the clouds, and who is unrepelled in battles: he is Indra.
O people, by whom this perishable world was made to stand firm, who made the destroying and base asura dwell in the cave that is hell, who conquered the enemy he had aimed at, and who, as a hunter takes possession of a deer, made the enemy's abundant riches his own: he is Indra.
Of him, the terror of the enemy, of whom they ask "Where is he?", the knowing say that he is not in one place only. That same Indra, causing alarm, destroys all round the cows, horses and the like that belong to the enemy and nourish him.

### Printed p. 370
O people, place faith in such a great Indra.
O people, he who gives wealth alike to the rich, to the poor, to the one who begs of him, and to the praising ṛtvij; who has fine cheeks, and who is the protector of the sacrificer who holds the pressing-stone in hand and has pressed the Soma: he is Indra.
O people, under whose rule, he being the inner controller of all, are horses, cows, villages and all chariots; who, having slain Vṛtra, created the sun and Uṣas; who, splitting the cloud, impels the waters: he is Indra.
O people, whom the divine host and the human host, sounding together, call for protection; whom both the best and the lowest enemies call; and whom the two charioteers, mounted on a chariot like Indra's chariot, call separately (for protection): he is Indra.
O people, without whom people cannot win victory, and therefore those engaged in battle call on him for protection; who is the representative of the whole world, and who made the immovable mountains and the like move: he is Indra.
O people, who slew with the thunderbolt the people who bore great sin, were many, and were full of arrogance; who gives no encouraging help to one without knowledge of the self; who is the destroyer of the enemy that causes decay: he is Indra.
O people, who searched out and finally found the asura Śambara, who lived hidden in the mountains for forty years, and slew that strong and murderous dānava: he is Indra.
O people, who, seven-rayed, rain-giving and mighty, freed the seven rivers such as the Gaṅgā from the serpent so that they might flow; who, thunderbolt in hand, slew the asura Rauhiṇa as he climbed the heavens: he is Indra.
Heaven and earth both bow humbly to this Indra, and from this Indra's might the mountains tremble. He who is a drinker of Soma, firm of body, with arms like the thunderbolt, who holds the thunderbolt in hand: he is Indra.

### Printed p. 371
O people, who protects the sacrificer who presses the Soma; who protects the one who cooks the puroḍāśa and the like; who protects those who ask for protection; who protects the praisers; and for whom the hymn, the Soma and the puroḍāśa and other foods are increasers: he is Indra.
O Indra, you who, unrepelled, give abundantly food and strength to the sacrificer who presses Soma and cooks puroḍāśa and the like, are you not of true nature? We, dear to you, and joined by your grace with sons, grandsons and others of good fortune, recite the hymn on all days.
Indra's origin; his parents and his wife.
Although Indra's greatness is described in a most excellent and poetic style, Indra is nowhere described as a supreme god without birth. As noted on many earlier occasions, Indra's mother and father are specified. His manner of birth too is praised at great length in many places. For example, some mantras quoted below speak of Indra's birth.
"O Indra, on the very day you were born you drank the juice of the Soma plant born on the mountain-slope and showed your great fondness for it. Your mother, young, who bore you, in the house of your father of great might gave you that Soma and satisfied you. This same Indra, as soon as born, approached his mother and found the Soma in her breast." (3-48-2, 3)
"O Indra, your father is very firm of body, as the atmosphere expects. The begetter of Indra, who roars in the atmosphere and is steady as the earth, is a most skilful doer of deeds. Indra has the utmost devotion to his father and to his mother." (4-17-4)
"The womb too is that same ancient door through which the gods were born of old. May the fully grown child come out through this door; may Indra, born from it, not needlessly hurt his mother." (4-18-1)
Knowing that Indra's origin would reveal a fault, Indra's mother hid him. Most powerful, he rose of himself as a most attractive bearer of weapons and at once pervaded heaven and earth both. (4-18-5)

### Printed p. 372
His mother brought forth the most powerful, firm-bodied, Indra of unrepelled power, heroic and robust, as a cow bears a calf, so that he might move freely by himself and show his strength. (4-18-10)
When Indra of great power was born, his mother, out of fondness for her son, warned him: "O son, none of these gods helped you; all have abandoned you." Then Indra said: "O Viṣṇu, since Vṛtra the asura must be slain, become one who has the form and power to pervade all worlds." (1-18-11) **NOTE**
"O Indra, who made your mother a widow? Who, when you were asleep or moving about, wished to kill you? Who was the god near you when your father was seized by the foot and harmed?" (4-8-12) **NOTE**
"The mighty father begot a son of strength fit to destroy enemies in battle; the radiant woman bore a radiant son." (7-20-5)
"O Indra, as soon as born you drank Soma to gain your strength. Your mother made your greatness manifest." (7-98-3)
"To show your unrepelled power you were born of fearsome form. Displaying anger, and making known your proud valour, you showed your self-confidence. When Indra's mother, full of wealth, bore Indra, the Maruts tended and fostered this mighty Indra so that he grew ever greater." (10 73-1)
The god who begot this Indra, of fearsome form and unrepelled power, is of the greatest might in the whole universe. (11-20-1) **NOTE**
"O Indra, as Uṣas pervades the whole world, so when you stood pervading all of heaven and earth, your mother, divine and of great form, bore you, the lord of all the gods, the best of the world's people." (8.0-134-1) **NOTE**
"As we have known before, this Indra is the son of Niṣṭigrī. (Sāyaṇa explains Niṣṭigrī as Aditi.)" (10-101-12) **NOTE**

### Printed p. 373
Although in the Purāṇas and the like Indra is famed as one of the Ādityas and as Varuṇa's companion (Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-85-4), in other parts of the Ṛk-Saṃhitā he is mostly not described in this way, that is, as one of the Ādityas. In 4-26-1 identity with Manu and Sūra is shown. In the mantras 8.8-2-1 and 4, 10.89.2 he is denoted by the word sūra. In 2-30-1 he is described by the epithet savitṛ.
In the Atharvaveda Indra's power is described by the passages quoted below.
एकाष्टका तपसा तप्यमाना जजान गर्भं महिमानमिंद्रं । तेन देवा अपहंत शत्रून् हंता दस्यूनामभवच्छचीपतिः ॥ (*ekāṣṭakā tapasā tapyamānā jajāna garbhaṃ mahimānamiṃdraṃ | tena devā apahaṃta śatrūn haṃtā dasyūnāmabhavacchacīpatiḥ ‖*)
(Atha. Saṃ. 3-10-12)
Ekāṣṭakā, practising powerful austerity, bore the great Indra. By the help of this Indra the gods conquered their enemies. Indra, lord of Śacī, became the slayer of the dasyus.
In the next Ṛk Ekāṣṭakā is specified as the mother of Indra and Soma and as the daughter of Prajāpati. In the Atharvaveda Indra's mother is addressed (6.38) but not named. The Mahābhārata says that Indra is one of the sons born to Kaśyapa of Dākṣāyaṇī, the daughter of Dakṣa, who has the other name Aditi. (Ā. Pa.) In Atharvaveda 8-58-4 he is called son of truth (सूनुं सत्यस्य (*sūnuṃ satyasya*)).
Elsewhere it is said that Indra was created by the gods to destroy enemies (3.49-1): घनं वृत्राणां जनयंत देवाः (*ghanaṃ vṛtrāṇāṃ janayaṃta devāḥ*) (2-13.5; 3-51.8).
The Puruṣasūkta says that Indra, with Agni, was born from the mouth of the Puruṣa (मुखादिंद्रश्चाग्निश्च (*mukhādiṃdraścāgniśca*)). (10-90-13)
Elsewhere in the Ṛk-Saṃhitā it is stated definitely that Indra is one of the gods born of Soma. (9-96-5)
Such a mighty Indra conquered heaven by the power of his austerity. (10-167-1)
In the Śatapatha and other Brāhmaṇas the story of Indra's origin is told in various ways. For example, the account in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa is as follows.

### Printed p. 374

ता वा एताः प्रजापतेरधि देवताः असृज्यंत अग्निरिंद्रः सोमः परमेष्ठी प्राजापत्यः । ताः सहस्रायुषो जज्जिरे । ता यथा नद्यै पारं परापश्येदेवं स्वस्यायुषः पारं पराचख्युः ॥ (*tā vā etāḥ prajāpateradhi devatāḥ asṛjyaṃta agniriṃdraḥ somaḥ parameṣṭhī prājāpatyaḥ | tāḥ sahasrāyuṣo jajjire | tā yathā nadyai pāraṃ parāpaśyedevaṃ svasyāyuṣaḥ pāraṃ parācakhyuḥ ‖*) (Śa. Brā. 11.1.6.14)

Agni, Indra, Soma and Pārameṣṭhi Prājāpatya are all deities created by Prajāpati. They all came into being with a thousand years of life. Just as a man can see the far bank of a river, so all of them were able to see beyond the limit of their own lifespan. The Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa tells of Indra's origin as follows:

प्रजापतिर्देवासुरानसृजत । स इंद्रमपि ना सृजत । तं देवा अब्रुवन् । इंद्रं नो जनयेति । सोऽब्रवीत् । यथाहं युष्माग्स्तपसासृक्षि । एवमिंद्रं जनयध्वमिति । ते तपोऽतप्यंत । त आत्मन्निंद्रमपश्यन् । तमब्रुवन् । जायस्वेति । सोऽब्रवीत् । किंभागधेयमभि जनिष्य इति । ऋतून्त्संवत्सरं । प्रजाः पशून् । इमान्लोकानित्यब्रुवन् । तं वै माहुत्याप्रजनयतेत्यब्रवीत् । तं चतुर्होत्रा प्राजनयन् । (*prajāpatirdevāsurānasṛjata | sa iṃdramapi nā sṛjata | taṃ devā abruvan | iṃdraṃ no janayeti | so 'bravīt | yathāhaṃ yuṣmāgstapasāsṛkṣi | evamiṃdraṃ janayadhvamiti | te tapo 'tapyaṃta | ta ātmanniṃdramapaśyan | tamabruvan | jāyasveti | so 'bravīt | kiṃbhāgadheyamabhi janiṣya iti | ṛtūntsaṃvatsaraṃ | prajāḥ paśūn | imānlokānityabruvan | taṃ vai māhutyāprajanayatetyabravīt | taṃ caturhotrā prājanayan |*) (Tai. Brā. 2-2-3-3, 4).

Prajāpati created the gods and the Asuras. Only Indra he did not create. Then the gods addressed Prajāpati and prayed, "Create Indra for us." Then he said to the gods, "Just as I, by the power of my austerity, caused all of you to come into being, so you also, as the fruit of the toil of austerity, create Indra." Then all those gods practised austerity. Then they found Indra within themselves. Afterwards they told him to receive a share of the oblation. Then Indra said, "For what purpose must I manifest myself outside?" They said, "You must be born for the nourishment of the seasons, and for the protection of the year, of all beings and of all worlds." But in another place in this same Brāhmaṇa the account of Indra's origin is somewhat different. It runs as follows:

प्रजापतिरिंद्रमसृजतानुजावरं देवानां । तं प्राहिणोत् । परेहि । एतेषां देवानामधिपतिरेधीति । तं देवा अब्रुवन् । कस्य मसि । वयं वै त्वच्छेयाग्‌ंसस्म इति । सोऽब्रवीत् । कस्यमसि वयं वै त्वच्छे याग्ंसस्स इति मा देवा अवोचन्निति । अथवा इदं तर्हि प्रजापतौ दर आसीत् । यदस्मिन्नादित्ये । तदेनमब्रवीत् । एतन्मे प्रयच्छ । अथा- हमेतेषां देवानामधिपतिर्भविष्यामीति.... ... ततो वा इंद्रो देवानामधिपतिरभवत् ॥ (*prajāpatiriṃdramasṛjatānujāvaraṃ devānāṃ | taṃ prāhiṇot | parehi | eteṣāṃ devānāmadhipatiredhīti | taṃ devā abruvan | kasya masi | vayaṃ vai tvaccheyāgṃsasma iti | so 'bravīt | kasyamasi vayaṃ vai tvacche yāgṃsassa iti mā devā avocanniti | athavā idaṃ tarhi prajāpatau dara āsīt | yadasminnāditye | tadenamabravīt | etanme prayaccha | athā- hameteṣāṃ devānāmadhipatirbhaviṣyāmīti.... ... tato vā iṃdro devānāmadhipatirabhavat ‖*) (Tai. Brā. 2-2-10 1, 2)

### Printed p. 375

After creating all the gods, Prajāpati created Indra last and made him lord over the remaining gods. Then the gods addressed Indra: "Who are you? We are all superior to you; how can you be lord over all of us?" Then Indra explained the situation and begged Prajāpati to provide him with Prajāpati's power, which confers the fitness to be lord over all the gods. Afterwards he obtained their lordship. So it is said. In the Taittirīya Saṃhitā:

इंद्रो वै देवानामानुजावर आसीत्स प्रजापतिमुपाधावत्तस्मा एतग्ं षोडशिनं प्रायच्छत्तमगृह्णीत ततो वै सोग्रं देवतानां परैत् (*iṃdro vai devānāmānujāvara āsītsa prajāpatimupādhāvattasmā etagṃ ṣoḍaśinaṃ prāyacchattamagṛhṇīta tato vai sograṃ devatānāṃ parait*) (Tai. Saṃ. 6-6-11-2)

Indra was the youngest of all the gods. Then, with the intention of going to Prajāpati, obtaining his help and attaining lordship over the gods, he offered the Ṣoḍaśin. Then Prajāpati granted his favour. As a result Indra obtained excellent fitness and became lord over the gods. So it is said. Moreover, in another part of the same Taittirīya Saṃhitā the same matter is stated somewhat differently:

तेनेंद्रं प्रजापतिरयाजयत्ततो वा इंद्र इंद्रोऽभवत् । (*teneṃdraṃ prajāpatirayājayattato vā iṃdra iṃdro 'bhavat |*) (Tai. Saṃ. 7-2-10-2)

Prajāpati had Indra perform a sacrifice by offering rice and the like according to the season. As a result Indra attained Indra-hood. It is said. In the same way, through the power of the sattra called Pañcadaśarātra, he obtained both the power to destroy the Asuras and the power to become lord over the gods. This is stated.
(Tai. Saṃ. 7-3-6-1)

A passage of the Ṛksaṃhitā states that Indra and Agni are twins, with the same father but different mothers.
(6-59-2)

In 10-55-1 the sons of Indra's brother are mentioned; it may be said that Heaven and Earth are these sons of the brother. In 6-55-5 Pūṣan is mentioned as Indra's brother.

### Printed p. 376

It is described that Indra displayed a warrior's prowess even in infancy. The description is as follows. "Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, as soon as he was born, took up his weapon and asked, 'Who are those warriors renowned as most valiant?'"
(8-45-4; 8-66-1)

"O Indra, you are by nature free of enemies, and aged (great)": thus a devotee praises Indra and expresses his devotion.
(1-102-8; 1.176-1; 10-133-2)

"O Indra, being greatly delighted, join your wife, and through union with her attain your satisfaction": the passage in which Indra's wife is mentioned describes an occasion on which Indra enjoys amorous beauty. समु पत्न्यामदः (*samu patnyāmadaḥ*).
(1-8-5, 6)

During this kind of domestic happiness a perplexing situation sometimes arises. On the one hand the soma-oblation which the sacrificers offer at the sacrifice is very attractive. The seer describes Indra's predicament: Indra often doubts which of the two he should accept and which he should give up. It runs thus:

"O Indra, the housewife is the house; she is the dwelling of the man. Therefore let your horses carry you to the place where your housewife is. But as soon as we have offered the soma-oblation, let Agni come to you to invite you." (3-254) **NOTE**

"O Indra, my brother, set out. Please come here. Both places are attractive to you. When your chariot stands, your horses are unyoked."

"O Indra, you have drunk the soma. Now set out for your home. In your home there is an attractive wife, and you have excellent domestic happiness. Wherever your chariot halts, there you should unyoke your horses." (3.25-6)

The name Indrāṇī is mentioned in many places, but it is not stated directly that she is Indra's wife. Yet from that naming one may confidently say that she is Indra's wife.
(1 22-12; 2-32.8; 5-46.8; 10-86 11, 12)

### Printed p. 377

In these places she is praised together with Agnāyī, Agni's wife, and with Varuṇānī, Varuṇa's wife, and she is also invited to the sacrifice along with them. But in the mantras 10-86-11 and 12 there is a somewhat special account of her.

"Of all these goddesses I have heard that Indrāṇī is the most fortunate. For her husband has no old age, and so no death as its consequence." So it is said.

A sentence of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa states precisely that Indrāṇī is Indra's wife and that she has an excellent head-ornament that takes on every form.
(Pa. Bri. 14-2-1-8) **NOTE**

The account in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa that describes Indrāṇī's good fortune is as follows:

इंद्राणी देवी सुभगा सुपत्नी । उदग्‌ंशेन पतिविद्यॆ जिगाय । त्रिग्ंशदस्या जघनं योजनानि । उपस्थ इंद्रग् स्थविरं बिभर्ति ॥ (*iṃdrāṇī devī subhagā supatnī | udagṃśena patividyè jigāya | trigṃśadasyā jaghanaṃ yojanāni | upastha iṃdrag sthaviraṃ bibharti ‖*)
(Tai. Brā. 2.4-2-7)

This says what was stated above, that the fortunate Indrāṇī is a giver of happiness to her husband. The Kāṭhaka passage is of another kind:

इंद्रो वै विलिष्टेंगां दानवीमकामयत । सोऽसुरेष्वचरत् स्त्रीव स्त्रीषु भवन् पुमान् पुंसु । स निर्यतिगृहीत इवामन्यत । स एतमैंद्रानैर्यतमपश्यत् ॥ (*iṃdro vai viliṣṭeṃgāṃ dānavīmakāmayata | so 'sureṣvacarat strīva strīṣu bhavan pumān puṃsu | sa niryatigṛhīta ivāmanyata | sa etamaiṃdrānairyatamapaśyat ‖*)
(Kā. Saṃ 13-5) **NOTE**

Indra was enamoured of a Dānava woman named Viliṣṭeṅgā. Then, joining the Asuras, he behaved among women like a woman and among men like a man. Then, feeling himself seized as if by Nirmuti (निर्मुतिगृहीत (*nirmutigṛhīta*)), that is, recognising his own bondage, he accepted an oblation in order to counteract it. **NOTE**  Besides this, in the Atharvaveda:

येनानि चक्रे आसुरी इंद्रं देवेभ्यस्परि । तेनानि कुर्वे त्वामहं यथा तेऽसामि सुप्रिया ॥ (*yenāni cakre āsurī iṃdraṃ devebhyaspari | tenāni kurve tvāmahaṃ yathā te 'sāmi supriyā ‖*)
(A. Ne 7.38.2) **NOTE**

"O Indra, you must love me. To bring that about, I make you mine with the help of this herb." So saying, with its help that woman drew Indra, who was among the gods, into her own company. So it is said. In this way different Śruti passages give different accounts of Indra's wife.

### Printed p. 378

**Epithets showing Indra's physical and mental qualities**

Epithets describing Indra's extraordinary qualities are very plentiful. First, the description of his youth and strength. This Indra is very young and yet ancient, exceedingly powerful and skilful in action.
(1-130.7; 2-22.4; 6-29-3; 8-24.9, 12; 8-58-7; 8-81-3)

There are also very many passages describing Indra's warrior qualities: that he has kṣatriya valour, is resplendent, ageless, conquers all, has boundless discernment, has unobstructed valour and vigour, and bears the thunderbolt.
(1-4-8; 1-16-9; 1-30-6, 15; 1-61-1; 1-81-2, 7; 1-84-2; 1-100-12; 1-102-6; 1 165-6; 2.21-1, 2, 3; 3.30-3; 3.32.7; 3-45-3; 3-46.0; 6.18-4; 7-20.4; 7-22-5; 8-81.8; 8-84-7)

In Indra's body there is valour, in his arms strength, in his hand the thunderbolt, in his head discernment.
(2.86-2)

Indra can assume many kinds of forms. All those forms are exceedingly beautiful and have the golden hue of the sun. (10.102-3)

The seers who beheld the Ṛksaṃhitā described this special beauty of Indra with many kinds of comparisons. The words suśipra and śiprin are the chief among them. These words mean one with fine cheeks or nose. This is Indra's personal quality.
(1-9-3; 1-29-2; 1-81-4; 1-101-10; 3-32-3; 3-36-10; 8-32.4 . 24. 8-33.7; 8-55.4; 10.105.5; 3-30-3; 8-17.4; 8-81-4)

In 8-65-10 it is described that Indra, having gained strength through drinking soma, savours the sweetness of the soma by smacking his lips. Epithets such as hariśipra, harikeśa and hariśmaśru are also very frequent; they mean one with golden cheeks, golden hair, golden beard and moustache.
(10-96.4, 9, 12; 10-96-5, 8; 10-23-4)

When he is greatly delighted, his beard and moustache bristle and move.
(2-11-17; 10-23-1)

### Printed p. 379

(In 6-46-3 Indra is also described as thousand-faced.)

The whole form of this Indra is golden. In many places his form is described as harivarpas and as of golden form.
(10-96-1; 8-55-3; 1-7-2)

But in some other places he is also said to be of iron form, that is, one whose body is made of iron.
(1-56.3; 10-96.4, 8)

His arms are spread far and wide. (pṛthū karasnā bahulā gabhasti).
(6-19-3; 8-32-10; 8-70-1)

A mantra that is not in the Ṛksaṃhitā, in the Sāmasaṃhitā, praises Indra's long arms and attractive form and describes them thus:

इंद्रस्य बाहू स्थविरौ युवानावनाधृष्ट्य सुप्रथितावसह्यौ । तौ युंजीत प्रथमौ योगे आगते याभ्यां जितमसुराणां सहो महत् ॥ (*iṃdrasya bāhū sthavirau yuvānāvanādhṛṣṭya suprathitāvasahyau | tau yuṃjīta prathamau yoge āgate yābhyāṃ jitamasurāṇāṃ saho mahat ‖*)
(Sā. Ve. 2-1219) **NOTE**

When the occasion arises for Indra to display his prowess, let him employ the arm which formerly destroyed the great power of the Asuras and won victory; which is powerful, youthful, of unobstructed strength, of charming form and invincible. So it is said.

But Indra's forms are endless. In many places it is said that by mere resolve he can take on any forms he likes:
(3-38-4; 3-48-4; 3-53.8)

रूपरूपं प्रतिरूपो बभूव तदस्य रूपं प्रतिचक्षणाय । इंद्रो मायाभिः पुरुरूप ईयते युक्ता ह्यस्य हरयः शता दश ॥ (*rūparūpaṃ pratirūpo babhūva tadasya rūpaṃ praticakṣaṇāya | iṃdro māyābhiḥ pururūpa īyate yuktā hyasya harayaḥ śatā daśa ‖*)
(Ṛ. Saṃ. 6-47-18)

**Indra's chariot and horses**

Indra, seated in his golden chariot, with a golden whip (kaśā) in his hand, sets out on his journey. That chariot has a thousand supporting pillars.
(6-29-2; 8-1-24; 8-58-16)

This chariot of Indra is swifter than the mind.
(10-112-2)

### Printed p. 380
This chariot is drawn by a pair of horses that are golden-hued, of unobstructed power, and that neigh wondrously. They have manes of golden form, and they are as attractive as peacock feathers. These horses are very swift in movement and can travel great distances. Just as a bird can travel with the help of its wings, so Indra too can fly throughout the atmosphere with the help of his horses.
(1.30.16; 1.81.3; 1-10.3; 1.82.6; 8.17-2; 8.32.29; 8.82-24; 3-45-1; 8-1-25; 2-16-3; 8-34-9).
In the prayer-mantras asking Indra to come to the Soma-drinking, borne by the horses that carry his chariot, Indra's immeasurable numbers of horses are specified. He is entreated to come with horses numbering two, four, six, eight, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, eighty, ninety and a hundred.
(2-18-4 to 7; 8-19)
In some other places this number even exceeds a thousand. For example: "Indra and Vāyu are both borne by horses numbering a thousand."
(4-46-3; 6-47-18; 8-1-24)
Because Indra's horses are of a supernatural nature, an exact knowledge of their form cannot be grasped by the human eye. Hence the question arises naturally: "Who is able to see Indra's two horses? Who has seen them?" हरी इंद्रस्य नि चिकाय कः स्मित् (*harī iṃdrasya ni cikāya kaḥ smit*).
(11-114-9)
It is well known that Indra's chariot and horses were made by the skilful craftsmen, the Ṛbhus.
(1-111-1; 5.31-4).
Some sentences, with the sense given below, tell of special qualities of Indra's chariot and horses. For example, the horses that carry Indra's chariot are described as having eyes like the sun (सूरचक्षसः (*sūracakṣasaḥ*)).
(1-6-2; 1-16.1, 2; 1-55.7; 1-84-6; 1.101.10; 3-11.6; 8-13-11, 97; 10-44-2)
Indra is praised sometimes as being carried by the horses of Sūrya, and at other times as being carried by the horses of Vāyu.
(10-49-7; 10-22-4 to 6)

### Printed p. 381
The description of Indra travelling at times as charioteer in Vāyu's chariot, and at other times as his friend, both seated in one chariot, shows in a striking way the relation between Indra and Vāyu and the speed of Indra's chariot.
(4-46-2; 4-48-2; 7-91-6)
Indra's horses, by the power of praise, come of themselves to the chariot and are yoked. ब्रह्मणा ते ब्रह्मयुजा युनज्मी हरी (*brahmaṇā te brahmayujā yunajmī harī*).
(3-35.4; 1-82-6; 2-18-3; 8-1-24; 8.17-2; 8 2-27; 8-45-39; 8-86-9)
The sense is that as soon as the prayer in the form of praise by the sacrificing patrons is recited, Indra at once yokes the horses to his chariot in order to come to their sacrifice. Since praises are the cause of yoking the horses to the chariot, the idea is that the yoking of the horses takes place through the power of praise. Thus, of the many Saṃhitā passages that describe Indra's majestic chariot and horses, which travel throughout earth and atmosphere, only a few have been explained above as examples.
Indra's thunderbolt and other implements
Indra's great thunderbolt is well known to have been made by Tvaṣṭṛ, the divine craftsman. It is also said that Tvaṣṭṛ made it for Indra alone (त्वष्टास्मै वज्रं स्वर्यं ततक्ष (*tvaṣṭāsmai vajraṃ svaryaṃ tatakṣa*)).
(1-32-2; 1-68-6; 1-85-9; 5.31-4; 6-17-10; 10-48-3)
But in some places alone it is stated precisely that it was made by Kāvya Uśanas and given to Indra for the slaying of the Asuras. (यं ते काव्य उशना................ततक्ष वज्रं (*yaṃ te kāvya uśanā................tatakṣa vajraṃ*)).
(1-28-2; 5-34.2)
On the creation of the thunderbolt and Indra's taking it up, a passage of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa says as follows—
देवा वै प्रथमेनाह्नेंद्राय वज्रं समभरंस्तं द्वितीयेनाह्नासिंचंस्तं तृतीयेनाह्ना प्रायच्छंस्तं चतुर्थेऽहन्प्राहरत् ॥ (*devā vai prathamenāhneṃdrāya vajraṃ samabharaṃstaṃ dvitīyenāhnāsiṃcaṃstaṃ tṛtīyenāhnā prāyacchaṃstaṃ caturthe 'hanprāharat ‖*) (Ai. Brā. 4-1)
The gods, for the proceedings of the first day, provided the thunderbolt for Indra; on the second day they consecrated it; on the third day they handed it over to him; on the fourth day Indra wielded that thunderbolt given by the gods. It is said. Moreover,
"The thunderbolt lies covered with water in the ocean situated in the atmosphere."
(8-100-9)

### Printed p. 382
In this account the natural order of origin of the thunderbolt is described. This thunderbolt is said in some places to be of golden form (1-57-2; 1-85.9; 8-57-3; 10-23-3), and in some places to be golden-hued mixed with green (10-96-3); in still other places it is said to be आयस (*āyasa*), that is, made of iron (आयसः (*āyasaḥ*)).
(1-52.8; 1-80-12; 1-81-4; 1-121-9; 8-85-3; 10-48-3; 10-96-3; 10-113-5)
Some passages hold that it has four edges. (4-22-2) (चतुरश्रिः (*caturaśriḥ*)). But there are also passages that call it शताश्रि (*śatāśri*) (6-17-10), meaning having a hundred edges. It is also described as having a hundred joints (शतपर्वन् (*śataparvan*)).
(1-80-6; 8-6-6; 8-63-2; 2-78-3)
There are also some contexts that call it a thousand-jointed.
(1-80-12; 1-85-9; 55-34-2; 6-17-10)
भीमा इंद्रस्य हतयश्वतभृष्टीरयस्मयिः (*bhīmā iṃdrasya hatayaśvatabhṛṣṭīrayasmayiḥ*) ।
(A. Ve. 4-37-8)
Indra's weapons, hundred-pointed and made of iron, are praised in the Atharvaveda as extremely terrifying. Elsewhere the same description occurs with the variant reading हिरण्ययीः (*hiraṇyayīḥ*) in place of आयस्मयिः (*āyasmayiḥ*).
(Ka. Pe. 8-5-19)
As a bull rubs its horn, Indra rubs his weapon and sharpens it (for slaying enemies). (शिशीते वज्रं (*śiśīte vajraṃ*)).
(C-55-2)
As the Āditya standing in the atmosphere shines with his divine radiance, so the thunderbolt placed in Indra's hand shines. (दिवे न सूर्यः (*dive na sūryaḥ*))
(8-59-2)
There are also some contexts in which Indra is described as a deity bearing arrows and bow.
(8-45-4; 8-66-6, 11; 10-103-2; 10.103-3)
Indra's arrows have three joints and sharp points. They are adorned with thousands of feathers and are golden.
(8-66-7; 8-66-11)
Indra is also described as bearing a goad. (दीर्घस्ते अस्त्वंकुशः (*dīrghaste astvaṃkuśaḥ*))

### Printed p. 383
"O Indra, may your goad, which helps to provide wealth for the patron who offers you the oblation, be long."
(8-17-10)
The same matter is stated in the Atharvaveda as follows.
यस्ते अंकुशो वसुदानो बृहन्निंद्र हिरण्ययः । तेनाजनीयते जायां मह्यं धेहि शचीपते (*yaste aṃkuśo vasudāno bṛhanniṃdra hiraṇyayaḥ | tenājanīyate jāyāṃ mahyaṃ dhehi śacīpate*) ‖
(A. Ve. 6-82-3)
"O Indra, I am very eager to obtain a wife. With the help of your goad, which provides wealth and is golden, grant me a wife," is the situation of the patron praying to Indra. Moreover,
O Indra, as a goat stretches its forefoot and catches the branch of a creeper, so you too stretch out your goad and draw to yourself the thing you desire. You bear such power.
(10-134-6)
A mantra giving the sense, "O Indra, this long goad, with which you destroy the powerful Asuras, I bring and present to you," conveys the same idea.
(10-44-9)
In the Atharvaveda, the description and praise of Indra's net (jāla) are as follows.
अंतरिक्षं जालमासीज्जालदंडा दिशो महीः । तेनाभिधाय दस्यूनां शक्रः सेनामपातयत् ॥ (*aṃtarikṣaṃ jālamāsījjāladaṃḍā diśo mahīḥ | tenābhidhāya dasyūnāṃ śakraḥ senāmapātayat ‖*)
(A. Ve. 8-8-5)
The atmosphere is Indra's net; the great quarters are the poles of this net. Spreading this net, which pervades all directions, Indra seized the enemies in the form of Dasyus and made them fall down.
बृहद्धि जालं बृहतश्यक्रस्य वाजिनीवतः । तेन शत्रूनभि सर्वान्न्युब्ब यथा न मुच्यातै कमश्चन एषां ॥ (*bṛhaddhi jālaṃ bṛhataśyakrasya vājinīvataḥ | tena śatrūnabhi sarvānnyubba yathā na mucyātai kamaścana eṣāṃ ‖*)
(A. Ve. 8-8-6)
The net of Indra, the giver of food and of great nature, is very extensive. If it is cast and spread, all the enemies are caught. Not one of them can escape from it.

### Printed p. 384
बृहत्ते जालं बृहत इंद्र शूर सहस्रार्घस्य शतवीर्यस्य । : ऽन सहस्रमयुतं न्यर्बुदं जघान शक्रो दस्यूनामभिधाय सेनया ॥ (*bṛhatte jālaṃ bṛhata iṃdra śūra sahasrārghasya śatavīryasya | : 'na sahasramayutaṃ nyarbudaṃ jaghāna śakro dasyūnāmabhidhāya senayā ‖*)
(A. Pe. 8-8-7)
O Indra of great nature, your net, O valiant one, is very extensive. You possess together the strength of a hundred … (तत्तुगळ (*tattugaḷa*)) **NOTE**. You can confront thousands of enemies at once. Indra, together with his retinue, caught in his net all the Dasyu people, numbering a thousand, ten thousand and ten crores, and struck them down with his weapon and killed them all.
अयं लोको जालमासीच्छक्रस्य महतो महान् । तेनाहमिंद्रजालेनामूंस्तमसाभिदधामि सर्वान् ॥ (*ayaṃ loko jālamāsīcchakrasya mahato mahān | tenāhamiṃdrajālenāmūṃstamasābhidadhāmi sarvān ‖*)
(A. Pe. A-A-A)
This world is the net of Indra, of great nature. With the help of that net I make all the enemies caught in pitch darkness.
Indra's … in the Soma-drinking **NOTE**
As soon as he is invoked by the patron for the Soma-drinking, Indra comes ready, seated in his chariot. And there too food for his horses is made ready. And as soon as he arrives, an abundant oblation in the form of Soma is prepared and offered for his drinking.
(3-35-6)
As soon as this Soma is drunk he gains exceeding joy, and from this he gains the enthusiasm needed for battle, and also strength useful for many other extraordinary deeds such as upholding heaven and earth. All kinds of strength and enthusiasm increase.
(2.15-3)
Here only the sense of a few of the many passages describing the manner of worshipping Indra is given. This Soma-juice produces imperishable vitality. The seer prays that, as Sūrya pervades the atmosphere and the other regions with his rays, this Soma-juice may make strength pervade Indra's whole body.
(2-15-1, 2; 2.19.1; 2.21.1; 3-36-3; 3-40.1; 3-42.1; 6-23-1, 5, 6; 6.27.1; 6-29-4; 7-22.1; 7-29.1; 8-3-1; 8-81-5, 6; 10-104-1)

### Printed p. 385
All the gods run eagerly to the share of Soma-juice that is to be offered to Indra.
(8-2-18)
"Along with Indra, the other gods and Agni have drunk. All the gods have been satisfied. But Indra's satisfaction is the greatest."
(1-104-9; 1-175-5; 2-14-1; 3-33-2; 8-2-4)
Among all the other gods, Indra's Soma-drinking is the most excessive. इंद्र इत् सोमपा एकः........अंतर्देवान् मर्त्यांश्च (*iṃdra it somapā ekaḥ........aṃtardevān martyāṃśca*) । (8-2-4). Among the gods and the rest, Indra alone is the true Soma-drinker. Therefore he alone is truly possessed of heroes.
(8-4-12; 8-6-40)
Since Indra's mother provided Soma to him on the very day of his birth, it is clear that Soma is the very life-sustainer (jīvātu) of Indra. (सद्यो यज्ञातो अपिबो ह सोमं (*sadyo yajñāto apibo ha somaṃ*)).
(3-32-9, 10; 3-48-2; 6-40-2; 7-98-3)
It is well known that he drank the Soma of thirty Droṇa vessels in a single gulp.
(8-66-4; 6-17-11; 8-7-10; Ni. 4-11)
His devotees call him to this Soma-drinking with great humility and devotion, and Indra, honouring their invitation, drinks hastily like a thirsty deer.
(8-4-10; 5-36-1; 8-33-2)
The belly (or bellies) of this Indra is like two lakes. Eager to fill it, Indra roars like a bull wandering for water in a waterless wilderness.
(5-36-1; 1-8-7; 1-104-9; 2-11-11; 2-14-10; 2-16-2; 3-35-6; 3.36-7, 8; 3-40-5; 3.47-1; 3.51-12; 8-12-23; 8-2-1; 8-17-5 to 8; 8.67-7; 8-81-22, 23, 24; 10.28-2; 10-43.7; 10-104-2; A. Ve. 2-5-1; 6.2-1)
At times the same description occurs when the patrons drink this Soma-juice. For example—
"As soon as I drink this Soma, it increases my body."
(6-47-3)
the seer says. In another context, describing the power of Soma-drinking—

### Printed p. 386

"We have drunk Soma, and therefore we have become free from death. No man can now harm us. O immortal Indra, by your grace we too shall ascend to the atmosphere together with you, without fear." So the seer proclaims. (8-48-3)

Birds fly to a tree full of leaves, and rivers full of water go and join the ocean; in the same way the stream of Soma juice goes and joins Indra. Just as grain and the like grow abundantly and strongly when rain falls, so the sacrificers, by offering Soma juice, make Indra grow strong. (19-43-4, 7)

Indra is prayed to drink the Soma offered by the sacrificers and to accept the praises offered by them, and to be satisfied by them, as a good husband loves his wife and longs for her company. (3.52-3 : 4-32-16)

To show in detail how the effect of Soma-drinking increases Indra's vigour, a seer in one sūkta has described Indra's nature thus; from it one learns in what various ways Indra, satisfied by Soma-drinking, shows his favour to the sacrificer:

"I have drunk Soma fully. Therefore I shall supply the sacrificer with cattle and horses. The stream of Soma that I have drunk has given me exceeding vigour. As a cow runs lovingly to her calf, the hymn made by the seer has come and joined me. As a carpenter goes around a chariot-seat and perfects it, I too have made that hymn pervade my heart. Even the five peoples, the Gandharvas and others, are small before me. That is the power of Soma. Even if heaven and earth were joined together, they would not equal half of me. I have a greatness that surpasses the greatness of these two, heaven and earth. I establish this earth according to my resolve. The atmosphere is one half of me; the other half I have lowered down. I have the power to rule in the atmosphere. As the fruit of this Soma-drinking I have the strength to carry the oblation to all the gods and distribute it." (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-19-1 to 3)

### Printed p. 387

Like the Soma offered to Indra, the hymns of praise and other kinds of worship offered by the sacrificer also greatly increase his valour and vigour. ब्रह्माणींद्र तवयानि वर्धना (*brahmāṇīṃdra tavayāni vardhanā*) (उक्थैर्वर्धमानाः (*ukthairvardhamānāḥ*)) (1-52-7, 1-54-8, 1-80-1, 2-11-2, 2-12-14, 3-32-12; 3-34-1, 5-31-10, 6-21-2; 6-44-13; 8-6-1, 21, 31, 35; 8-13-6, 8-14-5, 11; 8-82-27; 8-47-8: 10.50.4; 10.120 5).

To give exceeding power to the valour stimulated by that Soma-drinking, the gods and men place the thunderbolt in Indra's hand. (1-63-2; 2-20-8; 3.32.12)

Moreover, the other gods too place all their power in Indra himself. (1-80-15; 6.20-2; 10-48.3; 10-113-8; 10-120-3; 10.56-4; 8.15-8)

And they seat him in a chariot and make him ready for battle. (1-53-3; 1.131-1; 6.17-8)

In many places it is described that at the time of the slaying of the demon Vṛtra the Maruts give Indra encouragement and make his power stand firm and bring victory. That increases the effect of Soma-drinking still more. (या आभजो मरुत इंद्र सोमे ये त्वामवर्धन्नभवन् गणस्ते (*yā ābhajo maruta iṃdra some ye tvāmavardhannabhavan gaṇaste*)). (3.35.9; 3-32.4; 3.47.3; 6-7.11; 8-7-24; 10-23-1, 2; 10-113-3).

In this context it is necessary to state the natural relation and companionship of Indra and the Maruts. This section is to show Indra's regard for Soma. But since it also indicates how stimulating that Soma-drinking is for the slaying of Vṛtra and what part the Maruts play in this, the matter too is incidental.

In 1-165 a dispute between Indra and the Maruts is described. In 1-116-8 Indra boasts that he slew Vṛtra without the Maruts' help, by his own power. In 7.21-6 the same praise is made by Indra's devotee (स्वेना हि वृत्रं शवसा जघंथ (*svenā hi vṛtraṃ śavasā jaghaṃtha*)). Likewise in 10.138-6 too he is praised with एता त्या ते श्रुत्यानि केवला यदेकः (*etā tyā te śrutyāni kevalā yadekaḥ*) ... and so on. It is stated that because of this prowess all the gods fear Indra. (5.30.5). In 8-7-1 the Maruts are asked whether it was not an offence that they did not help their friend Indra in a time of difficulty, and how in such a situation they could be worthy of trust.

### Printed p. 388

In 4-18-11 Aditi, Indra's mother, grieved that all the other gods had abandoned her son without helping him, approaches Viṣṇu and prays that he help her son. But elsewhere there is a somewhat different account. It is stated that while Indra was fighting the demon Vṛtra, all the other gods, afraid of Vṛtra's terrible form, left Indra alone and fled, and that Indra, being a friend of the Maruts, destroyed Vṛtra with their help. (8-96-7). Sāyaṇa in this context has given the purport so that there is no contradiction between the earlier statements and this one. And he has supported his meaning by citing a passage of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa. The passage of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa is as follows:

इंद्रो वै वृत्रं हनिष्यन्सर्वा देवता अब्रवीदनु मोपतिष्ठध्वमुप मा ह्वयधृमिति तथेति तं हनिष्यंत आद्रवन्नॊऽवेन्मां वै हनिष्यंत आद्रवंति हंतेमान्षया इति तानभिप्राश्वसीत्तस्य श्वसथादीषमाणा विश्वे देवा अद्रवन् मरुतो हैनं नाजहुः प्रहर भगवो जहि वीरयस्वेत्येवैनमेशां वाचं वदंत उपातिष्ठंत ! तदेतदृषिः पश्यन्नभ्यनूवाच वृत्रस्य त्वा श्वसथादीषमाणा विश्वे देवा आजहुर्यॆ सखायः । मरुद्धिरिंद्र सख्यं ते अस्त्वथेमा विश्वाः पृजना जयासीति । सोऽवेदिमे वै किल मे सचिवा इमे माकामयंत हंतेमानस्मिन्नुक्क अभजा इति (*iṃdro vai vṛtraṃ haniṣyansarvā devatā abravīdanu mopatiṣṭhadhvamupa mā hvayadhṛmiti tatheti taṃ haniṣyaṃta ādravannò 'venmāṃ vai haniṣyaṃta ādravaṃti haṃtemānṣayā iti tānabhiprāśvasīttasya śvasathādīṣamāṇā viśve devā adravan maruto hainaṃ nājahuḥ prahara bhagavo jahi vīrayasvetyevainameśāṃ vācaṃ vadaṃta upātiṣṭhaṃta ! tadetadṛṣiḥ paśyannabhyanūvāca vṛtrasya tvā śvasathādīṣamāṇā viśve devā ājahuryè sakhāyaḥ | maruddhiriṃdra sakhyaṃ te astvathemā viśvāḥ pṛjanā jayāsīti | so 'vedime vai kila me sacivā ime mākāmayaṃta haṃtemānasminnukka abhajā iti*) (Ai. Brā. 3-20)

Indra, wishing to slay the demon Vṛtra, said to the gods: "O gods, follow me without wavering and be my helpers." They gave the assurance "We shall do so" and advanced to kill Vṛtra. Then Vṛtra, thinking "These gods are advancing to kill me; I shall frighten them," breathed out a mighty breath and made a terrible sound. Hearing that terrible sound all the gods were afraid and fled in all directions. But the Maruts alone did not abandon Indra. Standing right beside Indra they encouraged him: "O Indra, strike him. Show your prowess." Then the seer, praising the friendship of the Maruts, recited the mantra beginning वृत्रस्य त्वा (*vṛtrasya tvā*) and praised them (8-96-7). Then Indra said: "These Maruts are my true friends. They love me; therefore I shall give them a share too in the ukṣa mantra offered to me."

### Printed p. 389

In the Ṛksaṃhitā, in mantra 1.32-14, describing this same situation, he is praised with अहेर्यातारं (*aheryātāraṃ*). Here too the meaning is doubtful. It is stated here that Indra himself felt some fear at the time of Vṛtra's slaying. Two or three kinds of purport can be given, for example that from that fear he ran like a falcon, crossed the ninety-nine river-streams that he met on the way, and escaped. But that discussion is unnecessary at present. The matter of other gods who helped Indra is also praised in some places. For example:

"O Aśvins, lords of radiance, having drunk the sweet Soma together with Indra, you helped him when he was destroying the demon Namuci, and at that time you protected him." (10-13-4)

"O Indra, as parents protect their children, the two Aśvins protected Indra in a time of danger. When you drank Soma at the time of the display of your prowess, the goddess Sarasvatī stood at your side as helper with all her means of protection." (CO-C30-5)

**NOTE**

This episode is also told in the Vājasaneya Saṃhitā (10-33, 34). And in the Vājasaneya Saṃhitā Bhāṣya the commentator has cited a story told in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa. Its form is as follows:

इंद्रस्येंद्रियमन्नस्य रसग्ंसोमस्य भक्षग्ंसुरयासुरो नमुचिरहरत्योऽश्विनौ च सरस्वतीं चोपाधावछेपानोऽस्मि नमुचये न त्वा दिवा न नक्तग्ं हनानि न दण्णेन न धन्वना न पृथेन न मुष्टिना न शुष्केण नाद्रॆणार्थ म इदमहार्षिदिदं म आजिहीर्षथेति । (*iṃdrasyeṃdriyamannasya rasagṃsomasya bhakṣagṃsurayāsuro namuciraharatyo 'śvinau ca sarasvatīṃ copādhāvachepāno 'smi namucaye na tvā divā na naktagṃ hanāni na daṇṇena na dhanvanā na pṛthena na muṣṭinā na śuṣkeṇa nādrèṇārtha ma idamahārṣididaṃ ma ājihīrṣatheti |*) (Śa. Brā. 12-7-3-1)

Once the demon Namuci carried off Indra's valour, food, Soma and surā. Then Indra went to the Aśvins and to Sarasvatī and said: "I have given a promise that I shall not kill Namuci either by day or by night. Not only that, I have promised that I shall not kill him with wood, or with my hand, or with a fist, or with a dry instrument, or with a wet one. Because of this promise he has carried off my strength. Bring it back to me." They answered him as follows.

### Printed p. 390

अस्तु नोऽप्राप्यथाहरामेशि सह न एतदथाहरतेत्यब्रवीदिति । (*astu no 'prāpyathāharāmeśi saha na etadathāharatetyabravīditi |*)

They said it would do if we too were given a share in that valour and in the other Soma and the rest. Indra agreed to that.

तावश्विनी च सरस्वती च अपां फेनेन वज्रमसिंचन्न शुष्को नार्द्र इति तेनेंद्रो नमुचेरासुरस्य व्युष्टायाग्ं रात्रावनुदित आदित्ये न दिवा न नक्तमिति शिर उदवासयत् । (*tāvaśvinī ca sarasvatī ca apāṃ phenena vajramasiṃcanna śuṣko nārdra iti teneṃdro namucerāsurasya vyuṣṭāyāgṃ rātrāvanudita āditye na divā na naktamiti śira udavāsayat |*) (12-7-3-3)

Then the Aśvins and Sarasvatī smeared the thunderbolt with foam. Then it was neither wet nor dry. With it Indra struck Namuci. Since he struck at dawn, when the night had passed and the sun had not yet risen, it was neither day nor night. With it he cut off Namuci's head.

तस्मादेतदृषिणाभ्यनूक्तं . . . . . तस्य शीर्षंश्विन्ने लोहितमिश्रः सोमोऽतिष्ठत्तस्मादबीभत्संत त एतदंधसोर्निपानमपश्यन्सोमो राज्ञामृतग्ं सुत इति तेन्‌नग्ं स्वदयित्वात्मन्नदधत ॥ (*tasmādetadṛṣiṇābhyanūktaṃ . . . . . tasya śīrṣaṃśvinne lohitamiśraḥ somo 'tiṣṭhattasmādabībhatsaṃta ta etadaṃdhasornipānamapaśyansomo rājñāmṛtagṃ suta iti tennagṃ svadayitvātmannadadhata ‖*) (12-7-4)

As soon as Namuci's head was split, the Soma became mixed with blood. Then it became loathsome. Then they, thinking "Soma the king, as soon as it is poured, becomes immortal," poured that too with this Soma and drank it; so the description runs. But here, in this last part, which are the two Somas, "this Soma" and "that Soma", deserves examination. For the moment that is not relevant.

Likewise, in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, in yet another situation, when Indra's power was dulled, the Aśvins, the physicians of the gods, and Sarasvatī are said to have caused his valour to be re-established. (12-7-10; 12-8-3-1)

Just as Indra destroyed the power of the demons with the help of the Maruts, so with Bṛhaspati's help too Indra destroyed the enemies of the gods who opposed him. (8-85-12)

### Printed p. 391

Thus, delighted and stimulated by Soma-drinking, Indra goes to fight Vṛtra, sometimes accompanied by the Maruts and sometimes by Viṣṇu. (2-15-1; 2-19-2; 6-47-1, 2; 18-10-2)

With the help of these Maruts and of Viṣṇu he goes to fight the demons who block the waters from flowing in the atmosphere. (1-22-19; 1-85-7; 4-18-11; 6-20-2; 8-89-12; 7-99-4, 5)

The companionship of Indra and Viṣṇu is praised in many mantras. By such passages as आ यो विवाय सचथाय दैव्य इंद्राय विष्णुः सुकृते सुकृत्तरः (*ā yo vivāya sacathāya daivya iṃdrāya viṣṇuḥ sukṛte sukṛttaraḥ*) (1.156-5) the help given by Viṣṇu to Indra is made plain. (6-17-11; 8-12-27; 8-37-10; 10-13-2)

On the companionship of Indra and Viṣṇu the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa describes a situation in narrative form in the passages cited below.

वृत्रे ह वा इदमग्रे सर्वमास यदृचो यद्यजूग्ंषि यत्सामानि तस्मा इंद्रो वज्रं प्राजिहीर्षत् । (*vṛtre ha vā idamagre sarvamāsa yadṛco yadyajūgṃṣi yatsāmāni tasmā iṃdro vajraṃ prājihīrṣat |*) (Śa. Brā. 5-5-5-1)

In the beginning, Vṛtra, lord of the demons, had taken into himself all of the Ṛks, Yajus and Sāmans. With the aim of bringing them out and making them shine for the world, Indra tried to hurl the thunderbolt at that Vṛtra:

स ह विष्णुमुवाच । वृत्ताय वै वज्रं प्रहरिष्याम्यनुमा तिष्ठस्वेति तथेति ह विष्णुरुवाचानु त्वा स्वास्ये प्रहरेति तस्मा इंद्रो वज्रमुद्ययाम स उद्यताद्वज्राद्वृत्रो बिभयां चकार ॥ (*sa ha viṣṇumuvāca | vṛttāya vai vajraṃ prahariṣyāmyanumā tiṣṭhasveti tatheti ha viṣṇuruvācānu tvā svāsye prahareti tasmā iṃdro vajramudyayāma sa udyatādvajrādvṛtro bibhayāṃ cakāra ‖*) (5-5-5-2)

Then Indra said to Viṣṇu: "I intend to hurl the thunderbolt at Vṛtra in order to gather the Ṛks and the rest. You too help in this." Then Viṣṇu said: "So be it. I shall help in this work. Strike Vṛtra with the thunderbolt." On that assurance, when Indra hurled the thunderbolt at Vṛtra, Vṛtra was frightened. And he said to Indra as follows.

### Printed p. 392

Then Indra said to Viṣṇu, "I intend to hurl the vajra at Vṛtra in order to gather the Ṛk and the other Vedas. You too help in this." Viṣṇu said, "So be it. I shall help in this task. Strike Vṛtra with the vajra." On that assurance Indra hurled the vajra at Vṛtra, and Vṛtra was frightened. He told Indra as follows:

स होवाच । अस्ति वा इदं वीर्यं तन्नु ते प्रयच्छानि मा तु मे प्रहार्षीरिति तस्मै यजूग्ंषि प्रायच्छत्तस्मै द्वितीयमुद्ययाम ॥ (*sa hovāca | asti vā idaṃ vīryaṃ tannu te prayacchāni mā tu me prahārṣīriti tasmai yajūgṃṣi prāyacchattasmai dvitīyamudyayāma ‖*) (5-5-5-3)

"This power is lodged in me. I shall give it to you. Do not strike me." So saying, he handed the Yajus over to Indra. Indra, not content with that, and wishing to snatch away what remained, raised the vajra over him to strike a second time.

स होवाच । अस्ति वा इदं वीर्यं तन्नु ते प्रयच्छानि मा तु मे प्रहार्षीरिति तस्मा ऋचः प्रायच्छत्तस्यै तृतीयमुद्ययाम ॥ (*sa hovāca | asti vā idaṃ vīryaṃ tannu te prayacchāni mā tu me prahārṣīriti tasmā ṛcaḥ prāyacchattasyai tṛtīyamudyayāma ‖*) (5-21-5-4)

"I have power in yet another form. That too I shall give you. Do not strike me." So saying, he handed all the Ṛks over to Indra. Indra, not content even with that, and wishing to seize what remained, raised the vajra over him to strike a third time.

स होवाच । अस्ति पा इदं वीर्यं तन्नु ते प्रयच्छानि मा तु मे प्रहार्षीरिति तस्मै सामानि प्रायच्छत् तस्मादप्येतर्ह्येव मेवैतैर्वेदैर्यज्ञं तन्नते यजुर्भिरेवाग्रेऽथर्भि रथ सामभिरेवग्ग्यस्मा एतत्पायच्छत् ॥ (*sa hovāca | asti pā idaṃ vīryaṃ tannu te prayacchāni mā tu me prahārṣīriti tasmai sāmāni prāyacchat tasmādapyetarhyeva mevaitairvedairyajñaṃ tannate yajurbhirevāgre 'tharbhi ratha sāmabhirevaggyasmā etatpāyacchat ‖*) (Śa. Brā. 5-21.5-5)

"O Indra, in me there is yet another kind of instrument of strength. That too I offer you. Please do not strike me." So saying, he offered the Sāmans also to Indra.

इंद्रो हि वज्रमुद्यच्छद्विष्णुरस्वतिष्ठत । (*iṃdro hi vajramudyacchadviṣṇurasvatiṣṭhata |*) (5-5-5-2)

Even so, when Indra raised the vajra and tried to strike, Viṣṇu too stood by him, it is said.

The same kind of story is told in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā. But there it is stated that, in return for the powers in the form of Ṛk, Yajus and Sāman, Vṛtra gave Indra three kinds of Uktha, one each time; and since Viṣṇu too helped Indra, Viṣṇu also has a share in it. (Tai. Saṃ. 6-5-1-1) In Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-109-5, 7, 8; 3-12-4, 6; 10-65-2 and similar places it is stated that Agni, the destroyer of Vṛtra, who is of dense form, killed Vṛtra together with Indra.

### Printed p. 393

"O Indra and Agni, I have heard that at the time of distributing wealth to all the worshippers you two, standing face to face, proved supremely capable in the work of destroying the asura Vṛtra." (1-109-5)

Epithets such as "vajra-armed" and "fort-destroyer" are common to both. In one or two contexts it is stated that Varuṇa too helped Indra.

"O Indra and Varuṇa, against this Vṛtra of unequalled power, you two together hurled the shining and mighty vajra." (4-41.4)

These asuras, the causes of famines, are known by many names: Vṛtra, Ahi, Śuṣṇa, Namuci, Pipu, Śambara, Uraṇa and others. (1-121-9, 10; 2-14.4; 8.32-2, 3)

If we take as examples some passages that speak of them and describe their destruction and the like, their deformed nature becomes known. In some places all their names are mentioned together. All of them are Dānavas; Danu is their mother. It is stated that she too sometimes takes part in the fight to protect her sons. For example:

"At the time of the slaying of the asura Vṛtra, his mother came to protect her son from the blow of the vajra. Then Indra weakened her strength and struck her hard on the lower part of her body. After she was struck with the vajra, the mother came to lie on top. The son was caught beneath and lay there. As a cow lies with her calf, the Dānavī, the mother, lay dead together with her son Vṛtra." (1-3-9)

तद्वै एष एव इंद्रो य एष तपति । अथ एष एव वृत्रो यच्चंद्रमाः ॥ (*tadvai eṣa eva iṃdro ya eṣa tapati | atha eṣa eva vṛtro yaccaṃdramāḥ ‖*) (Śa. Brā. 1-6-4-18)

The one who shines in the sky is the Sun. The Moon is the asura Vṛtra, as is stated in the passage of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa. It is stated in the Ṛk Saṃhitā too that Indra himself is of the form of the Sun. All these asuras take up their various weapons and make ready for battle. (1-3-2)

But their attempt to resist the gods proves merely a delusion. Vṛtra, covered in the form of a cloud, resisted Indra; that attempt came to nothing and he was defeated by Indra,

### Printed p. 394

and this is clearly stated. (2-30-3) When Indra roars, even heaven and earth tremble with fear. (1-80-11, 14; 2-11-9, 10; 4.17-9)

Though Tvaṣṭā is the maker of the vajra, and though he created it for Indra himself, yet when Indra, bearing the vajra, faces his enemies, roars and shows his wrath, the same Tvaṣṭā too is afraid. (त्वष्टा चित्तव मान्यव इंद्र विविज्यते भिया (*tvaṣṭā cittava mānyava iṃdra vivijyate bhiyā*)) (1.80-14)

As soon as this steel weapon of Indra is hurled, it pierces the vital parts of the enemies and scatters them all completely. (1-32.5; 1.57.6; 1-60.80; 2-19-3; 10-89.7; 6-27.4; 8.6-13)

As soon as Indra by his prowess releases the waters held back by the asuras, they, filled with abundant water in the form of floods, descend from the atmosphere to the earth, fill all the rivers, flow on and join the ocean. (1-32.5; 1-32-1; 1, 57.6; 1-61-10 **NOTE**; 1-103-2; 2.11-2; 2-12-1; 2.14.2; 2-15.3; 2.19-3; 3-32.6; 4.17-1; 5-32-1; 6-30-4; 8.65.3; 10-135.2)

As soon as Indra shows his prowess and resolves, all the clouds in the atmosphere scatter and the darkness is destroyed. The Sun too, regaining his natural state, spreads everywhere the radiance that gives light to the whole world. (1-32-4; 1-51.4; 1-51.8; 2-19-3)

Regarding the matter described in mantra 1-51-4, Sāyaṇa gives his opinion as follows. The original is:

वृत्रं यदिंद्र शवसावधीरहिमादित्सूर्यं दिव्यारोहयो दृशे । (*vṛtraṃ yadiṃdra śavasāvadhīrahimāditsūryaṃ divyārohayo dṛśe |*)

Explaining its purport, Sāyaṇa says:

वृत्रेणावृतं सूर्यं तस्माद्वृत्तात् अमूमुच इत्यर्थः ॥ (*vṛtreṇāvṛtaṃ sūryaṃ tasmādvṛttāt amūmuca ityarthaḥ ‖*)

that is, the purport is that Indra caused the Sun, enveloped by Vṛtra, to be freed. But if the original sentence is examined, it gives the meaning that after slaying Vṛtra he established the Sun in the atmosphere. On the whole, its purport is that Indra became the cause of the destruction of darkness.

### Printed p. 395

Such a battle with Vṛtra, who is of the nature of darkness, is described in many places in the Ṛk Saṃhitā. The aim of the battle is to destroy the darkness and spread light. (1-4.8; 1.32.1; 1-52.2; 1-54.4; 1-80-1; 1-103-2; 2-11.5; 5-32.1; 1.89-7; 10.103-6)

And this description is poetic, full of various metaphors. Because clouds take most wondrous shapes, they are described in many ways: sometimes as mountains, at other times as strongholds of the asuras, and as dense cities of the asuras. (2-14-6; 8-17-14; 8-87-6)

These masses of clouds, which move and obstruct the light, are described as made of ayas (steel) and as made of stone. It is also stated that these are the cities of the asuras, and that Indra destroyed these very cities, which give shelter to the asuras of the atmosphere, by hurling the vajra. (1-51-5; 1-63-7: 1-103 3; 1-130-7; 1-174-8; 2-19-6; 2-20-7; 3-12-6; 4-20-3; 4-30-13; 8-82-2; 10-89-7)

Indra picks out all the asuras sleeping in the mountains of the atmosphere, beats them down, and rolls them all down from the atmosphere. (1-32-2; 1-130-7; 2-12-11; 4-30-14; 6-26-5)

And when they wish to occupy the whole atmosphere, he drives them all back. (2-12-12; 8-14-14)

One of those asuras he treads down under his foot, and he torments with frost. (1-5-6; 8-32-26)

He strikes the head of Namuci with the foam of water. (8-14-13)

(8-14-13)

Of the asuras who are Indra's enemies, one named Uraṇa has ninety-nine arms and is a monster; his deformed form is described. Another is said to have had three heads and six eyes. (2-14-4) (10-99-6)

Such forms and imaginative descriptions are also fitting for natural events. It is natural that people scorched by the burning heat of the summer season look for rain as soon as summer ends. But there are also many occasions when dense clouds spread over the whole atmosphere and yet do not pour rain.

### Printed p. 396

On such occasions it is natural that the belief arises that some asuric power is obstructing the rain. It is likewise natural that a kind of faith arises in the divine power that destroys this asuric power. The appearance of thunder and lightning is described as the clash, in the atmosphere, of two powers, the divine and the asuric.

Indra is the presiding deity who reflects this divine power. This power of Indra, beneficent to devotees and destroyer of enemies, supplies wealth to the sacrificer and others and spares them the affliction of the asuras. The masses of clouds moving in the atmosphere are described as chariots, as chariot-horses, and as Indra's conveyances.

This Indra is understood to be a deity of a nature different from Parjanya. Since there are passages that compare Indra and Parjanya, there is full scope to say that they are separate deities of distinct nature. Many hymns addressed to Parjanya too show that he is a deity distinct from Indra. (8-6-1)

But there are also many passages that state the identity of Indra and the Sun.

Description of Indra's greatness

It may be said that, throughout the Ṛk Saṃhitā, the epithets showing the highest position among the gods are applied to Indra most of all. They also show Indra's universal lordship. Only some of them are selected here, and their purport is given.

In the first maṇḍala:

Indra has established the Sun in the atmosphere so that he can be seen even from very far. (1-2-3)

O Indra, you bear in your arms the vajra made of steel, and you have established the Sun in the atmosphere. (8.25.8)

Dwelling on the farther shore of the atmosphere, displaying your divine power, and standing here on this earth too for the benefit of us humans, you have pervaded the heavenly world also through the ocean of the atmosphere, and spread your influence in all three worlds. (Printed reference unclear: "C.-53-12")

### Printed p. 397

O Indra, you are the representative of this earth. You are the lord of the atmosphere. And by your greatness you have pervaded the whole heavenly world. Among gods, men and the rest there is no one at all with greatness equal to yours. (1-52-13)

Neither the earth nor the heavenly world has reached your superiority. The ocean of the atmosphere too has not reached your extent. In all three worlds, everything is firmly established in its fixed place by you. (1-52-14; 1-55-1; 1-60-9)

As soon as Indra was born, the immovable mountain and heaven and earth trembled, fearing to appear before him. (1-61-14)

"Indra has pervaded the whole earth. In the atmosphere he has established all the orbs of light. O Indra, none of divine qualities like yours has been born till now, nor will be born hereafter. You stand beyond the whole universe." (1-81.5)

This same Indra is the sovereign of heaven and earth. Neither gods, nor men, nor Yakṣas and Gandharvas, nor the deities have attained the greatness of this Indra, nor can they attain it. (Printed reference unclear: "C-C00-C") (1-100-1)

Indra is the master of the whole world, whatever world there is, made of the immovable and the moving, and endowed with life. (1-101.5)

O Indra, the three worlds and the masses of light of the three worlds are your representatives. Standing beyond the three worlds, you, free of enemies, the lord of the universe, have made your sovereignty shine everywhere. (1-802-8)

Indra established the earth and spread it out. He struck with his vajra and made the water flow. He slew Ahi (Vṛtra). (Printed reference unclear: "C-C.03.9")

Indra is a support for the atmosphere like a prop. And for four-footed animals and for two-footed men and the rest he has held the atmosphere and kept it from falling down. (1-12-2)

**The nature of the favour Indra shows to his devotees**
There are many sentences showing the direct relation between Indra and his devotees. Some sentences also describe Indra's moral character. Of the many sentences showing faith in Indra, the purport of some is now given.
When Indra, at the time of destroying enemies, whirls his thunderbolt again and again, all people, fearing his terrible form, place faith in him.
(1-55-5)
O Indra, the sun and the moon (under your control) carry on their revolving work in alternation. All who behold such a world-order show devotion and faith in you because you have such extraordinary power. (1-102-2)

(1-104-6)

(1-104-6)

(1-108.6)

It is Indra's nature to determine our future and to act independently of his own accord. Seers afflicted with distress have in many places voiced their lament that in such descriptions of independence there are situations that take away even human freedom.

No one but Indra knows Indra's wondrous power. Of his own will he first sets one work going and afterwards makes another go; and it is he who shows the distinctions of earlier and later. Indra acts as he pleases. He may leave the present sacrificer and go to another and join him there. Even when the former sacrificer's rites are excellent, he sometimes leaves them and desires the rites of another sacrificer that are deficient. No one can obstruct his independence. But the occasions when he stays near those who worship him are the more frequent. (6 47 12)

In the passage quoted above, that is, in stating the purport of verse 6-47-16, one point calls for some discussion. In verse 16 विधमानद्विट् (*vidhamānadviṭ*) is an epithet of Indra and tells his nature. The word विधमान (*vidhamāna*) means "prospering," that is, endowed with wealth and the like and with mental comforts. But is Indra one who fosters enmity with those who are rich? Is there no distinction of friend and foe in him? Such a question arises naturally. Therefore on this occasion Sāyaṇa has explained him as the enemy of असुन्वतां विधमानानां (*asunvatāṃ vidhamānānāṃ*), the selfish who have grown in wealth and yet do not offer oblations in sacrificial rites

### Printed p. 415
and the like. Thus: विधमानद्विट् (*vidhamānadviṭ*) is something that generally applies to all the gods. It becomes clear from this that the gods cannot tolerate the advancement of men. The sense of the next verse supports the same view. The scholar Wilson says as follows:

"He is also represented in the same hymn as of a capricious temperament, neglecting those who serve him, and favouring those who pay him no adoration; a notion somewhat at variance with a doctrine, previously inculcated that the ceremonial worship of Indra is able to atone for the most atrocious crimes."

(Quoted by Muir. Original Sanskrit Text. Vol. V. p. 111).

The purport of these sentences is as follows. One might say that the meaning given by the English commentators for विधमानिद्विट् (*vidhamānidviṭ*) is natural. For immediately after this verse, the next verse says: "Indra acts as he pleases; Indra is ready to leave the sacrificer who offers oblations and go to the one who does not." This statement supports the purport above. In the verses whose purport is that even the gravest sins are destroyed if an oblation is offered to Indra in the sacrifice (5-34-4), what is described is wholly contrary to what is said in the present verses. This is the opinion of the same scholar Wilson. For this contradiction to disappear, as Sāyaṇa and the Nirukta authors say, विधमानानां वर्धमानानां असुन्वतां द्विट् (*vidhamānānāṃ vardhamānānāṃ asunvatāṃ dviṭ*) must be taken to mean "enemy of all who are prospering without offering oblations." That suits the context.

Some apparent inconsistencies in the description of Indra's nature, to the gross view, and their resolution.
For those who have no acquaintance with the Ṛk-saṃhitā, whether through study of the original or through translation, it is natural that some contradictory points should appear in the description of Indra's nature given above. Examined only from the gross point of view, there is no doubt that inconsistency appears in the above accounts. The description of Indra as the supreme deity who governs and supports the universe is contrary to the other, ordinary descriptions of qualities. For example—
In Soma-drinking and in other dealings too, Indra is described as having the desires and so on of ordinary men. Sometimes even sensual desire seems intense. Such a description does not fit with the great qualities of Indra, which are extraordinary, supramundane, guiding the whole universe, and spiritual. There are also contexts in which such contrary descriptions occur in a single sūkta. But if one examines the matter from the spiritual point of view, it becomes clear that such a nature is only natural. How? All elements of the universe may be seen to have two kinds of nature: one eternal, the other non-eternal; one sensory, the other spiritual; one ordinary, the other extraordinary; thus this duality is plainly present in every human being. There is no inconsistency in the ordinary qualities natural to the universe and the extraordinary, supramundane, divine qualities, because he transcends the universe, being found together. Even if one supposes that qualities like desire show a terrestrial nature in Indra, it is established that this is not a description of sensual desire in the modern cultural sense. The desire for the Soma juice, the means of immortality, in Soma-drinking and the like through which Indra procures nectar, is itself a supramundane, divine desire; it is certain that it is no fault. Since these contrary qualities are described by one and the same seer, it is not right to say that such a seer's utterance is inconsistent. Some such contexts may be examined. For example—
"Indra established the heaven in the empty region. He pervaded and stood throughout heaven and earth. He upheld the earth and made it spread out widely. All these extraordinary deeds Indra did by the power of drinking the Soma juice."
(2-15-2)

### Printed p. 420
O Indra, of most wonderful prowess, producer of the atmosphere, maker of the earth, drink the Soma that gives you supreme delight.
(8-36-4)
As explained before, in all the Ṛks such as 8-78-5, Indra's drinking of Soma juice, the vigour arising from it, and the supramundane deeds that Indra performs as the fruit of that vigour are well known.
"By this Soma-drinking, which produces most intense and excellent delight, Indra's vigour grew, and by its power Indra conquered all the worlds and became the lord who governs the whole universe." (8-92-6)
From such passages it cannot be said that Indra's desire to drink Soma is sensual desire, nor that the vigour born of it is merely worldly vigour, nor that such descriptions state anything contrary to Indra's divine qualities. Even when examined from the spiritual point of view, there is no doubt that these descriptions describe Indra's divine qualities.
Some passages describing the mutual relationship of Indra and Varuṇa
In the early maṇḍalas of the Ṛk-saṃhitā the sūktas addressed to Indra are more numerous; in the last maṇḍalas the sūktas addressed to Varuṇa are in greater number. For this reason some English scholars have held that in the early period of the composition of the Ṛk-saṃhitā Indra had greater prominence than Varuṇa, and that in the last period Varuṇa was shown greater reverence than Indra. This opinion has no proper basis, and it may be called a wrong opinion. The Saṃhitā's own sentences state, and it has been explained before and will be stated again, that all the practical differences such as Indra and Varuṇa are different special manifestations of one principle, and that these names are not divisions of deities with differences of principle. (इंद्रं मित्रं वरुणमग्निमाहुः (*iṃdraṃ mitraṃ varuṇamagnimāhuḥ*)) Even so, to establish that there is no room for such a difference even in describing the special manifestations of the one principle, some contexts in which these two deities are described, together or individually, may be examined.
In sūktas such as 1-17, 4-41, 4-42, 6-68, 7-82, 7-83, 7-84, 7-85, equal reverence is shown to both Indra and Varuṇa. At the very beginning Indra and Varuṇa are both designated as sovereigns who support the whole world.
इंद्रावरुणयोरहं सम्राजोरव आ वृणॆः । ता नो मृळात ईवृतॆ (*iṃdrāvaruṇayorahaṃ samrājorava ā vṛṇèḥ | tā no mṛḷāta īvṛtè*)
(1-2-1)

### Printed p. 421

(1-17-2)

But in many contexts this power applies to Indra alone. In 7-82-2 Varuṇa is praised with the epithet samrāṭ and Indra with the epithet svarāṭ. (सम्राळन्य: स्वराळन्य उच्यते (*samrāḷanya: svarāḷanya ucyate*)).
(See mantras such as 3-46-1; 1-61-9)
In this same sūkta and in other sūktas too, the individual acts and qualities of Indra and Varuṇa are described separately.
O Indra and Varuṇa, when you created all the creatures of the world and manifested your power, Mitra shone in a tranquil manner with Varuṇa, and the terrible Indra with the Maruts.
(7-82-5)
Varuṇa conquers the destructive enemy. Indra, with the help of the Maruts alone, drives numerous enemies far away.
(7-82-6)
Indra shows his delight in destroying enemies in battle. Varuṇa's duty is to keep the law, being Dhṛtavrata.
(7-83-9)
May Varuṇa's wrath not harm us but remain far from us. May Indra provide us wide room.
(7-84-2)
The one, Varuṇa, bears many kinds of vital powers. The other, Indra, utterly destroys endless enemy armies.
(2-85-3) **NOTE**

### Printed p. 422

All of the above are descriptions of the personal deeds of these gods. Next, some of the descriptions of their well-coordinated, mutually helpful major undertakings may be examined.
(7-85-3)
O Indra and Varuṇa, you both, by your power, removed the obstruction that held back the waters and made them fit to flow. You made the Sun, the illuminator of the world, lord of the atmosphere. As the fruit of the joy born of drinking Soma, you made all the banks of the river fertile. Be gracious and make the purpose of our sacrificial rite fruitful.
(7-82-3)
O Indra and Varuṇa, by your great power you have created all the beings of the world.
(7-82-5)
All the other gods too fill Indra and Varuṇa, who dwell in the loftiest region of the atmosphere, with water and brilliance. (7-82-2)
In the same way, in some other mantras Indra and Viṣṇu are praised together.
Indra and Viṣṇu, the unobstructed and great ones, stand in splendour on the lofty region of the clouds that are like mountain peaks, as if mounting tamed horses and climbing to high places. To Indra and Viṣṇu, the mighty and heroic, offer your nourishing food in the form of Soma.
(7-1552-0)**NOTE**
O Indra and Viṣṇu, through Agni the bestower of desired things, you always supply to the human sacrificer the food and other things to be received as the fruit of sacrifice. The sacrificer worships the radiant and united coming of you two, who thus perform acts such as granting desires.
(1-25-2)
For the sake of giving living beings the power of procreation and the capacity to enjoy pleasures, he distributes to heaven and earth great manly power. By the grace of Viṣṇu, every man obtains this power, established in the orb of the intensely shining Āditya, in the form named sons, grandsons and so on.
(C-2538-2 : C.77-5)**NOTE**
The companionship of Indra and Agni too is praised in many places. (1-25 : 1-27), for example—

### Printed p. 423

O Indra and Agni, you have made your auspicious name famous as always joint and united; and as slayers of Vṛtra you were united even at the time of the slaying of Vṛtra. Therefore, O Indra and Agni, bestowers of desires, come together, sit on the sacrificial altar and drink the flowing Soma juice of your share.
(1-108-3)
O Indra and Agni, who hold the thunderbolt in your hand, bring wealth for us and give it to us. Protect us, who perform the sacrifice, by your heroic deeds. By those same rays of Indra in the form of the Sun, by which our fathers, grandfathers and others together reached the world of Brahmā, may these very rays, visible to our eyes, favour us too.
(1-109-7 ; 3-12 ; 55-86 ; 6-59)
In the same way, joint descriptions and praises such as Indra–Vāyu, Indra–Pūṣan and Indra–Soma are very numerous.
(4-46 to 8) Indra–Vāyu; (6-57) Indra–Pūṣan; (6-72; 7-104) Indra–Soma.
What is described in the mantras that use the word असिंद्र (*asiṃdra*) deserves notice. This word is used in many contexts.
(1-133-1 ; 4-23-6 ; 5.2-3 ; 7.18-16 ; 10-27-6 ; 10-48-7)
अनिंद्र (*aniṃdra*) means one who is not a worshipper of Indra. By this word may be meant either non-Āryas who did not worship Indra and the other gods, or the demonic powers hostile to Indra.
In the twelfth sūkta of the second maṇḍala the description of Indra's great qualities is most excellent. Only some of it may be examined here. They describe Indra's power of governing the universe.
The extremely wise Indra, as soon as he was born, surpassed by his great power all the other gods. O men, know that he is Indra, at whose power and might heaven and earth trembled. (2-12-1)
O men, know that he is Indra who made the trembling earth stand firm, who made the agitated mountains immovable, who created the very wide atmosphere and who supports the heavenly world. (2-12-2)
"I, the divine self, have obtained extremely mighty power, an unconquerable state and unobstructed valour only with the help of Ādityas and other gods.

### Printed p. 424

Therefore I shall not cause any harm to the excellent states of the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the adopted-son Maruts." These words of Indra (10.48-11) show the occasion on which Indra expresses his gratitude towards the other gods.
We conclude this section by stating the purport of some of the laudatory statements that Indra alone accomplished extraordinary deeds impossible for other gods.
Indra alone, who surpasses men and does not seek the help of others, possesses power greater than all living beings, and also power that no one can conquer.
(8-6-2)
All the other gods too praise Indra's excellent valour and prowess and thereby show their humility.
(8-63-7)
May our praise addressed to Indra be truthful, with no untruth in it of any kind. Extremely severe calamity befalls one who does not offer Soma juice to Indra; but the devotee who worships Indra with an offering of Soma obtains abundant wealth together with great light.
(8-6-2)
There is no god equal to Indra. Therefore there is no possibility of any god having qualities surpassing his.
(4-30-1)
This Indra alone conquered all the gods in battle; and even the most ancient gods, recognizing Indra's might, showed their humility before him and accepted his lordship. (7-21-7)
All the other gods, Varuṇa, Sūrya and the rest, bow to the ordinance laid down by Indra and perform their duties.
(1-101-3)
