#### Ṛk 3

##### ॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)

> म॒मत्तु॑ त्वा दि॒व्यः सोम॑ इंद्र म॒मत्तु॒ यः सू॒यते॒  ॑
> पार्थि॑वेषु ।  
> म॒मत्तु॒ येन॒ वरि॑वश्च॒कर्थ॑ म॒मत्तु॒ येन॑ निरि॒णासि॒ शत्रू॑न् ॥३॥

##### ॥ पदपाठः ॥ (Pada-pāṭha)

> ममत्तु । त्वा । दिव्यः । सोमः । इंद्र । ममत्तु । यः । सूयते । पार्थिवेषु ।  
> ममत्तु । येन । वरिवः । चकर्थ । ममत्तु । येन । निरिणासि । शत्रून् ॥ ३ ॥

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> हे इंद्र त्वा त्वां दिव्यो दिवि भवः सोमो ममत्तु । आत्मीयकलाप्रदानेन
> मादयतु । देवा ह्यपरपक्षे सोमस्य कलां पिबंति ॥ मदेर्लोटि व्यत्ययेन
> श्लुः । भीह्रीत्यादिना । पा.६-१-१९२ । पितः पूर्वस्योदात्तत्वं ॥ तथा पार्थिवेषु
> पृथिव्यां भवेषु देवयजनेषु यः सोमोऽस्माभिः सूयते अभिषूयते सो-
> sप्यस्माभिर्दत्तो ममत्तु । त्वां हर्षयतु । येन सोमेन वरिवो वरणेयं
> धनं चकर्थ कृतवानसि स च ममत्तु ॥ करोतेर्लिट् । यद्योगादनिघाते लित्स्वरः ॥
> किंच येन शत्रून्निरिणासि निर्गमयसि । सोऽपि ममत्तु । त्वां मादयतु ॥ रिणासि ।
> री गतिरेषणयोः क्रादिः । प्वादीनां ह्रस्वत्वं ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

O Indra, may the heavenly Soma delight you by giving its own digit (the gods drink a digit of Soma in the dark fortnight). Likewise the Soma that is pressed by us in the earthly places of divine worship, being offered by us, may it delight you. The Soma by which you have made वरिवः (*varivaḥ*), choice wealth, may it also delight you. And the Soma by which you drive out the enemies, may it too delight you.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- इंद्र (*iṃdra*)—O Indra
- त्वा (*tvā*)—you
- दिव्यः (*divyaḥ*)—that is in the heavenly world
- सोमः (*somaḥ*)—Soma
- ममत्तु (*mamattu*)—may it gladden (and)
- पार्थिवेषु (*pārthiveṣu*)—in the sacrifices performed on earth
- यः (*yaḥ*)—the Soma juice that
- सूयते (*sūyate*)—is pressed and offered by us
- ममत्तु (*mamattu*)—may it make you delighted
- येन (*yena*)—by drinking which Soma
- वरिवः (*varivaḥ*)—the desired wealth
- चकर्थ (*cakartha*)—you provide, may that Soma
- ममत्तु (*mamattu*)—gladden you
- येन (*yena*)—by which Soma, being invigorated, you
- शत्रून् (*śatrūn*)—the enemies
- निरिणासि (*niriṇāsi*)—destroy, such Soma juice
- ममत्तु (*mamattu*)—may it gladden you

### Printed p. 530

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

O Indra, may the Soma that is in the world of heaven gladden you. May the Soma that we press and prepare at the many sacrifices spread out on the earth also bring you joy. May that Soma-juice gladden you, delighted by which you provide us the wealth we desire; and may that Soma-juice gladden you, by which, filled with zeal, you destroy enemies.

##### English translation
May the celestial Soma exhilarate you, Indra; may that which is effused at terrestrial rites exhilaratingate you; may that exhilaratingate you through the influence of which you have bestowed wealth; may that exhilaratingate you whereby you scatter foes.

#### Ṛk 4

##### ॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)

> आ द्वि॒बर्हा॑ अमि॒नो या॒त्विंद्रो॒ वृषा॒ हरि॑भ्यां॒ परि॑षिक्त॒मंधः॑।  
> गव्या सु॒तस्य॒ प्रभृ॑तस्य॒ मध्वः॑ स॒त्रा खेदा॑मरुश॒हा वृ॑षस्व ॥ ४ ॥

##### ॥ पदपाठः ॥ (Pada-pāṭha)

> आ । द्विबर्हाः । अमिनः । यातु । इंद्रः । वृषा । हरिभ्यां । परिसिक्तं । अंधः ।  
> गवि । आ । सुतस्य । प्रभृतस्य । मध्वः । सत्रा । खेदां । अरुशहा । आ । वृषस्व ॥ ४ ॥

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> द्विबर्हा द्वयोर्लोकयोः परिवृढः । यद्वा । द्वाभ्यां स्तुतशस्त्राभ्यां वर्धनीयः ॥ वृहेर्वर्धनार्थस्य कर्तरि कर्मणि वासुन् ॥ अमिनः । अमतेर्गत्यर्थादौ.
> णादिक इनच् । सर्वत्र गंता । यद्वा । कांत्यर्थात् । सर्वैः काम्यमानः । आत एव
> वृषाभिलषितानां वर्षक इंद्रः परिषिक्तं वसतीवरीभिः परितः सिक्तमंधोऽस्मदीयं
> सोमलक्षणमन्नं प्रति हरिभ्यामेतन्नामकाभ्यामश्वाभ्यां सहा यातु । आगच्छतु ।
> अथ प्रत्यक्षः । हे इंद्र अरुशहा । अरुशाः शत्रवः । तेषां हंता ॥ आर्तॆरौणादिक

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

द्विबर्हा (*dvibarhā*) means "overpowering in the two worlds"; or "to be magnified by the two, the praise (stotra) and the recitation (śastra)." अमिनः (*aminaḥ*) means "going everywhere"; or, from the sense of desire, "desired by all." Hence Indra, the showerer who rains what is wished for, is to come with his two horses of that name (the Haris) to our Soma-food, the अंधः (*aṃdhaḥ*), sprinkled all round with the Vasatīvarī waters. Then, addressing him directly: O Indra, अरुशहा (*aruśahā*), "slayer of the अरुशाः (*aruśāḥ*), the enemies."

### Printed p. 531

> उशन् । बहुलं छंदसीति हंतेः क्विप् ॥ सत्रा । सप्तम्याः डादेशः । अस्मदीये
> सत्रे यज्ञे गव्यानडुहे चर्मणि सुतस्याभिषुतस्य प्रभृतस्य पात्रेषु प्रहृतस्य ॥
> हृग्रहोर्भः ॥ ईदृशस्य मध्यो मदकरस्य सोमस्य पानेन हृष्टः सन् खेदां
> खिद्यमानानां शत्रुणामुत्पित्तय अभिमुख्येन वृषस्व । वृष इवाचर ॥ वृषशब्दादाचारार्थे क्विप् । व्यत्ययेनात्मनेपदं । खेदां । खिद दैन्ये । कर्मणि घइंतस्यामि
> नुडागमाभावश्चांदसः ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

सत्रा (*satrā*) is a locative with the ending ḍā: at our sacrificial session (sattra), on the cow-hide (गव्यानडुहे चर्मणि (*gavyānaḍuhe carmaṇi*)), the Soma that has been pressed and drawn into the vessels. Gladdened by drinking such sweet, intoxicating Soma, वृषस्व (*vṛṣasva*), act like a bull, charging head-on to bring about the ruin of the distressed enemies. खेदां (*khedāṃ*) is from the root खिद (*khida*) in the sense of distress.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- द्विबर्हाः (*dvibarhāḥ*)—one who grows in both worlds, or who grows through the two kinds of praise and recitation mantras
- अमिनः (*aminaḥ*)—one who moves everywhere, or who is prayed to by all
- वृषा (*vṛṣā*)—the granter of desired ends
- इंद्रः (*iṃdraḥ*)—Indra
- परिषिक्तं (*pariṣiktaṃ*)—mixed with the Vasatīvarī water
- अंधः (*aṃdhaḥ*)—the food in the form of Soma, aiming at it
- हरिभ्यां (*haribhyāṃ*)—together with his two horses called Hari
- आ यातु (*ā yātu*)—may he come to our sacrificial ground (O Indra)
- अरुशहा (*aruśahā*)—you, slayer of enemies
- सत्रा (*satrā*)—at this sacrifice that we are performing
- गवि (*gavi*)—upon the cow-hide
- सुतस्य (*sutasya*)—which has been pounded and pressed with the plants laid down
- प्रभृतस्य (*prabhṛtasya*)—which has been filled into the vessels
- मध्वः (*madhvaḥ*)—by drinking the tasty Soma-juice
- खेदां (*khedāṃ*)—for the destruction of the enemies afflicted, that is, seized by anxiety
- वृषस्व (*vṛṣasva*)—act like a bull, that is, rush forward against them

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

Indra, who grows in both worlds, or who is praised with the two kinds of mantras, stotra and śastra, who moves everywhere and grants desired ends, may he graciously come to our sacrificial ground with his two horses, the Haris, to drink the Soma mixed with the Vasatīvarī water. O Indra, slayer of enemies, gladdened by drinking the tasty Soma-juice, pounded and pressed with the plants laid on the cow-hide and filled into the vessels, rush upon the enemies, overcome by distress, as a bull charges.

##### English translation
May Indra, who deserves the twofold adoration, (of praise and prayer), who goes everywhere, the showerer benefits, come to the offered sacrificial food with his two bay horses; O slayer of enemies, (exhilarated) at our sacrifice (by drinking) of the Soma-juice effuse upon the cow-hide and poured (into the cups), rush like a bull upon the dispirited (foe).

### Printed p. 532
#### Ṛk 5

##### ॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)

> नि ति॒ग्मानि॑ भ्रा॒शय॒न्फाश्या॒न्यव॑ स्थि॒रा त॑नुहि यातु॒जूनां॑ ।  
> उ॒ग्राय॑ ते॒ सहो॒ बलं॑ ददामि प्र॒तीत्या॒ शत्रू॑न्विग॒देषु॑  
> वृश्च ॥ ५ ॥

##### ॥ पदपाठः ॥ (Pada-pāṭha)

> नि । तिग्मानि । भ्राशयन् । भ्राश्यानि । अव । स्थिरा । तनुहि । यातुजूनां ।  
> उग्राय । ते । सहः । बलं । ददामि । प्रतिइत्य । शत्रुन् । विगदेषु । वृश्च ॥ ५ ॥

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> हे इंद्र भ्राश्यानि प्रकाश्यानि तिग्मानि तीक्ष्णान्यायुधानि नितरां भ्राशयन्
> प्रकाशयन् ॥ भ्रातृ दीप्तौ ॥ स त्वं यातुजूनां ॥ जु इति सौत्रो धातुः । भ्राजभासेत्यत्र जवतेर्दिीर्घः । का- ३-२-१७७-१ । क्विष्टेति क्विप् । दीर्घस्यामि नुडागमश्चांदसः ॥ यातुधानानां स्थिरा स्थिराणि दृढान्यपि शरीराण्यव तनुहि । अवस्तात्तनुभूतान्नातॆय । उग्रायोद्दूर्णबलाय ते तुभ्यं सहः शत्रुसहनसमर्थ० बलं
> बलहेतुकं हनिर्ददामि । अहं प्रयच्छामि । ततो विगदेषु । विविधं गदंति शब्दायंते ॥ गदेर्घइर्थे कविधानमित्यधिकरणे कः ॥ शत्रुन्मतीत्य प्रतिगम्य प्रतिकूलं
> गत्वा वृश्च । तांश्चिंदि ॥ ओव्रश्च छेदने तौदादिकस्य लोट् ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

O Indra, brandishing (भ्राशयन् (*bhrāśayan*), "making shine") your bright (भ्राश्यानि (*bhrāśyāni*)) and sharp (तिग्मानि (*tigmāni*)) weapons, bring down the bodies of the Yātudhānas, firm though they be: अव तनुहि (*ava tanuhi*) means stretch them downward. जु (*ju*) is a sautra root. To you, the fierce, of surging strength, I give strength (सहः (*sahaḥ*)), able to withstand enemies, a strength-producing oblation. Then, विगदेषु (*vigadeṣu*), in battles where men variously cry out, go against the enemies, assail them and cut them down: वृश्च (*vṛśca*) is the imperative of the root व्रश्च (*vraśca*) in the sense of cutting.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- (O Indra) भ्राश्यानि (*bhrāśyāni*)—shining
- तिग्मानि (*tigmāni*)—sharp, your weapons
- नि भ्राशयन् (*ni bhrāśayan*)—brandishing
- यातुजूनां (*yātujūnāṃ*)—of the hosts of rakṣas beginning with the Yātudhānas
- स्थिरा (*sthirā*)—the firm bodies
- अव तनुहि (*ava tanuhi*)—make them fall face downward
- उग्राय (*ugrāya*)—to you of exceeding strength
- ते (*te*)—to you
- सहः (*sahaḥ*)—able to endure the enemies' blows
- बलं (*balaṃ*)—the strength-giving oblation
- ददामि (*dadāmi*)—I offer
- विगदेषु (*vigadeṣu*)—in tumultuous battles
- शत्रून् प्रतीत्य (*śatrūn pratītya*)—rushing upon the enemies
- वृश्च (*vṛśca*)—cut them down

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

O Indra, brandishing your shining and sharp weapons, bring down the firm bodies of the Yātudhānas face downward. To you, endowed with exceeding strength, I offer an oblation that gives strength and can withstand the enemies'

### Printed p. 533
blows. In the tumultuous battles rush upon the enemies and cut them down.

##### English translation
Brandishing your sharp, shining weapons, pierce the solid bodies of the evil spirits. I give to you who are ficrce, foe-subding strength ; having assailed the enemies cut them to pieces in the midst of their clamour.

#### Ṛk 6

##### ॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)

> व्य१॒॑गर्य इं॑द्र तनुहि॒ श्रवां॒स्योजः॑ स्थि॒रेव॒ धन्व॑नो॒भिमा॑तीः ।  
> अ॒स्म॒द्र॑ग्व्यावृधा॒नः सहो॑भि॒रनि॑भृष्टस्त॒न्वं॑ वावृधस्व ॥ ६ ॥

##### ॥ पदपाठः ॥ (Pada-pāṭha)

> वि । अर्यः । इंद्र । तनुहि । श्रवांसि । ओजः । स्थिराइव । धन्वनः । अभिमातीः ।  
> अस्मद्र्यक् । ववृधानः । सहभिः । अनिभृष्टः । तन्वं । ववृधस्व ॥ ६ ॥

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> हे इंद्र आर्यः स्वामी त्वं श्रवांस्यन्नानि । श्रव इत्यन्ननाम । अस्मभ्यं वि
> तनुहि । विस्तारय । प्रयच्छ ॥ तनोतेर्लोट्युतश्च प्रत्ययाच्छंदसि वावचनं ।
> पा. ६-४-१०६-१ । इति हेर्लुगभावः ॥ तथाभिमातीः । अभितो मातिर्मानं येषां
> तेऽभिमातयः शत्रवः । तान्प्रत्योज आत्मीयं वीर्यं स्थिरेव स्थिराण्येव धन्वनो
> धनूंषि च विस्तारय । तैः शत्रुञ्छहीत्यर्थः । अपि चास्मद्र्यगस्मदभिमुखांचनः ॥
> विश्वद्गेवयोश्च टेरद्रंचतावित्यद्रादेशः । पा. ६-३-९२ । आद्रिसध्वरंतोदात्तत्वेन निपातनात् । पा. ६-३-९५-१ । उदात्तस्वरितयोर्यण इति धातोरकारस्यानुदात्तस्य स्वरितत्वं ॥ सहोभिरात्मीयैर्बलैर्वावृधानः प्रवृद्धः अत एवानिभृष्टः
> शत्रुभिरपरिभवनीयस्त्वं तन्नमात्मीयं शरीरं वावृधस्व । वर्धय । यद्वा। तन्नं ।
> तन्यत इति तनूर्यज्ञः । तं वर्धय । त्वदागमनेन हि यज्यो वर्धते ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

O Indra, आर्यः (*āryaḥ*), the lord, stretch out (वि तनुहि (*vi tanuhi*), extend, bestow) on us श्रवांसि (*śravāṃsi*), foods; "श्रव (*śrava*)" is a name for food. Likewise, against the अभिमातीः (*abhimātīḥ*), the enemies (those whose conceit, *mātiḥ*, is all around), extend your own might as if firm, and your bows; that is, strike the enemies with them. Further, अस्मद्र्यक् (*asmadryak*) means turned toward us. Strengthened by your own powers (सहोभिः (*sahobhiḥ*)), grown great and so unassailed by enemies, increase your own body (तन्वं (*tanvaṃ*)). Or else: तनू (*tanū*) is the sacrifice, "that which is extended"; increase it, for by your coming the sacrifice thrives.

### Printed p. 534

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- इंद्र (*iṃdra*)—O Indra
- आर्यः (*āryaḥ*)—you, the lord of all
- श्रवांसि (*śravāṃsi*)—foods and other provisions
- वि तनुहि (*vi tanuhi*)—provide us abundantly
- अभिमातीः (*abhimātīḥ*)—upon the enemies who stand against us
- ओजः (*ojaḥ*)—your splendour
- स्थिरेव (*sthireva*)—casting it so that it stays firm
- धन्वनः (*dhanvanaḥ*)—employ your bows
- अस्मद्रक् (*asmadrak*)—the people who are before us
- सहोभिः (*sahobhiḥ*)—by your strength and powers
- नावृधानः (*nāvṛdhānaḥ*)—making them zealous
- अनिभृष्टः (*anibhṛṣṭaḥ*)—you who are not defeated by enemies
- तन्नं (*tannaṃ*)—your body, that is, your own might
- नावृधस्व (*nāvṛdhasva*)—increase it still more [or तन्नं (*tannaṃ*)—the sacrifice; नावृधस्व (*nāvṛdhasva*)—make it go forward]

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

O Indra, lord of all, provide us abundantly with food and other provisions. Casting your splendour firmly upon the enemies who stand before us, employ your bow against them. Rousing our people who stand before us with your strength and powers, you who are not defeated by enemies, increase still more the might of your body; or else, increase our sacrifice.

##### English translation
Stretch out for us, lord Indra, varied food, (stretch out) your strength like strong bows against our enemies; mighty in our presence by your vigour and irresistible, still augment your form.

#### Ṛk 7

##### ॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)

> इ॒दं ह॒विम॑घव॒न्नुभ्यं॑ रा॒तं प्रति॑ सम्रा॒ळहृ॑णानो गृभाय ।  
> तुभ्यं॑ सु॒तो म॑घव॒न्नुभ्यं॑ प॒क्वो॒३॒॑ ३ द्धीं॑द्र॒ पिब॑ च॒ प्रस्थि॑तस्य ॥ ७ ॥

##### ॥ पदपाठः ॥ (Pada-pāṭha)

> इदं । हविः । मघवन् । तुभ्यं । रातं । प्रति । संराट् । अहृणानः । गृभाय ।  
> तुभ्यं । सुतः । मघवन् । तुभ्यं । पक्वः । अद्धि । इंद्र । पिब । च । प्रस्थितस्य ॥ ७ ॥

### Printed p. 535

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> हे मघवन्थनवन् सम्राट् सम्यग्राजमान सर्वेषामीश्वरेति ना इदं
> सोमादिलक्षणं रातमस्माभिर्दत्तं हविर्हे इंद्र तुभ्यमहृणानोऽक्रुद्धन् प्रति
> गृभाय । प्रतिगृहाण ॥ ग्रहेर्लोटि श्नाप्रत्ययस्य च्छंदसि शायजपीति शायजादेशः।
> हृग्रहोर्भ इति भः । संनिपातपरिभाषाया अनित्यत्वाद्धेर्लुक् ॥ हे मघवन्
> तुभ्यमेवायं सोमः सुतः ॥ जयि च । पा. ६-१-२१२ । इत्याद्युदात्तत्वं ॥
> तुभ्यमेवायं पुरोडाशादिः पक्वः । हे इंद्र तं पुरोडाशमद्धि । भक्षय । किंच
> प्रस्थितस्य हविर्धानादुत्तरवेदिं प्रति प्रस्थापितं सोमं पिब ॥ वाक्यभेदादनिघातः ।
> यद्वा । आमंत्रितस्याविद्यमानत्वेन तिज उत्तरत्वादनिघातः ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

O Maghavan, wealthy one, सम्राट् (*samrāṭ*), the fully shining, lord of all: this oblation (हविः (*haviḥ*)) of Soma and the rest, given (रातं (*rātaṃ*)) by us, accept (प्रति गृभाय (*prati gṛbhāya*)), O Indra, not angry (अहृणानः (*ahṛṇānaḥ*)). For you alone this Soma has been pressed, and for you alone this puroḍāśa and the like has been cooked. O Indra, eat that cake (अद्धि (*addhi*), consume). And further, drink the Soma that has been sent forth (प्रस्थितस्य (*prasthitasya*)) from the havirdhāna toward the northern altar.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- मघवन् (*maghavan*)—wealthy one
- सम्राट् (*samrāṭ*)—O Indra, lord of all
- तुभ्यं (*tubhyaṃ*)—for you
- रातं (*rātaṃ*)—offered by us
- इदं हविः (*idaṃ haviḥ*)—this oblation
- अहृणानः (*ahṛṇānaḥ*)—without anger
- प्रति गृभाय (*prati gṛbhāya*)—accept
- मघवन् (*maghavan*)—O Indra
- तुभ्यं (*tubhyaṃ*)—for you alone
- सुतः (*sutaḥ*)—this Soma-juice has been pressed and made ready
- तुभ्यं (*tubhyaṃ*)—for you alone
- पक्वः (*pakvaḥ*)—this oblation, puroḍāśa and the like, has been cooked
- इंद्र (*iṃdra*)—O Indra
- (तं (*taṃ*)—that puroḍāśa) अद्दि (*addi*)—eat
- प्रस्थितस्य (*prasthitasya*)—the Soma that is ready, filled in the vessel
- पिब (*piba*)—drink

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

O Indra, wealthy and lord of all, accept without anger this oblation offered by us for you. O Indra, this Soma-juice has been pressed and made ready for you alone. This puroḍāśa also has been cooked for you alone. Eat it. O Indra, drink the Soma-juice that is ready, filled in the vessel.

##### English translation
Imperial Maghavan, to you this oblation is offered; aecept it, not displeased : for you, Maghavan, the libation is effused, for you (the cake is) toasted ; eat it, Indra, and drink the libation poured (upon the altar).

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

On the question whether the deities, like men, have bodily forms, limbs such as hands, eating of food, drinking of Soma and similar actions, or not, Yāska has given as an example the phrase of this Ṛk, अद्धींद्रपिब च प्रस्थितस्य (*addhīṃdrapiba ca prasthitasya*). His explanation on this matter is as follows—

### Printed p. 536
Although there is a difference of opinion on the question whether the gods have limbs such as hands and feet, as human beings have, in the Ṛgveda the seers are seen to praise Indra and the other gods as possessing limbs such as hands and feet. On this point Yāska says:
अथाकारचिंतनं देवतानां । पुरुषविधाः स्युरित्येकं । चेतनावद्वद्धि स्तुतॆयो भवंति । तथाभिधानानि । अथापि पौरुषविधिकैरंगैः संस्तूयंते । ऋष्वात इंद्र स्थविरस्य बाहू । यत्संगृभ्जा मघवन् काशिरित्ते । (*athākāraciṃtanaṃ devatānāṃ | puruṣavidhāḥ syurityekaṃ | cetanāvadvaddhi stutèyo bhavaṃti | tathābhidhānāni | athāpi pauruṣavidhikairaṃgaiḥ saṃstūyaṃte | ṛṣvāta iṃdra sthavirasya bāhū | yatsaṃgṛbhjā maghavan kāśiritte |*) (Ni. 7-6)
Thus he has stated the explanation. Now let us examine the forms, shapes and so on of the gods. Some hold that the gods have hands and other limbs as men have. Considering that the gods, like men, possess consciousness, intelligence and so on, and that, having hands and other limbs and a form as men have, they are conscious beings, they are praised accordingly. For this very reason it is customary, when describing Indra and the other gods, to describe their hands and the like. In the third pāda of the present Ṛk, ऋष्वात इंद्र स्थविरस्य बाहू (*ṛṣvāta iṃdra sthavirasya bāhū*), there is a description of Indra's arms. Likewise in the Ṛk
उताभये पुरुहूत श्रवोभिरेको दृळमवदो वृत्रहा सन् । इमे चिदिंद्र रोदसी अपारे यत्संगृभ्णा मघवन् काशिरित्ते ॥ (*utābhaye puruhūta śravobhireko dṛḷamavado vṛtrahā san | ime cidiṃdra rodasī apāre yatsaṃgṛbhṇā maghavan kāśiritte ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 3-30-5)
the author of the Nirukta has cited a description of Indra's limbs. There are many descriptions that the gods have, besides human forms, association with various kinds of things, as men have:
अथापि पौरुषविधिकैर्द्रव्यसंयोगैः । (*athāpi pauruṣavidhikairdravyasaṃyogaiḥ |*) (Ni. 7-6)
On this point he cites the Ṛk
आ द्वाभ्यां हरिभ्यामिंद्र याह्या चतुर्भिरा षड्भिर्हूयमानः । आष्टाभिर्दशभिः सोमपेयमयं सुतः सुमख मा मृधस्कः ॥ (*ā dvābhyāṃ haribhyāmiṃdra yāhyā caturbhirā ṣaḍbhirhūyamānaḥ | āṣṭābhirdaśabhiḥ somapeyamayaṃ sutaḥ sumakha mā mṛdhaskaḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 2-18-4)
and in this Ṛk it is clearly explained that, as men have cows, horses and so on, so Indra and the other gods have them. "O Indra, come to our sacrifice with your two horses named Hari, seated in the chariot, or else

### Printed p. 537
with four, six, eight or ten horses, here for the drinking of Soma." Since this is said, the sense is plain that, as men have possessions in worldly dealings, so the gods have horses and the like. And again
अपाः सोममस्तमिंद्र प्र याहि कल्याणीर्जाया सुरणं गृहे ते । यत्रा रथस्य बृहतो निधानं विमोचनं वाजिनो दक्षिणावत् ॥ (*apāḥ somamastamiṃdra pra yāhi kalyāṇīrjāyā suraṇaṃ gṛhe te | yatrā rathasya bṛhato nidhānaṃ vimocanaṃ vājino dakṣiṇāvat ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 3-53-6)
In this Ṛk there is mention of Indra, like men, having a wife, a chariot and horses in his house.
Further, in support of the view that the gods have actions like those of men, he gives some examples:
अथापि पौरुषविधिकैः कर्मभिः । (*athāpi pauruṣavidhikaiḥ karmabhiḥ |*) (Ni. 7-6)
इदं हविर्मघवन् तुभ्यं रातं प्रति सम्राळहृणानो गृभाय । तुभ्यं सुतो मघवन् तुभ्यं पक्वोऽद्धींद्र पिब च प्रस्थितस्य ॥ (*idaṃ havirmaghavan tubhyaṃ rātaṃ prati samrāḷahṛṇāno gṛbhāya | tubhyaṃ suto maghavan tubhyaṃ pakvo 'ddhīṃdra piba ca prasthitasya ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-116-7)
आश्रुत्कर्ण श्रुधी हवं नू चिद्दधिष्ट मे गिरः । इंद्र सोममिमं मम कृष्णा युजश्चिदंतरं । (*āśrutkarṇa śrudhī havaṃ nū ciddadhiṣṭa me giraḥ | iṃdra somamimaṃ mama kṛṣṇā yujaścidaṃtaraṃ |*)
These Ṛks are given as examples. In the first Ṛk it is said that the oblation and Soma are offered for Indra and that he is prayed to drink it. In the second Ṛk there is a prayer that he should hear our invocation and our praise. That is, actions fitting human beings, such as eating the oblation as men do, drinking the Soma juice, and listening to the invocation and the praise, are attributed to Indra and the other gods, and they are praised accordingly. Thus it is the contention of some that the gods have a form, hands and other limbs, and actions such as eating, as men have. Others hold that the gods have no forms and the like as men have, that their actions also are different from those performed by men, and that they are so described by way of exaggeration, to depict the greatness of the gods:
अपुरुषविधाः स्युरित्यपरं ॥ (*apuruṣavidhāḥ syurityaparaṃ ‖*) (Ni. 7-7)
Others hold that the gods do not have form, shape, action and so on as men have, and that their distinctive character is of another kind. How so?

### Printed p. 538
अपि तु यद्दृश्यतेऽपुरुषविधं तद्यथाग्निर्वायुरादित्यः पृथिवी चंद्रमा इति (*api tu yaddṛśyate 'puruṣavidhaṃ tadyathāgnirvāyurādityaḥ pṛthivī caṃdramā iti*) (Ni. 7-7)
Although the forms and actions of some gods appear like those of men, they are not so. Although the forms and actions of the gods Agni, Vāyu, Āditya, Pṛthivī, Candramā and so on appear like the actions of men, their manner is quite different. There is a marked difference between those actions and the actions of men.
यथो एतच्छेतनावद्वद्धि स्तुतयो भवंतीत्यचेतनान्यप्येवं स्तूयंते यथाक्षप्रभृतीनोषधिपर्यंतानि ॥ (*yatho etacchetanāvadvaddhi stutayo bhavaṃtītyacetanānyapyevaṃ stūyaṃte yathākṣaprabhṛtīnoṣadhiparyaṃtāni ‖*) (Ni. 7-7)
That is, when gods such as Agni are praised, they are praised as though conceived to be like conscious beings. In gambling men address the dice; though the dice are without consciousness, they address them as if they were conscious creatures. They also address the herbs, that is, plants, trees and creepers, conceiving them as conscious.
यथो एतत्पौरुषविधिकैरंग्यैः संस्तूयंत इत्यचेतनेष्वप्येतद्भवत्यभिक्रदंति हरितेभिरासभिरिति ग्रावस्तुतिः ॥ (*yatho etatpauruṣavidhikairaṃgyaiḥ saṃstūyaṃta ityacetaneṣvapyetadbhavatyabhikradaṃti haritebhirāsabhiriti grāvastutiḥ ‖*) (Ni. 7-7)
In the same way, unconscious things too are praised as if they had limbs belonging to a man. Herbs and the stones that crush the Soma are unconscious. Yet the sound that arises when Soma plants are crushed with stones is described thus: those stones cry out with their green mouths. Since stones are unconscious they have no mouths as living beings have; still the seer describes, figuratively, the sound made when the plant is laid on the stone and crushed as made by the stones themselves from their mouths. When Soma plants are crushed, the green colour of the plants sticks to the stones; to indicate that the mouths of the stones are green, the description that their mouths are green is made with exaggeration.
यथो एतत्पौरुषविधिकैर्द्रव्यसंयोगैरित्येतदपि तादृशमेव । सुखं रथं युयुजे सिंधुरश्विनं इति नदीस्तुतिः ॥ (*yatho etatpauruṣavidhikairdravyasaṃyogairityetadapi tādṛśameva | sukhaṃ rathaṃ yuyuje siṃdhuraśvinaṃ iti nadīstutiḥ ‖*) (Ni. 7-7)
On the point that unconscious things too have association with objects as men have: as in sentences such as "the river (Sindhu) yoked her horses to a pleasant chariot", the river is unconscious and has no chariot. Yet in praising the river the seer praises it by attributing to it, as to men, association with objects (the possession of property).

### Printed p. 539
यथो एतत्पौरुषविधिकैः कर्मभिरित्येतदपि तादृशमेव । होतुश्चित्पूर्वो हविरद्यमाशत इति ग्रावस्तुतिरेव ॥ (*yatho etatpauruṣavidhikaiḥ karmabhirityetadapi tādṛśameva | hotuścitpūrvo haviradyamāśata iti grāvastutireva ‖*) (Ni. 7-7)
In the matter of actions also, agency is attributed to unconscious things such as stones, as to men, and they are praised so. When Soma plants are crushed with a stone, it is natural that the juice that comes out touches the stone. This the seer describes: the stones, the instruments of pressing the Soma, taste the Soma juice even before the sacrificers such as the Hotṛ. A stone has no mouth and no capacity to taste. Yet since the juice that comes out when the plant is crushed with the stone touches the stone, to describe that the stone tastes the Soma juice before everyone is exaggeration and figurative. That in reality stones, being unconscious, have neither mouth nor capacity to taste is a matter of everyone's experience.
अपि वोभयविधाः स्युः । अपि ना पुरुषविधानामेव सतां कर्मात्मान एते स्युर्यथा यज्ञो यजमानस्य । एष चाख्यानसमयः ॥ (*api vobhayavidhāḥ syuḥ | api nā puruṣavidhānāmeva satāṃ karmātmāna ete syuryathā yajño yajamānasya | eṣa cākhyānasamayaḥ ‖*) (Ni. 7-7)
Hence room exists for both kinds of view. Although things such as the earth are unconscious, they behave as if endowed with consciousness; so, though there is a difference of opinion in conceiving them in both ways, as conscious and as unconscious, both ways may be accepted as right. In the sentence यज्ञो यज्ञमानस्य (*yajño yajñamānasya*) the sacrificer is conscious. The sacrifice is unconscious; yet in speaking of the sacrifice, in sentences such as "the sacrifice provides the sacrificer with heaven, the best place", the sacrifice is treated as if conscious. Therefore there is no fault in describing unconscious things as if they were conscious. To give an example: पृथिवी स्त्रीरूपेण भारावतरणाय ब्रह्माणं ययाचे ! अग्निश्च ब्राह्मणरूपेण वासुदेवार्जुनावुभौ खांडवं ययाचे । पुरुषरूपेणाग्निरूपेण च खांडवं ददाह । (*pṛthivī strīrūpeṇa bhārāvataraṇāya brahmāṇaṃ yayāce ! agniśca brāhmaṇarūpeṇa vāsudevārjunāvubhau khāṃḍavaṃ yayāce | puruṣarūpeṇāgnirūpeṇa ca khāṃḍavaṃ dadāha |*) The Earth, taking the form of a woman, begged Brahmā to relieve her of her burden; Agni, in the form of a Brahmin, approached Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna and begged Indra's Khāṇḍava forest; Agni, as a man and in his fire form, burnt the Khāṇḍava forest. In such sentences there are many descriptions also in the Purāṇas and elsewhere that lifeless things such as Agni and the Earth, or their presiding deities, took human form and did various deeds. Hence the main purport of the explanation is that it is right to conceive these in both ways, as conscious and unconscious; this is the conclusion.

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> हे इंद्र प्रस्थिता प्रस्थितान्युत्तरवेदिं प्रतीमेमानि ॥ उभयत्र डादेशः ॥
> हवींष्यद्दीत् । इदवधारणे । भक्षयैव । चनः । चन इत्यन्ननाम । तद्दधिष्ट! धारय।
> उदरे प्रक्षिप ॥ दधातेर्लोटि चृंदस्युभयथेति थास आर्धधातुकत्वादिडागमः ॥
> पचता पचतानि सवनीयपुरोडाशादीनि च धारय ॥ पचेर्भृमृदृशीत्यादिना
> कर्मण्यतच् प्रत्ययः ॥ उतापि च सोमं पिब । ततः प्रयस्वंतः । प्रीणयतीति
> प्रयोऽन्नं । तेन तद्वंतः संतस्त्वा त्वां प्रति हर्यामसि । हर्यामः । कामयामहे धनादीनि ॥ हर्यतिः प्रेप्साकर्मा । इदंतो मसिः ॥ तस्माद्यजमानस्य यागं
> कुर्वाणस्य कामा धनादिविषया अभिलाषाः सत्या यथार्थाः संतु !! पूज्यजोः
> शानन् । पा. ३-२-१२८ । इति यजेः शानन्प्रत्ययः । शित्वादाद्युदात्तः ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

"O Indra, *prasthitā* means these oblations that have been set out toward the Uttaravedi" (in both places the substitution of ḍa applies). Eat these oblations without fail: इत् (*it*) is for emphasis. चनः (*canaḥ*) is a name of food; take it in, that is, put it into your belly. Likewise take in the cooked foods, the cakes of the Soma pressing and the rest. And drink the Soma too. Then प्रयस्वंतः (*prayasvaṃtaḥ*): *praya* is food, since it gratifies; possessing it, we seek you; हर्यामः (*haryāmaḥ*) means we desire wealth and the like; हर्यति (*haryati*) is a root of the sense of wishing. Therefore let the desires of the sacrificer who performs the sacrifice, longings for wealth and the like, be true, that is, fulfilled. The affix śānac applies to यजेः (*yajeḥ*) by पूज्यजोः शानन् (*pūjyajoḥ śānan*) (Pā. 3-2-128).

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- इंद्र (*iṃdra*)—O Indra
- प्रस्थिता (*prasthitā*)—brought and placed on the Uttaravedi
- इमा हवींषि (*imā havīṃṣi*)—these oblations
- अद्धि इत् (*addhi it*)—eat certainly
- चनः (*canaḥ*)—the food also
- पचता (*pacatā*)—the cooked cakes and the like
- दधिष्व (*dadhiṣva*)—fill into the belly
- उत (*uta*)—and
- सोमं (*somaṃ*)—drink the Soma juice

### Printed p. 541
- प्रयस्वंतः (*prayasvaṃtaḥ*)—we, who are ready to offer satisfying food
- त्वा प्रति (*tvā prati*)—approaching you
- हर्यामसि (*haryāmasi*)—we pray for wealth and the like
- यजमानस्य (*yajamānasya*)—of the sacrificer who performs the sacrifice
- कामः (*kāmaḥ*)—the desires
- सत्याः संतु (*satyāḥ saṃtu*)—let them surely be fulfilled

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

O Indra, eat without fail these oblations brought and made ready on the Uttaravedi. Likewise fill your belly with the food and the cooked cakes and the like. And drink the Soma juice. We, who offer satisfying food, approach you and ask for wealth and the like. May all the desires (wishes) of the sacrificer who performs the sacrifice be fulfilled.

##### English translation
Eat, Indra, these oblations placed (upon the altar); accept the food the toasted (cakes), and the Soma. Provided with sacrificial vainds we delight you; let the desires of the institutor of the rite be fulfilled.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

Yāska has given the following explanation for the words चनः (*canaḥ*) and पचता (*pacatā*) in this Ṛk:
चनः । पचता ॥ अद्धीदिंद्र प्रस्थितेमा हवींषि चनो दधिष्ट पचतोत सोमं॥ अद्धींद्र प्रस्थितानीमानि हवींषि चनो दधिष्ट । चन इत्यन्न नाम । पचतिर्नामीभूतः । तं मेदस्तः प्रति पचताग्रभीष्वां इत्यपि निगमो भवति॥ (*canaḥ | pacatā ‖ addhīdiṃdra prasthitemā havīṃṣi cano dadhiṣṭa pacatota somaṃ‖ addhīṃdra prasthitānīmāni havīṃṣi cano dadhiṣṭa | cana ityanna nāma | pacatirnāmībhūtaḥ | taṃ medastaḥ prati pacatāgrabhīṣvāṃ ityapi nigamo bhavati‖*) (Ni. 6-16)
The sense of the sentence is: O Indra, take into your belly the oblations and the food prepared here. Here चनः (*canaḥ*) is a word denoting the meaning "food"; चनः (*canaḥ*) means food. On this point the Śruti sentence अद्दीदिंद्र (*addīdiṃdra*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-116-8) is the example. Though the word पचति (*pacati*) is a verb, in many contexts it is used like a noun. On this the Śruti sentence तं मेदस्तः प्रति पचिताग्रभीष्टां (*taṃ medastaḥ prati pacitāgrabhīṣṭāṃ*) supports it.

> अर्कॆः ।

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> इंद्राग्निभ्यां देवाभ्यां सुवचस्यां ॥ छंदसि चेति यत्प्रत्ययः ॥ सुवचनार्हां स्तुतिमहं प्रेयर्मि । प्रेरयामि ॥ ऋ गतौ चौहोत्यादिकः । आर्तिपिपर्योश्चेत्यभ्यासस्यॆत्वं । देवताद्वंद्वे चेतींद्राग्योरुभयपदप्रकृतिस्वरत्वे
> प्राप्ते नोत्तरपदेऽनुदात्तादाविति प्रतिषेधः ॥ सिंधाविव सिंधौ नद्यां यथा नावं
> प्रेरयंति तद्वदर्कैरर्चनीयैर्मंत्रैः सहितां स्तुतिं प्रेरयं । प्रावादिषं ॥
> ईर गत् । ण्यंतस्य लज्युत्तमस्यामादेशः ॥ स्तुतास्ते देवा अया इव । आयंति
> कर्मकरणार्थं गच्छंत्यया ऋत्विजः कर्मकरा ना । तद्वत्परि चरंति । आस्मान्थनादिदानेन
> पूजयंति । ये देवा अस्मभ्यं धनदा धनस्य दातार उद्भिदोऽस्मच्छत्रूणामुद्भेत्तारश्च ये संति ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

For the two deities Indra and Agni, I send forth a praise worthy of good speech (सुवचस्यां (*suvacasyāṃ*)). Sāyaṇa takes प्रेयर्मि (*preyarmi*) as "I send forth", from the root ऋ (*ṛ*) in the sense of going. As men launch a boat on a river, so I have sent forth a praise accompanied by venerable mantras (*arkaiḥ*); प्रेरयं (*prerayaṃ*) means "I have recited". The gods so praised, like अयाः (*ayāḥ*) (priests, workers, who go to perform rites), attend upon us (परि चरंति (*pari caraṃti*)), honouring us with gifts of wealth and the like: those gods who are givers of wealth to us and breakers-out (destroyers) of our enemies.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- इंद्राग्निभ्यां (*iṃdrāgnibhyāṃ*)—addressing the deities Indra and Agni
- सुवचस्यां (*suvacasyāṃ*)—this hymn composed of excellent words
- प्र इयर्मि (*pra iyarmi*)—I offer of my own impulse
- सिंधाविव (*siṃdhāviva*)—in the river Sindhu
- नावं (*nāvaṃ*)—as one launches and steers a boat
- आर्कैः (*ārkaiḥ*)—a hymn accompanied by mantras
- प्र ईरयं (*pra īrayaṃ*)—I have offered of my own impulse
- ये (*ye*)—which gods
- अस्मभ्यं (*asmabhyaṃ*)—to us
- धनदाः (*dhanadāḥ*)—givers of wealth
- च (*ca*)—and who
- उद्भिदः (*udbhidaḥ*)—destroyers of our enemies, such

### Printed p. 543
- देवाः (*devāḥ*)—the gods
- अया इव (*ayā iva*)—like roving priests or workers
- परि चरंति (*pari caraṃti*)—they attend us with wealth and the like, that is, they gladden us

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

To Indra and Agni I offer this hymn made of excellent words, of my own impulse alone. As a boat is launched and pushed on the river Sindhu, I have composed and offered this mantra-accompanied praise of my own impulse. The gods who are our givers of wealth and who destroy our enemies, like roving priests, attend upon us with gifts of wealth and so on and gladden us.

##### English translation
I direct my eulogy to Indra and Agni; with sacred prayers I directed (my praise) like a vessel (launched) upon the ocean ; like holy priests, the gods themselves reverence us being the donors (to us) of wealth and the extirpators (of our foes).

## Sūkta 117 (Maṇḍala 10)
**Introduction**
The deity of this sūkta is the praise of food (अन्नस्तुति (*annastuti*)). As Śaunaka says in his Ṛgvidhāna (Ṛgvi. 1-27), it has been a custom among the Āryas from of old to honour food or nourishment with devotion and worship, then to give a portion to guests and others, and only afterwards to eat oneself. It is necessary to consider here a little the importance of food. The word अन्न (*anna*) is formed from the root अद (*ada*) in the sense of eating (अद् (*ad*), "eat"). On the origin of food:
तस्माद्वा एतस्मादात्मन आकाशः संभूतः । आकाशाद्वायुः । वायोरग्निः । अग्नेरापः । अद्भ्यः पृथिवी । पृथिव्या ओषधयः । ओषधीभ्योऽन्नं । अन्नात्पुरुषः ॥ (*tasmādvā etasmādātmana ākāśaḥ saṃbhūtaḥ | ākāśādvāyuḥ | vāyoragniḥ | agnerāpaḥ | adbhyaḥ pṛthivī | pṛthivyā oṣadhayaḥ | oṣadhībhyo 'nnaṃ | annātpuruṣaḥ ‖*)
(Kṛ. U. 2-1)

### Printed p. 544
**NOTE**
This Vedic text says that at the creation of the world, of the five elements, space first arose from the supreme Brahman (the Supreme Self), from space air, from air fire, from fire water, from water earth, from earth the plants (herbs and the like), and from plants food. From such food arose man (and the other creatures too). The answers to questions such as what is the excellence of food, what use comes of food, and why food is called annam are given there itself:
अन्नाद्वै प्रजाः प्रजा मंते । याः काश्च पृथिवीग् श्रिताः । अथो अन्नेनैव जीवंति । अथैनदपियत्यंततः । अन्नग्ंहि भूतानां ज्येष्ठं । तस्मात्सर्वषधमुच्यते । सर्वं वै तेऽन्नमाप्पुवंति । येऽन्नं ब्रह्मोपासते । अन्नग्ंहि भूतानां ज्येष्ठं । तस्मात्सर्वौषधमुच्यते । अन्नाद्भूतानि जायंते । जातान्यन्नेन वर्धंते । अद्यतेऽत्ति च भूतानि । तस्मादन्नं तॆदुच्यत इत (*annādvai prajāḥ prajā maṃte | yāḥ kāśca pṛthivīg śritāḥ | atho annenaiva jīvaṃti | athainadapiyatyaṃtataḥ | annagṃhi bhūtānāṃ jyeṣṭhaṃ | tasmātsarvaṣadhamucyate | sarvaṃ vai te 'nnamāppuvaṃti | ye 'nnaṃ brahmopāsate | annagṃhi bhūtānāṃ jyeṣṭhaṃ | tasmātsarvauṣadhamucyate | annādbhūtāni jāyaṃte | jātānyannena vardhaṃte | adyate 'tti ca bhūtāni | tasmādannaṃ tèducyata ita*)
(Tai. U. 2-2)
That is: all creatures dwelling on earth are born of food, live by food, and at the end are dissolved in it. Among the beings (or among things created from the five great elements) food is the eldest of all; therefore it is called the "all-herb" (सर्वौषध (*sarvauṣadha*)). Those who worship Brahman in the form of food obtain all food, that is, they get food in abundance. Food is the eldest among all beings.
The beings (bhūtas) are the five great elements: earth, water, fire (heat), air and space. These five elements exist as food in their original form. How? Earth means solid substance. In the food we eat there are solid things such as grains; these are the earth part. The second is water. We drink water; besides, in other things we eat or drink (milk and so on) there is a watery part. Living beings need more water than earth-part (solid) food; in our body too the watery part (blood) predominates. The third is fire (tejas), that is, heat. Creatures cannot live without heat. We get heat from the food we take and from the warmth in sunshine, air and so on around us. When heat is lacking in the body, death occurs at once. From birth to death there must be heat in the body.

### Printed p. 545
Therefore there is no need to say how necessary heat or tejas is. We need one measure more of fire than of water. The fourth is air. When we draw breath we attract the air outside and take it into the body. We cannot be without breathing for a moment; as soon as breathing stops, life departs, that is, death occurs. From birth till death air is absolutely necessary to all creatures, and it is needed in greater measure than the solid earth-food, water and heat described above. The fifth is space (room). Without space neither we nor other creatures could exist; space is needed for our movements and the body's needs. Although fire, air and space are not visible to our eyes, they are indispensable for the nourishment of the body. Moreover, we (and other creatures) need one measure more of water than of solid earth-food; more heat than water; more air than heat; more space than air. And a further point: in food belonging to the earth part, water, heat, air and space are mixed; in heat, air and space are present; in air, space is included. Thus the five elements and their mixtures, that is, herbs and trees, are arranged as food for creatures. This kind of food is called annam; therefore it is called the "all-herb".
From food beings (creatures) are born; the born creatures grow and flourish by food alone. It is eaten, and it also eats creatures. Therefore it is called annam. Here the last sentence (food is eaten and it eats creatures) needs explanation. For creatures moving in the world, apart from the five elements such as water in their original form, all other food is produced by living creatures. There is no food in the world other than what relates to living things. Thus flesh-eating animals eat plant-eating animals, plant-eaters eat plants; plants too have life (how could a lifeless plant grow?), and living moving creatures must live by eating one another. Since the plant kingdom does not belong to the moving class, plants take their food directly from the earth or the five elements and grow. Hence moving creatures cannot live without food from living creatures or from plants. Therefore creatures eat food; and food eats creatures, that is, food arises from creatures

### Printed p. 546
as said above. The main point is that in the world moving creatures (men too) must live by eating one another; without food related to creatures they cannot live at all. This is the intention stated in the sentences अद्यतेऽत्ति च भूतानि । तस्मादन्नं तदुच्यते (*adyate 'tti ca bhūtāni | tasmādannaṃ taducyate*).
There are also Vedic texts on the point that food should be worshipped and held in respect:
अन्नं न निंद्यात् । तद्व्रतं । प्राणो वा अन्नं । शरीरमन्नादं । प्राणे शरीरं प्रतिष्ठितं । शरीरॆ प्राणः प्रतिष्ठितः । तदेतदन्नमन्ने प्रतिष्ठितं । स य एतदन्नमन्ने प्रतिष्ठितं वेद प्रतितिष्ठति । अन्नवानन्नादो भवति । महान्भवति प्रजया पशुभिर्ब्रह्मवर्चसेन । महान्कर्त्या ॥ (*annaṃ na niṃdyāt | tadvrataṃ | prāṇo vā annaṃ | śarīramannādaṃ | prāṇe śarīraṃ pratiṣṭhitaṃ | śarīrè prāṇaḥ pratiṣṭhitaḥ | tadetadannamanne pratiṣṭhitaṃ | sa ya etadannamanne pratiṣṭhitaṃ veda pratitiṣṭhati | annavānannādo bhavati | mahānbhavati prajayā paśubhirbrahmavarcasena | mahānkartyā ‖*)
(Tai. U. 3-7)
Food should not be reviled; one should regard this as a vow (a duty). Breath is food. The body eats food and grows by it. In breath the body is established; in the body breath is established. Hence breath and body are related to each other. Both are established in food; that is, by food alone the growth and protection of body and breath come about. Without food neither body nor breath can be. One who knows that food is established in food (in Brahman in the form of food) is honoured. He becomes rich in food and an eater of food. Endowed with progeny (children and so on), cattle, Brahmanical radiance and fame, he becomes the best and most honoured among men.
अन्नं न परिचक्षीत । तद्व्रतं । आपो वा अन्नं । ज्योतिरन्नादं । अप्सु ज्योतिः प्रतिष्ठितं । ज्योतिष्यापः प्रतिष्ठिताः । तदेतदन्नमन्ने प्रतिष्ठितं । स य एतदन्नमन्ने प्रतिष्ठितं वेद प्रतितिष्ठति । अन्नवानन्नादो भवति । महान्भवति प्रजया पशुभिर्ब्रह्मवर्चसेन । महान्कर्त्या ॥ (*annaṃ na paricakṣīta | tadvrataṃ | āpo vā annaṃ | jyotirannādaṃ | apsu jyotiḥ pratiṣṭhitaṃ | jyotiṣyāpaḥ pratiṣṭhitāḥ | tadetadannamanne pratiṣṭhitaṃ | sa ya etadannamanne pratiṣṭhitaṃ veda pratitiṣṭhati | annavānannādo bhavati | mahānbhavati prajayā paśubhirbrahmavarcasena | mahānkartyā ‖*)
(Tai. U. 3-8)
Do not despise food; regard this very act as a vow. Water is food; fire (light) eats food. In water fire is established; in fire water is established. These two, fire and water, are established in food (food has heat and a watery part). One who knows that food is established in food (in Brahman in the form of food) is honoured. He becomes rich in food and an enjoyer of food. Endowed with progeny, cattle, Brahmanical radiance and fame, he becomes the best and most honoured among men.

### Printed p. 547
There are also many Vedic authorities for the point that one should give food to guests and visitors and only then eat oneself.
मोघमन्नं विंदते अप्रचेताः सत्यं ब्रवीमि वध इत्स तस्य । नार्यमणं पुष्यति नो सखायं केवलाघो भवति केवलादी ॥ (*moghamannaṃ viṃdate apracetāḥ satyaṃ bravīmi vadha itsa tasya | nāryamaṇaṃ puṣyati no sakhāyaṃ kevalāgho bhavati kevalādī ‖*)
(Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-117-6)
That is: the food which a miser who gives nothing to anyone obtains is vain. By the food he gets no benefit comes to him; it becomes the cause of his death (ruin). "I tell the truth," says the seer. The man who does not give oblations and the like to Aryaman and other gods, that is, does not offer food to the gods, and who does not satisfy with food a friend or a guest who comes to the house like a friend, but eats alone, is said to be a great sinner. And:
न स सखा यो न ददाति सख्ये सचाभुवे सचमानाय पित्वः । अपास्मात्प्रेयॊन्न तदोको अस्ति पृणंतमन्यमरणं चिदिच्छेत् ॥ (*na sa sakhā yo na dadāti sakhye sacābhuve sacamānāya pitvaḥ | apāsmātpreyònna tadoko asti pṛṇaṃtamanyamaraṇaṃ cidicchet ‖*)
(Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-117-4)
He who gives no food to a friend, to his companion, to one near him, is no friend at all. Therefore one should leave the house of such a man. That is not the only house; there are houses of generous people who give food; it is good to go there. So the seer describes. Therefore good householders should prepare in the house a little more food than suffices for themselves, for the entertainment of guests and visitors. On this point:
अन्नं बहु कुर्वीत । तद्व्रतं पृथिवी वा अन्नं । आकाशोऽन्नादः । पृथिव्यामाकाशः प्रतिष्ठितः । आकाशे पृथिवी प्रतिष्ठिता । तदेतदन्नमन्ने प्रतिष्ठितं । स य एतदन्नमन्ने प्रतिष्ठितं वेद प्रतितिष्ठति । अन्नवानन्नादो भवति । महान्भवति प्रजया पशुभिर्ब्रह्मवर्चसेन । महान् कीर्त्या ॥ (*annaṃ bahu kurvīta | tadvrataṃ pṛthivī vā annaṃ | ākāśo 'nnādaḥ | pṛthivyāmākāśaḥ pratiṣṭhitaḥ | ākāśe pṛthivī pratiṣṭhitā | tadetadannamanne pratiṣṭhitaṃ | sa ya etadannamanne pratiṣṭhitaṃ veda pratitiṣṭhati | annavānannādo bhavati | mahānbhavati prajayā paśubhirbrahmavarcasena | mahān kīrtyā ‖*)
(Kṛ. U. 3-9)
Food should be made plentiful; one should regard doing so as a vow. Earth is food. Space eats food; that is, plants, grains and the like grown on earth are eaten, as oblations, by the gods dwelling in the atmosphere (heaven). In earth space is established; in space earth is established. Both (earth and space) are established in food. That food is established in food (in Brahman in the form of food). One who knows that food is established in food

### Printed p. 548
…knows this is established, or lives with honour. He becomes rich in food and an enjoyer of food. He also becomes endowed with sons, grandsons and other progeny, possessed of cattle, and, together with Brahma-radiance and fame, gains esteem among men. And further: न कंचन वसतौ (*na kaṃcana vasatau*) … य एवं वेद । इत्युपनिषत् (*ya evaṃ veda | ityupaniṣat*) **NOTE** (Kṛ. U. 3-10) **NOTE**

These sentences quoted above were spoken by the Veda-Puruṣa himself. One must not turn anyone away by saying there is no room in the house; that very thing is to be regarded as the vow. Therefore, by whatever means, one must obtain plenty of food. It is said, "Prepare food for him (the guest)." This is the preparation of food with the utmost respect. Parameśvara himself has said that in preparing food and giving it to a worthy recipient there are three kinds: sāttvika, rājasa and tāmasa.

दातव्यमिति यद्दानं दीयतेनुपकारिणे । देशे काले च पात्रे च तद्दानं सात्विकं स्मृतं ॥ (*dātavyamiti yaddānaṃ dīyatenupakāriṇe | deśe kāle ca pātre ca taddānaṃ sātvikaṃ smṛtaṃ ‖*)

### Printed p. 549

यदन्नं संपादितमस्येतदेवान्नं मुखतो राद्धं भवति । मुख्ये देशे तीर्थक्षेत्रविशेषे मुख्यकाले संक्रांत्यमावास्यादिरूपे मुख्यायाभ्यागताय वेदशास्त्र तदध्ययनानुष्ठानपराय मुख्यया वृत्ता श्रद्धाप्रणिपातसत्कारादिपरया मुख्येन दात्रा सात्विकेन दत्तमित्यर्थः । यः पुमानेवं सात्विकं दानप्रकारं वेद विदित्वानुतिष्ठति अस्मै जन्मांतरे मुख्यक्रमेणैवान्नं संपद्यते । (*yadannaṃ saṃpāditamasyetadevānnaṃ mukhato rāddhaṃ bhavati | mukhye deśe tīrthakṣetraviśeṣe mukhyakāle saṃkrāṃtyamāvāsyādirūpe mukhyāyābhyāgatāya vedaśāstra tadadhyayanānuṣṭhānaparāya mukhyayā vṛttā śraddhāpraṇipātasatkārādiparayā mukhyena dātrā sātvikena dattamityarthaḥ | yaḥ pumānevaṃ sātvikaṃ dānaprakāraṃ veda viditvānutiṣṭhati asmai janmāṃtare mukhyakrameṇaivānnaṃ saṃpadyate |*)

Sāttvika gift means this: while giving, the giver must not hold any hope that the receiver will do him some return service later on. A gift given in a spirit of sincere devotion, with no hope of any return service, after considering place and time and the worthy or unworthy recipient, is called a sāttvika gift. That is, one should give food at holy places such as sacred bathing-places and sacred fields, on principal days such as Saṅkrānti and Amāvāsyā, to a guest or visitor who comes whether invited or of his own accord. If that guest is accomplished in the study of the Veda and the śāstras, practises them, and is endowed with good conduct, that is better still; one should honour such a man with faith, attend on him with respect and the like, and give him food. If food is given to any man afflicted by hunger, and especially to guests and visitors with the qualities mentioned above, it is not only a sāttvika gift but the giver, in other births, enjoys happiness amply provided with wealth of food. This is set out here in the sentences एतद्वै मुखतोऽन्नग्ं राद्धं । मुखतोऽस्मा अन्नग्ं राज्यते (*etadvai mukhato 'nnagṃ rāddhaṃ | mukhato 'smā annagṃ rājyate*) **NOTE**. Now the second and third kinds, rājasa and tāmasa gifts, are as follows:

यत्तु प्रत्युपकारार्थं फलमुद्दिश्य वा पुनः । दीयते च परिक्लिष्टं तद्राजसमुदाहृतं ॥ (*yattu pratyupakārārthaṃ phalamuddiśya vā punaḥ | dīyate ca parikliṣṭaṃ tadrājasamudāhṛtaṃ ‖*)
ं ॥ अदेशकाले यद्दानमपात्रेभ्यश्च दीयते । असत्कृतमवज्ञातं तत्तामसमुदाहृतं ॥ (*ṃ ‖ adeśakāle yaddānamapātrebhyaśca dīyate | asatkṛtamavajñātaṃ tattāmasamudāhṛtaṃ ‖*)

The gift made by a man who gives in expectation of a return service is called a rājasa gift. For example: "If today I give food to this man, then tomorrow, or some day hereafter, he too will honour me in the same way"; a gift made with such a thought is called rājasa. Such a gift is set out here in the sentences एतद्वै मध्यतोऽन्नग्ं राद्धं । मध्यतोऽस्मा अन्नग्ं राज्यते (*etadvai madhyato 'nnagṃ rāddhaṃ | madhyato 'smā annagṃ rājyate*).

Further, a gift made without regard to place, time, or the worthy or unworthy recipient, without proper honour, merely for self-praise, is called tāmasa; that is, at a place of one's own whim, that is, at a censured place,

### Printed p. 550

at an improper time, that is, at an unseasonable time such as midnight, to an unworthy recipient, that is, one who is not troubled by hunger, has eaten up to his throat and has no need of any food, a hospitality or gift made out of vanity, so that another may see one's hospitality to guests and admire it, is called tāmasa. This is set out here in the sentences एतद्वा अंततोन्नग्ं राद्धं । अंततोऽस्या अन्नग्ं राज्यते (*etadvā aṃtatonnagṃ rāddhaṃ | aṃtato 'syā annagṃ rājyate*). Therefore, knowing all these matters well, one should give food at the right time to a fit and worthy recipient.

It is explained that a man who regards food as the form of the supreme Brahma and worships it with a certain thought obtains its fruit according to his thought. Thus: तत्प्रतिष्ठेत्युपासीत! प्रतिष्ठावान्भवति (*tatpratiṣṭhetyupāsīta! pratiṣṭhāvānbhavati*). If one worships it, thinking of it as pratiṣṭhā (support), one becomes endowed with the means of comfort such as food and clothing and possessed of standing. One who worships it as radiance (mahaḥ) becomes prosperous in wealth and the like, endowed with the qualities of greatness, and worthy of honour. One who worships it as manaḥ (mind) becomes possessed of mental power. One who worships it as namaḥ (worthy of salutation) is saluted by all and brings all under his sway. For him all desires, that is, all his wishes, come under control, that is, are fulfilled. One who worships it as Brahma comes to know the Vedas and the secrets of the truth of the Vedic meaning. For one who worships it as तद्ब्रह्मणः परिमर (*tadbrahmaṇaḥ parimara*), the enemies and afflictions around him are all destroyed. All enemies, haters and disliked persons perish completely. The one who is in this person and the one who is in the sun are Brahma alone. One who has such knowledge departs from this world, passes beyond the states of the self called annamaya, prāṇamaya, manomaya, vijñānamaya and ānandamaya, becomes a vidyādhara (that is, a deity with the power to assume whatever forms he wishes), and, enjoying his desires, roams here and there singing these (following) sāman verses. What a marvel this is! "I am food; I am the eater of food; I am the praiser; I was born before the truth (ṛta); before the gods, in the navel of immortality (in the middle), I was born. Whoever offers (food) to me becomes just like me. I am food. I eat the one who eats food. I overcome this whole world, this universe. One who knows this becomes like golden light." In this way there are many descriptions of food, or of the deity (Brahma) who is the lord of food. There are many more mantras in the Vedas containing matters concerning food; for fear of the extent of the book they cannot all be set out here.

### Printed p. 551

In this sūkta wealth and food are praised. The seer has described it in another way (by contrast). He has described, so as to touch the heart, the experience and sufferings of a beggar who, without food, famished and emaciated, wanders from door to door for alms. For describing it thus, there are sufficient grounds to guess that the seer of the sūkta himself must have undergone such an experience. Likewise, the seer Kavaṣa, son of Iluṣa, is not a Brāhmaṇa. He belonged to the Śūdra caste engaged in farming (agriculture). He used to gamble with dice, counters and the like. Having lost a great deal of property in gambling, he fell into distress without food and other provisions. His parents, relatives and brothers drove him away without admitting him to the house. The seer has described all this very well in his sūkta (the 34th sūkta of the 10th Maṇḍala). He has also described well the thoughts that arise in the minds of players as the dice roll in the game, "Shall I win or lose?"; how those who are not gamblers work hard, earn wealth and live happily; and how one engaged in farming lives happily on the crop he has grown. Once, when the seer Agastya was walking on grass, suspecting that a snake might have bitten him, he described snakes, their wicked nature, the method of removing poison and other related matters in the 191st sūkta of the 1st Maṇḍala. All these are matters described from one's own experience.

It is noteworthy that in some sūktas the name of the deity praised is also the name of the seer of that sūkta. An example is that the seer of the sūkta praising the deity Manyu (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10th Maṇḍala, sūktas 83 and 84) is a seer named Manyu, and the seer of the sūktas praising Viśvakarman (10th Maṇḍala, sūktas 81 and 82) is a seer named Viśvakarman. There are many such sūktas. Therefore it can be guessed that Bhikṣu of the Aṅgirasa line, the seer of the present sūkta, once begged alms for food, and it seems that for this very reason the name Bhikṣu came into use for him. Even if he had another name, it is not well known.

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> न वा इति नवर्चंपंचमं:सूक्तं। भिक्षुर्नामांगिरस ऋषिः । प्रथमाद्वितीये
> जगत्या शिष्टाः सप्त त्रिष्टुभः । अत्र धनस्यान्नस्य च दानं स्तूयते । अतस्तद्दैवत्यमिदं । तथा चानुक्रांतं । न वा उ भिक्षुर्धनान्नदानप्रशंसाद्ये जगत्याविति ॥ गतो
> विनियोगः ॥
> கெட்டது நல்லது

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

This is the fifth sūkta, of nine verses. The seer is Bhikṣu of the Aṅgirasa line. The first two verses are in Jagatī; the remaining seven are in Triṣṭubh. Here the giving of wealth and of food is praised, so this sūkta has that as its deity. He cites the Anukramaṇī accordingly: न वा उ भिक्षुर्धनान्नदानप्रशंसाद्ये जगत्याविति (*na vā u bhikṣurdhanānnadānapraśaṃsādye jagatyāviti*). The viniyoga has already been given.

### Printed p. 552

##### Anuvāda

This sūkta beginning "न वा (*na vā*)" is the fifth sūkta in the tenth anuvāka. It has nine ṛks. The seer of this sūkta is Bhikṣu of the Aṅgirasa gotra; its first two ṛks are in the Jagatī metre; the remaining ṛks are in the Triṣṭup metre. In this sūkta the praise of the giving of wealth and food is stated. Therefore the praise of the giving of wealth and food is the deity of this sūkta. In the Anukramaṇī it is said: न वा उ भिक्षुर्धनान्नदानप्रशंसाद्ये जगत्यौ (*na vā u bhikṣurdhanānnadānapraśaṃsādye jagatyau*). The viniyoga has been stated earlier.

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Bhikṣu first praises the giving of food by way of contrast. The gods, indeed, did not give hunger to all; they did not bestow it, but gave only death (वधमिद्वधमेव (*vadhamidvadhameva*)).

> वधरूपां क्षुधमन्नदानेन यः शमयति स दाता खलु । उ इति पूरणः । योऽदत्ता
> भुंक्ते तमाशितं भुंजानं पुरुषमपि मृत्यवो मरणान्युप गच्छंति । समापे
> यांति ॥ अशितः कर्ता! पा. ६-१-२०७ । इत्याद्युदात्तत्वं ॥ क्षुधार्तानां भोक्त्वाणां
> च मरणं समानं । किं दानेन धननाशरूपेण । अत आह । उतो । उतशब्दोऽप्यर्थे । पृणतः प्रयच्छतः पुरुषस्य रयिर्धनं नोप दस्यति । नोपक्षीयते ॥ दसु
> उपक्षये दैवादिकः । पृण दाने तौदादिकः । तस्य शत्रंतस्य शतुरनुमो नद्यजादी
> इति विभक्तेराद्युदात्तत्वं ॥ दानप्रसंगेनादातारं दूषयति । अपृणन्न प्रयच्छन्
> पुरुषस्तु मर्डितारमात्मनः सुखयितारं न विंदते । न कुत्रापि लभते । इह
> बंधवोऽप्रदानान्न सुखयंति देवा अपि हविष्पदानाभावात् ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

He who allays this hunger, which is of the nature of death, by the giving of food is truly a giver. उ (*u*) is an expletive. Deaths approach even the man who has eaten (आशितं (*āśitaṃ*)), who enjoys without giving. The death of those afflicted by hunger and of those who only eat is alike; what is the use of giving, which amounts to loss of wealth? Hence he says उतो (*uto*): the word उत (*uta*) is in the sense of "also". The wealth (रयिः (*rayiḥ*)) of a man who fills (पृणतः (*pṛṇataḥ*)), that is, gives, does not waste away (नोप दस्यति (*nopa dasyati*), does not diminish). Incidentally to the matter of giving, he censures the non-giver: the man who does not fill, that is, does not give, does not find one who makes him happy (मर्डितारं (*marḍitāraṃ*)); he gets him nowhere. Here relatives do not make him happy because of his non-giving, and the gods too, for lack of the gift of oblations.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- देवाः वै (*devāḥ vai*)—the gods (to all)
- क्षुधं (*kṣudhaṃ*)—hunger (the affliction of hunger)
- न ददुः (*na daduḥ*)—did not give; but,
- वधं इत् (*vadhaṃ it*)—gave only death
- उत (*uta*)—and
- आशितं (*āśitaṃ*)—even the man who has eaten food
- मृत्यवः (*mṛtyavaḥ*)—deaths
- उप गच्छंति (*upa gacchaṃti*)—approach
- उतो (*uto*)—moreover
- पृणतः (*pṛṇataḥ*)—of the man who gives
- रयिः (*rayiḥ*)—wealth
- न उप दस्यति (*na upa dasyati*)—does not diminish
- उत (*uta*)—and
- अपृणन् (*apṛṇan*)—the man who gives nothing to anyone
- मर्डितारं (*marḍitāraṃ*)—another man who would bring him happiness (or good)
- न विंदते (*na viṃdate*)—does not obtain

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

When the gods created human beings, they did not ordain that they should suffer from hunger, or the affliction of hunger, and that as a result of that affliction they should meet death. Even a man who, not knowing what the burning of hunger is, is always eating food well becomes subject to death. Moreover, for a man who gives wealth or food his wealth does not diminish. But for a miserly man who never gives anything to anyone, neither happiness nor help is obtained from anyone.

##### English translation
The gods have not assigned hunger as (the cause of) death, for deaths approach the man who has eaten; the riches of one who gives do not diminish, he who gives not finds no consoler.

### Printed p. 554

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

When the gods created human beings, they laid down the rule that however long people may live, each must die one day in the end. But they did not ordain that anyone should die for lack of food and the like. For even a man who is never short of food, who always eats as much as he likes and lives in comfort, must still fall under the power of death by some other cause. It is true that one dies if there is no food, but this is not a divine ordinance. By some means or other a man can earn his food and live. So if a man dies without food, it is not divinely appointed; the cause is that he was unable to earn his food. Death shows no partiality, saying "this man is fasting without food, while that one eats as he wishes." Whether there is food or not, all must fall under the power of death. Therefore, so as not to fall under death's power, a man must earn his food by his own effort. He must give up the foolish belief that death caused by lack of food is divinely ordained, and earn his own food himself.

If a man, for some reason, is unable to earn his own food (grain), he may obtain it by begging from others. In that case, does the giver not lose by giving food or wealth to the one who begs? Certainly not. For in return for the small part he gives, immense merit accrues to him. By this meritorious act he becomes worthy of the gods' favour and obtains wealth many times what he gave. Besides, through the help he gives he gains many friends and well-wishers. But as for the miser who never gives anyone any kind of gift or food, no one wishes him well. He has no friends. How could others help, in his time of trouble, one who has never helped another with food, gifts and the like? Therefore, for his own benefit, welfare and acquisition of merit, one must help (with food and the like) another who is in distress; this is the view the seer has expressed.

> लभते ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

The man who, though himself possessed of food, hardens his mind against one who is weak (आध्र (*ādhra*), "feeble", from अधार्यते (*adhāryate*)) and desires food (पित्वः (*pitvaḥ*), foods), who is afflicted (रफित (*raphita*), from रफति (*raphati*), to harm) by poverty and has come to his house — that is, he fixes his mind firmly on not giving; thereby he torments the beggar. Nor is that all: पुरा (*purā*), before him, he enjoys his own food. Such a man finds no one who gladdens him (मर्डितारं (*marḍitāraṃ*)) — he gets none anywhere. The rest of the block gives the derivation of कृणुते (*kṛṇute*) and its accent.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- यः (*yaḥ*)—which man
- अन्नवान् सन् (*annavān san*)—though himself possessed of food
- आध्राय (*ādhrāya*)—to the feeble one who deserves help
- पित्वः (*pitvaḥ*)—food
- चकमानाय (*cakamānāya*)—to one who is begging
- रफिताय (*raphitāya*)—to one who is afflicted by the burning of poverty
- उपजग्मुषे (*upajagmuṣe*)—to the guest who has come to his house, that is, in the matter of the guest
- मनः (*manaḥ*)—his mind, (resolving) "nothing must be given to this man"
- स्थिरं कुरुते (*sthiraṃ kurute*)—makes firm
- उतो (*uto*)—and
- पुरा चित् (*purā cit*)—even before giving to the guest, or in front of him
- सेवते (*sevate*)—he himself eats the food
- नः (*naḥ*)—that man
- मर्डितारं (*marḍitāraṃ*)—one who brings him happiness
- न विंदते (*na viṃdate*)—does not find

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

The man who, though he has as much food as he needs, hardens his heart without pity towards a guest who is helpless, worn out by poverty and has come to his house begging for food, firmly resolving to give him nothing, and who eats before giving food

### Printed p. 556

to the man who begs of him — for that man no one shows compassion. No one wishes that he may be happy.

##### English translation
He who, possessed of food, hardens his heart against the feeble man craving nourishment, against the sufferer comming to him (for help), and pursues (his own enjoyment even) before him, that man finds no consoler.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

In this Ṛk the nature of the miser who gives no food (or wealth) is described. The meaning is clear, so no further explanation is needed. The main point is this: no one wishes welfare or happiness for such a miser — the man who, though he has food enough to eat his fill and to give to others, gives to no one; who eats without giving food to a guest or visitor who has come to him, or eats before they have eaten; who, though a man worn out by poverty and hunger comes begging at his door, gives him nothing.

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

He praises by the positive way. He alone is भोजः (*bhojaḥ*), a liberal giver, who gives to the गृहवे (*gṛhave*) (the word is formed with the affix ku, from *graheḥ*, by the rule मृगय्यादित्वात् (*mṛgayyāditvāt*), Uṇ. Sū. 1-38), that is, to the recipient, who desires food (अन्नकामाय (*annakāmāya*)), asking for food, who has come about to his house (चरते (*carate*)), who is lean (कृशाय (*kṛśāya*)) through poverty — to such a guest he gives food. The accent of ददाति (*dadāti*) is initial-acute by the rule on reduplicated forms. यामहूत् (*yāmahūt*):

### Printed p. 557

यामा (*yāmā*) are the gods who come; here the affix man is added by the Uṇādi rule beginning यातेरर्तिस्तुसुहुसृ (*yāterartistusuhusṛ*) (Uṇ. Sū. 1-139). यामहूति (*yāmahūti*) is the sacrifice, where they are invoked. In it, for this giver, the fruit is अरं (*araṃ*), ample, sufficient; that is, his desires are fulfilled. उतापि चापरीषु (*utāpi cāparīṣu*): the form is made with जीप् (*jīp*) (Pā. Sū. 4-1-30 **NOTE**); among others, among hostile armies, he makes a friend; that is, he behaves like one. All are his friends, none are enemies.

> देवाः ॥ अत्र यातेरर्तिस्तुसुहुसृ । उ. १-१३९ । इत्यादिना मन्प्रत्ययः ॥ त आहूयंतेऽत्रेति यामहूतिर्यज्ञः । तस्मिन्नस्मै दात्रे फलमरमलं पर्याप्तं भवति ।

> सखाय एव न शत्रव इत्यर्थः ॥

- गृहवे (*gṛhave*)—who accepts it if given

- भोजः (*bhojaḥ*)—is called a giver of food
- यामहूत् (*yāmahūt*)—in the sacrifice
- अस्मै (*asmai*)—for this giver of food, the fruit of performing the sacrifice
- अरं (*araṃ*)—quickly
- भवति (*bhavati*)—is obtained

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

(In this Ṛk the giver of food is praised.) The man who gives food to a poor guest or beggar who has come to his house, lean for want of food and asking for it, is the true giver of food. In the sacrifice, such a giver of food quickly obtains the fruit of performing the sacrifice. In the case of this giver of food, even his enemies become friends. He has no enemies; all are his friends.

##### English translation
He is liberal who gives to the suppliant desiring food, wandering about distressed ; to him there is an ample (recompense), and he contracts friendship with his adversaries.

> अपा॑स्मा॒त्प्रेया॒न्न तदोको॑ अस्ति पृ॒णंत॑म॒न्यमर॑णं चिदिच्छेत् ॥ ४ ॥

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> व्यतिरेकेण निंदामाह । स पुरुषः सखा न भवति यः पुरुषः सचाभुवे

> गतौ । लिजि यासुट् ॥ तर्हि तदोको निवासः सदनं नास्ति । न भवति । सदनं हि

> स्वामिनमेवेच्छेत् । कामयेत ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

He states the censure by the negative way. That man is no friend who does not give food (पित्वः (*pitvaḥ*), foods) to a friend (सख्ये (*sakhye*)) who is सचाभुवे (*sacābhuve*), always accompanying him, सचमानाय (*sacamānāya*), serving him, subordinate to him. He is no true friend. From this non-giving friend one should go away (अप प्रेयात् (*apa preyāt*)), if one leaves him and goes (root इण् (*iṇ*) in the sense of going; यासुट् (*yāsuṭ*) in the optative). Then तदोकः (*tadokaḥ*), that dwelling, is not a dwelling: a dwelling is one surrounded by kinsmen. The one who has gone should seek (इच्छेत् (*icchet*), should desire) another master, अरणं चित् (*araṇaṃ cit*), who gives food and the like (पृणंतं (*pṛṇaṃtaṃ*)).

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- यः (*yaḥ*)—which man
- सचाभुवे (*sacābhuve*)—who is always with him
- सचमानाय (*sacamānāya*)—who follows him, or is his well-wisher
- सख्यॆ (*sakhyè*)—to his friend
- पित्वः (*pitvaḥ*)—food
- न ददाति (*na dadāti*)—does not give
- सः (*saḥ*)—that man
- न सखा (*na sakhā*)—is no friend at all
- अस्मात् (*asmāt*)—from such a man who gives no food (one who merely pretends to be a friend in name)
- अप प्रेयात् (*apa preyāt*)—one must go far away
- तदोकः (*tadokaḥ*)—the house of such a man
- न अस्ति (*na asti*)—does not count as a house (therefore the one who begs for food)
- पृणंतं (*pṛṇaṃtaṃ*)—who gives food and the like
- अन्यं अरणं (*anyaṃ araṇaṃ*)—another master
- इच्छेत् (*icchet*)—must go and seek

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

The man who does not give food to a friend who is always with him, follows him and wishes only his good, is not a true friend at all. One who needs food should leave such a man and go to another man who gives food.

### Printed p. 559

##### English translation
He is not a friend who gives not food to a friend, to an associate, to
a companion ; let him turn away from him, that is not a (fitting) dwelling;
let him seek another more liberal lord.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

In this Ṛk the censure of the man who gives no food, and the duty and qualities of a friend, are described. A friend is one who wishes one's good. For the word सखायः (*sakhāyaḥ*), which means friends, Yāska gives the etymology सहमदनं समानख्यानाः (*sahamadanaṃ samānakhyānāḥ*) (Ni. 7-30). That is: friends are those who rejoice together, the joy of one being the joy of the other, who are mutually glad; and समानख्यानाः (*samānakhyānāḥ*) means those who speak in one way — those whose views agree with one another in the same manner are called friends. In worldly usage too the marks of friends are stated thus:
ददाति प्रतिगृह्णाति गुह्यमाख्याति पृच्छति । भुंक्ते च भोजयत्येव षड्विधं मित्रलक्षणं ॥ (*dadāti pratigṛhṇāti guhyamākhyāti pṛcchati | bhuṃkte ca bhojayatyeva ṣaḍvidhaṃ mitralakṣaṇaṃ ‖*)
Where there are two friends, giving to one another, accepting what is given, telling and asking one another secrets (matters kept hidden), eating in one another's house, and one who has eaten making the other eat as well — these six are said to be the marks of friends. Taking the matter of food in the present context, mutual eating and feeding are said to be a mark of friendship. Without dealings in food there is no friendship. That is, if a man, for some reason, is without food and tormented by hunger, and his friend, though he has food, does not give it to him, that friendship is not true friendship; it is feigned and self-interested. However much friends may differ in opinion in other matters, when one is hungry without food, the one who is called his friend must help. This is the true duty of friendship. Therefore the seer describes that one should leave the man who gives no food to a friend in time of trouble, who merely pretends to be a friend, who is a miser, and take refuge in another man who is worthy, a giver of food, and a helper in time of trouble.

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> धनवंतं पुरुषं दाने प्रेरयति । तव्यांस्तवीयान्धनैरतिशयेन प्रवृद्धः
> पुरुषो नाधमानाय याचमानायातिथये पृणीयादित् । धनानि दद्यादेव ॥

> दीर्घशब्दादीयसुनि प्रियस्थिरेत्यादिना द्राघीत्यादेशः ॥ दीर्घतमं पंथां पंथानं
> सुकृतमार्गमनु पश्येत । अनुपश्येत् ॥ व्यत्ययेनात्मनेपदं । तत्र कारणमाह ।
> रायो धनान्यो हि । आ उ । आवर्तंते खलु। एकत्र न तिष्ठंतीत्यर्थः। तत्र दृष्टांतः।
> रथ्येव यथा रथ्यानि ॥ रथाद्यत् । पा. ४-३-१२१ । इति तस्येदमित्यर्थे यत् ॥ रथसंबंधीनि चक्राण्युपर्यधोभावेनावर्तंते तद्वदावृत्तिमेव दर्शयति । अन्यमन्यं
> पुरुषं धनान्युप तिष्ठंत । उपतिष्ठंते । समवेतानि भवंति ॥ उपाद्देवपूजासंगतिकरणेति । का. १-३-२५-१ । आत्मनेपदं ॥ तस्माद्भनानि देयानीति भावः ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Sāyaṇa says that the verse urges a wealthy man to give. A man greatly grown in wealth should not fail to satisfy a petitioning guest; he should certainly give his riches. If he gives, he will look forward to the longest path, that is, the path of good deeds. The reason is that riches turn from one to another and do not stay in one place. The illustration: as the wheels belonging to a chariot turn, one above and then below, so riches keep recurring, going to one man after another and attending him. Therefore, he concludes, wealth should be given.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- तव्यान् (*tavyān*)—the man grown great in wealth
- नाधमानाय (*nādhamānāya*)—to the guest (or beggar) who is asking
- पृणीयात् इत् (*pṛṇīyāt it*)—must give wealth and the like (if he gives thus, that man)
- द्राघीयांसं (*drāghīyāṃsaṃ*)—long
- पंथां (*paṃthāṃ*)—the best path, that is, progressive increase
- अनु पश्यत (*anu paśyata*)—will surely look forward to (because)
- रायः (*rāyaḥ*)—riches, wealth and the like
- रथ्येव चक्रा (*rathyeva cakrā*)—like the wheels of a chariot
- ओ हि वर्तंते (*o hi vartaṃte*)—keep moving (those riches)
- अन्यमन्यं (*anyamanyaṃ*)—from one man to another
- उप तिष्ठंत (*upa tiṣṭhaṃta*)—go and settle

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

A rich man endowed with wealth must give wealth and the like to the guest who asks him. If he gives thus, his riches will increase further and further. For riches, like a chariot wheel, do not stand fixed in one place but pass from one man to another and settle there.

### Printed p. 561

##### English translation
Let the very rich man satisfy his suitor, let him look forward to a more protracted route, for riches revolve from one man to another, as the wheels of a chariot turn round.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

Here the seer explains why a wealthy man should give, what benefit comes from giving, and what is lost by not giving. When a man is rich and in favourable circumstances, it is the duty of every person to help with wealth and the like a poor man who asks him, in order to relieve his distress. As to the benefit of giving: by helping the deserving with wealth, the rich man's wealth is not lost, that is, it does not diminish. It will increase even more than it is now, and he will attain a still better state. If he does not give, what is the loss? Riches are not permanent. The wealth that is with him today goes tomorrow to another. A man in favourable circumstances today may fall into a low state tomorrow, and likewise a man in a low state may rise to a better one. As, when a chariot wheel turns, the lower part comes up and at once the upper part comes down, so wealth too does not stay always with one man but settles among different people. The destitute becomes rich; the rich becomes destitute. Hence the main sense is that when in favourable circumstances the rich man does well to help the poor with wealth and gain merit and welfare.

> अदातारं दूषयति । अप्रचेता अप्रकृष्टज्ञानः दाने चेतो मनो यस्य
> न भवति स मोघं व्यर्थमेवान्नं विंदते । लभते ॥ विद्ल लाभे तौदादिकः । शे

> उपलक्षणमिदं । सर्वान्देवानर्यमादीन्न पुष्यति हविष्ट्रदानेन न पोषयति नो
> नापि सखायं समानख्यानमभ्यागतमतिथिं मित्रवर्गं च न पोषयति ॥ पुष पुष्पौ
> दैवादिकः । यच्छब्दाध्याहारादनिघातः ॥ अत एव केवलादी ॥ अदेः सुप्यजातौ ।
> पा. ३-२-७८ । इति णिनिः । आत उपधालक्षणावृद्धिः ॥ केवलमसाक्षिकमन्नं भुंजानः स
> केवलाघो भवति । केवलपापवान्भवति । अघमेव केवलं तस्य शिष्यते । ऐहिकामुष्मिकमिति । तस्माद्यथाकथंचिद्दातव्यमित्यभिप्रायः ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Sāyaṇa censures the non-giver. The man who is अप्रचेताः (*apracetāḥ*), of undeveloped understanding, whose mind is not set on giving, obtains food in vain. The seer says: "I speak this as true." It is not merely useless; for that man it is his very slaying, वध इत् (*vadha it*), the word "that" (स (*sa*)) referring to the food and taking the masculine gender by agreement with वध (*vadha*). Alternatively: he is a worthless slaying who does not nourish Aryaman. This is indicative: he does not nourish with offerings all the gods beginning with Aryaman, nor a friend, that is, a guest who has come, nor the circle of his friends. Hence he is केवलादी (*kevalādī*), one who eats alone. Eating food without a witness, he becomes केवलाघः (*kevalāghaḥ*), wholly sinful; only sin remains to him, nothing of this world or the next. The intention is that one must give in whatever way one can.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- अप्रचेताः (*apracetāḥ*)—the unintelligent one who has no mind for giving food
- सः (*saḥ*)—that man
- मोघं (*moghaṃ*)—vain
- अन्नं (*annaṃ*)—food
- विंदते (*viṃdate*)—has obtained
- सत्यं (*satyaṃ*)—that this is true
- ब्रवीमि (*bravīmi*)—I say
- तस्य (*tasya*)—of that man (the food)
- स वध इत् (*sa vadha it*)—is for him like death itself
- यः (*yaḥ*)—the man who
- अर्यमणं (*aryamaṇaṃ*)—Aryaman and all the gods
- न पुष्यति (*na puṣyati*)—does not nourish with offerings and the like
- सखायं (*sakhāyaṃ*)—his friend and his circle of friends
- नो (*no*)—does not nourish with gifts of food and the like (and) the man who
- केवलादी (*kevalādī*)—sits and eats by himself with no companion
- केवलाघः (*kevalāghaḥ*)—becomes very sinful

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

The food of a man who has no mind to give food is in vain. I say this truly. The food that such a man has is itself death-like for him. The man who does not honour and nourish Aryaman and the other gods with offerings and the like, who does not nourish his friend with gifts of food, who at his meal takes no one as companion but eats alone, becomes very sinful.

### Printed p. 563

##### English translation
The inhospitable man acquires food in vain. I speak the truth—it verily is his death. He cherishes not Aryaman nor a friend; he who eats alone is nothing but a sinner.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

In explaining the section that Ṛks have various kinds according to sense, Yāska, as an example of a Ṛk that points to censure, gives the explanation of the phrase केवलाघो भवति केवलादी (*kevalāgho bhavati kevalādī*) of this Ṛk (Ni. 7-3). There is a householder's rule that at meals he should welcome and honour guests and visitors and eat only after they have eaten. Here a guest may be any man or animal tormented by hunger. In giving food there is no distinction of woman and man, nor of caste such as Brahmin. The Purāṇas and other works say that any man or animal oppressed by hunger is fit to receive food, and that among gifts the gift of food is the best. Therefore the seer explains in this Ṛk that one should not sit and eat alone, and that if one does so, great sin arises.

### Printed p. 564

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> वदञ्ञास्त्रार्थं ब्रुवाणो ब्रह्मा ब्राह्मणोऽवदतः शास्त्रार्थमब्रुवानाज्जनाद्वनीयान् । संभक्तृतमः प्रियकरो भवति ॥ वनतेस्तृजंतस्येयसुनि तुरिष्ठेमेयः
> स्थिति तृचो लोपः ॥ ते यथा स्वकर्मणि प्रवर्तमानाः परेषामुपकारकाः तथा
> पृणन् दाता पुरुषोऽपृणंतमदातारं जनमभ्यभिलक्ष्यापिः स्यात् । बंधुर्भवेत् ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

The Brahmin who speaks, expounding the meaning of the śāstra, is more worthy of service (वनीयान् (*vanīyān*)), more beloved, than the person who does not expound the meaning of the śāstra. As these, acting in their own work, are helpful to others, so the giver, पृणन् (*pṛṇan*), looking towards the non-giver, the person who does not give, should be a kinsman (आपिः (*āpiḥ*)).

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- कृषन् (*kṛṣan*)—doing cultivation (agriculture), that is, ploughing the earth
- फालः (*phālaḥ*)—the plough
- आशितं (*āśitaṃ*)—makes the cultivating farmer eat food
- कृणोति (*kṛṇoti*)—makes (likewise)
- अध्वानं (*adhvānaṃ*)—the road
- यन् (*yan*)—the man who goes, passing over it
- चरित्रॆः (*caritrèḥ*)—by his travelling
- अप वृंक्ते (*apa vṛṃkte*)—earns and gives wealth to his master
- वदन् (*vadan*)—who knows and tells the meaning of the śāstra (the Veda)
- ब्रह्मा (*brahmā*)—the Brahmin
- अवदतः (*avadataḥ*)—than a Brahmin who does not know the meaning of the śāstra (the Veda)
- वनीयान् (*vanīyān*)—is held better
- पृणन् (*pṛṇan*)—the giver, that is, one who helps others
- अप्पणंतं अभि (*appaṇaṃtaṃ abhi*)—towards the miser who does not give
- आपि स्यात् (*āpi syāt*)—let him be a kinsman

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

For the cultivating farmer his plough provides food. The servant who travels for his master's work helps his lord to gain wealth. The Brahmin who knows the meaning of the Veda and tells it to others is better than a Brahmin who does not know it. Let the benefactor-giver be a kinsman to the miser who does not give; that is, let the non-giving miser take on the giver's quality and become like him.

##### English translation
The ploughshare furrowing (the field) provides food (for the plough-man); a man travelling along a road aquires (wealth for his master) by his movements; a Brahman expounding (the Veda) is better than one not expounding it; (so) let the man who gives become a kinsman to the man who gives not.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

The matters in this Ṛk are described by the seer through some illustrations: that the giver is better than the miser who does not give, and that the miser should take on the giver's quality and do good to others as he does. But those illustrations or comparisons do not fit the context. Even so, they indicate a kind of moral, that a good thing is better than a bad one.

### Printed p. 565
The plough, the instrument of cultivation, provides food for the cultivator; this is known in the world. The lazy man who does not cultivate suffers without food. So the cultivator is better than the non-cultivator. In the same way the giver is better than the miser who does not give. The man who goes where he must go for his master's work and toils for him becomes the cause of his master's prosperity; that is, the one who toils gets the fruit of it. The one who does not toil gets no gain. So the toiling man is better than the idle one who does no work. In the same way the giving man is better than the miser who does not give.

The Brahmin who has the ability to know and tell the meaning of the Vedas and śāstras is better than a man who knows nothing, that is, an unlearned man. In the same way the giver is better than the miser who does not give.

Therefore "let the giver be a kinsman to the miser who does not give": the seer expresses the assurance that the giver's good qualities may come to the miser too, so that he also may give gifts and the like to others, help them, and be devoted to doing good to others.
