##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> उरुव्यचा विस्तीर्णव्यापनो महिषो महान्ज्यो ना पुरुहूतो बहुभिर्यजमानैराहूतः पुरुक्षुर्बहुनिवासः ॥ क्षियतेर्मितद्वादिभ्य उपसंख्यानं ।
> पा. ३-२-१८०-१ । इति डुप्रत्ययः ॥ यद्वा। पुरुभिर्बहुभिः शब्द्यमानः स्तूयमानः ॥
> पूर्ववड्डु प्रत्ययः । औणादिके कर्मणि क्विपि वानित्यमागमशासनमिति तुगभावः ॥
> ईदृश इंद्रोऽस्मिन्हवे यज्ञे ! हूयंतेऽस्मिन्हवींषीति हवो यज्ञः ॥ जुहोतेs
> रधिकरणेऽप् ॥ यद्वा! अस्मिन्हवे त्वद्विषय आह्वाने ॥ भावेनुपसर्गस्यॆति ह्वयतेरप् संप्रसारणं च ॥ नोऽस्मभ्यं शर्म सुखं यंसत् । यच्छतु । ददात्वित्यर्थः ॥
> यमेर्लॆट्यडामः । सिब्बहुलमिति सिप् ॥ हे हर्यश्व हरी आश्वा यस्य तादृश हे
> इंद्र स त्वं नोऽस्माकं प्रजायै । द्वितीयार्थे चतुर्थि । प्रजां पुत्रपौत्रादिकां
> मृळॆय । सुखयॆ । नोऽस्मान्मा रीरिषः । मा हिंसीः । मा च परा दाः । परादानं
> परित्यागः । मा परित्याक्षीरित्यर्थः ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

उरुव्यचा (*uruvyacā*) means "pervading widely". महिषः (*mahiṣaḥ*) means "great". पुरुहूतः (*puruhūtaḥ*) means "called by many sacrificers". पुरुक्षुः (*purukṣuḥ*) means "of many dwellings". The affix ḍu is added here by Pā. 3-2-180-1. Alternatively, पुरुक्षुः (*purukṣuḥ*) means "praised (शब्द्यमानः (*śabdyamānaḥ*)) by many". The affix is added as in the earlier case. In the Uṇādi usage, where kvip comes after a karman, the augment is optional, so there is no tuk. Such an Indra, in this हवे (*have*) (the sacrifice, in which oblations are offered), is to be understood. Alternatively, अस्मिन् हवे (*asmin have*) means "in this invocation directed to you". नः (*naḥ*) is "to us". May he grant (यंसत् (*yaṃsat*) = यच्छतु (*yacchatu*), *dadātu*) शर्म (*śarma*), happiness. "O Indra, whose horses are the two bays (हरी (*harī*)), you, for our offspring (the dative stands in the sense of the accusative) — our sons, grandsons and the rest — make them happy. Do not harm us (मा रीरिषः (*mā rīriṣaḥ*) = मा हिंसीः (*mā hiṃsīḥ*)). And do not abandon (मा परा दाः (*mā parā dāḥ*)); परादानं (*parādānaṃ*) is abandonment, so the meaning is: do not forsake us."

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- उरुव्यचाः (*uruvyacāḥ*)—one who pervades all places
- महिषः (*mahiṣaḥ*)—one of great nature, or the worshipful
- पुरुहूतः (*puruhūtaḥ*)—one who is prayed to and called by many sacrificers
- पुरुक्षुः (*purukṣuḥ*)—one who has many dwelling places, or who goes to the dwellings of many (the sacrificial houses), or who is praised by many people; (this is) Indra
- अस्मिन् हवे (*asmin have*)—in this sacrifice
- नः (*naḥ*)—to us
- शर्म (*śarma*)—happiness
- यंसत् (*yaṃsat*)—may he give
- हर्यश्व (*haryaśva*)—one accompanied by the horses called Hari
- इंद्र (*iṃdra*)—O Indra
- सः (*saḥ*)—you
- नः (*naḥ*)—to us
- प्रजाय्कॆ (*prajāykè*)—giving offspring, sons, grandsons and so on
- मृळय (*mṛḷaya*)—bring happiness
- नः (*naḥ*)—us
- मा रीरिषः (*mā rīriṣaḥ*)—do not harm
- मा परा दाः (*mā parā dāḥ*)—do not abandon us

### Printed p. 743

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

May Indra — all-pervading, worshipful or of great majesty, worthy of the invocation of many, possessing many dwellings or praised by many — bring us happiness in this sacrifice. That is: may he cause the sacrifice to be completed without any obstacle, and make the happiness that is the fruit of the sacrifice come to us. O Indra, accompanied by your two horses called Hari, give us offspring such as sons, and make us live happily. Do not harm us, and do not abandon us.

##### English translation
May the omnipresent (Indra), the mighty one, who is invoked by many, and lauded by many, bestow a blessing on this our sacrifice; be gracious to our offspring, Indra, lord of bay horses; harm us not, desert us not.

##### ॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)

> वस॑वो रु॒द्रा आ॑दि॒त्या उ॑परि॒स्पृशं॑ मो॒ग्रं चेत्ता॑रमधिरा॒जम॑क्रन् ॥ ९ ॥

> ये । नः । सपत्नाः । अपे । ते । भवंतु । इंद्राग्निभ्यां । अव । बाधामहे । तान् ।  
> वसवः । रुद्राः । आदित्याः । उपरिस्पृशं । मा । उग्रं । चेत्तारं । अधिराजं ।  
> अक्रन् ॥ ९ ॥

### Printed p. 744

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> नोऽस्माकं ये सपत्नाः शत्रवस्तेऽप भवंतु । अपगता भवंतु । स्वस्थानादपगताः प्रच्युता भवंतु । तान्सपत्नानिंद्राग्निभ्यां हविर्भिः स्तुत्या च प्रसन्नाभ्यामनु
> गृहीता वयमन बाधामहे । निकृष्टतरं विनाशयामः । अपि च वसवो रुद्रा
> आदित्याश्च मा मामुपरिस्पृशमुन्नतपदस्य संस्पष्टारं सर्वेभ्यः श्रेष्ठमक्रन् ।
> कुर्वंतु । तथोग्रमुद्दूर्णबलं चेत्तारं चेतितारं ॥ छांदस इडभावः ॥ सर्वस्य
> ज्ञातारमधिराजं सर्वेषामधीश्वरं च मां कुर्वंतु ॥ करोतेश्छांदसे लुजि
> मंत्रे घसेत्यादिना चेर्लुक् ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

नः (*naḥ*) is "our". Those who are our rivals (सपत्नाः (*sapatnāḥ*), enemies), let them be gone (अप भवंतु (*apa bhavaṃtu*)): let them be driven away and dislodged from their own place. We, favoured by Indra and Agni, who are pleased by oblations and praise, drive those rivals down (अव बाधामहे (*ava bādhāmahe*)), that is, destroy them utterly. Moreover, may the Vasus, Rudras and Ādityas make me (मा (*mā*)) उपरिस्पृशं (*uparispṛśaṃ*), one who touches the high position, the best of all. Likewise उग्रं (*ugraṃ*), of surging strength; चेत्तारं (*cettāraṃ*) (= चेतितारं (*cetitāraṃ*), the absence of the augment iṭ being Vedic), the knower of all; and अधिराजं (*adhirājaṃ*), the lord over all — may they make me these.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- नः (*naḥ*)—our
- ये सपत्नाः (*ye sapatnāḥ*)—whatever enemies there are
- ते (*te*)—they
- अप भवंतु (*apa bhavaṃtu*)—let them be defeated and go away
- तान् (*tān*)—those enemies
- इंद्राग्निभ्यां (*iṃdrāgnibhyāṃ*)—with the help of Indra and Agni
- अव बाधामहे (*ava bādhāmahe*)—may we be able to harm and destroy (them); and
- वसवः (*vasavaḥ*)—the eight Vasus
- रुद्राः (*rudrāḥ*)—the eleven Rudras
- आदित्याः (*ādityāḥ*)—the twelve Ādityas also
- मां (*māṃ*)—me
- उपरिस्पृशं (*uparispṛśaṃ*)—one fit for a high position, or the best of all
- उग्रं (*ugraṃ*)—one possessed of great strength
- चेत्तारं (*cettāraṃ*)—all-knowing
- अधिराजं (*adhirājaṃ*)—lord of all
- अक्रन् (*akran*)—let them make

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

May our enemies be defeated by us and go away backwards. Praising Indra and Agni with oblations and the like, may we, with their help, harm and destroy those enemies of ours. May the eight Vasus, the eleven Rudras and the twelve Ādityas also make us worthy of a high position or the best of all, possessed of great strength, all-knowing, and lord of all.

##### English translation
May those who are our foes be driven off ; may we through Indra and Agni destroy them; may the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Adityas make me the high-reaching, fierce, intelligent, supreme ruler.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

### Printed p. 749

## Sūkta 129 (Maṇḍala 10)

The one hundred and twenty-ninth sūkta.

**Introduction**

The present sūkta describes the state that existed before creation. It then indicates how creation began. Among the sūktas that describe creation, the chief ones are Maṇḍala 10, sūktas 81, 82, 90, 129, 130 and 190. These sūktas are the basis of the principles and Vedāntic topics stated in the Upaniṣads and the Vedānta works. On their basis the Upaniṣads that describe the Supreme Brahman, and chiefly the ten principal Upaniṣads, were composed. In these Upaniṣads the nature of Brahman, the non-existent (asat) and the existent (sat), Prakṛti and Puruṣa, the Self and the Supreme Self, the state before the creation of the world, the cause of its creation afterwards, the course of creation, its continuance, its dissolution and similar matters are described in many ways. To explain them all at length would require many separate books, so it is not possible to do so here. Only the matters that belong to the present context will be examined, as the context requires.

When the seer describes the state before creation, he asks: what was Brahman like, which pervaded everything? The worlds of earth, atmosphere, heaven and the rest, which are now seen, did not exist. What, then, filled all that? There was neither death nor deathlessness, neither day nor night. Nothing existed except Brahman, whose nature is consciousness. Deep darkness covered everything. Water filled every place. Then in that Supreme Brahman the desire of tapas, or meditation (resolve), arose. That desire is the original cause of the creation of the world. How the manifest existent came from the unmanifest non-existent, and what relation there is between the non-existent and the existent, the seers found out by their meditation. Their meditation went further still. They learned what the cause of the world is.

### Printed p. 750

They learned that the enjoyer is greater than the object of enjoyment. Yet who knows this creation, its cause, its states and its destruction? The gods too had not yet been created at that time; they were created afterwards. How, then, can they know the state that existed before their own creation? Only the Supreme Brahman, from whom the world and the rest arose, knows the secret of creation. Others do not know it. If there is anyone who knows it, it is that Supreme Brahman and no one else. If even he does not know, who else should know? No one knows. Thus the seer expresses his doubt.

This sūkta has 7 Ṛks. In the first 2 Ṛks and in the first half of the third, the state before the creation of the world is described. In the second half of the third Ṛk and in the fourth Ṛk it is said that the cause of the creation of the world is the Supreme Self's desire in the form of tapas (meditation). The resolve to create is the seed, that is, the fundamental cause, of the creation of the world. At the end of the fourth Ṛk it is said that the seers found by the path of their meditation the relation between sat and asat, and, in the fifth Ṛk, the seed of the world, and that the Supreme Self, the enjoyer, is greater than the world and the rest, which are objects of enjoyment. In the sixth Ṛk the question is: who indeed knows the particulars of this creation? Do the gods know? Since they too had not then come into being, they have no reason to know it. How should those who came into being later know what came before? Such is the description. In the seventh Ṛk: only he from whom this world and the rest arose knows its secret; he certainly knows it. If he should say that he too does not know, who else should know? The seer thus states plainly that no one knows.

It has been said that the present sūkta contains an account of the state before creation. After that creation proceeds. Then comes continuance: the created world and the rest remain for some time in that state. Afterwards they are destroyed and return to the very state in which they were before creation. After some time, from that same state, creation, continuance and destruction (dissolution) take place again. That is, creation, continuance and dissolution do not occur only once. Like the turning of a wheel, one follows another without interruption. Therefore the state before the creation of the world described here has occurred many times in the past and will occur again. Creation, continuance, dissolution and the state after dissolution go on countless times, one after another. This has neither beginning nor end. Among those countless states, the state described here is only one that occurred once. Since all of them are of one kind, describing the one that occurred once amounts to describing all.

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

In the eleventh anuvāka there are twenty-three sūktas. Of these, the first is the seven-Ṛk sūkta beginning नासदासीत् (*nāsadāsīt*), in the Triṣṭubh metre. The seer is the Prajāpati named Parameṣṭhin. Since the origin, continuance and dissolution of ether and the other elements are set forth here, their maker, the Supreme Self, is the deity. He cites the Anukramaṇī: नासत्सप्त प्रजापतिः परमेष्ठि भाववृत्तं त्विति (*nāsatsapta prajāpatiḥ parameṣṭhi bhāvavṛttaṃ tviti*). The viniyoga has already been given.

##### Anuvāda

In the eleventh anuvāka of the tenth maṇḍala there are twenty-three sūktas in all. Among them this sūkta, नासदासीत् (*nāsadāsīt*), is the first; it has seven Ṛks. The seer of this sūkta is the Prajāpati known by the name Parameṣṭhin. Because this sūkta sets forth the elements such as ether and their creation, continuance and dissolution, the Supreme Self, their creator, is the deity of this sūkta. In the Anukramaṇī it is said: नासत्सप्तः प्रजापतिः परमेष्ठि भाववृत्तं तु (*nāsatsaptaḥ prajāpatiḥ parameṣṭhi bhāvavṛttaṃ tu*). The viniyoga was stated earlier.

Sūkta 128. Maṇḍala 10; Anuvāka 11; Sūkta 129; Aṣṭaka 8; Adhyāya 7; Varga 17. Number of Ṛks in the sūkta: 7. Seer: Prajāpati Parameṣṭhin. Deity: Bhāvavṛtta. Metre: Triṣṭubh.

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Creation will be set forth further on, beginning *tapasastanmahinājāyataikam*. For now the state of dissolution is described, the state before creation, in which the whole manifold world is withdrawn. At that time, in the condition of dissolution, the root cause of this world was not an asat, like a hare's horn, that cannot be spoken of. For from such a cause the origin of this existing world is not possible. Nor was it sat in the sense of being "existent" like the Self; it was inexpressible as existent. Although the existent and the non-existent are each distinct in nature, existence and non-existence could still coexist; how then could they be identical? So it was distinct from both and indeed inexpressible. An objection: *no sat* denies real existence, so the Self too would become inexpressible. Reply: no; its existence is stated further on, in *ānīdavātam*, so by elimination it is the existence of Māyā that is denied here. Even so, the qualifier *tadānīm* would be pointless, since Māyā has no real existence even in the state of ordinary experience. Another objection: since earth and the other elements exist in the empirical sense, how can existence be denied? To this he answers with नासीद्रज (*nāsīdraja*) and the rest. He cites Yāska: the worlds are called rajas (Ni. 4-19). The singular is used with a general sense. Because व्योम (*vyoma*) is mentioned next, the worlds below it, from Pātāla down to the earth, did not exist. Likewise व्योम (*vyoma*), the atmosphere, was not. परः (*paraḥ*) means "beyond"; so whatever exists above, from the heaven-world to the Satya-world, also was not. By this the egg of Brahmā, with its fourteen worlds within, is denied in its own form. Then the elements known from the Purāṇas as its coverings, such as ether, the places where they stand, and the cause of their covering are denied in order, by way of question: किमावरीवः (*kimāvarīvaḥ*). What principle could cover, since there was nothing to be covered? So the covering too did not exist. Or else *kim* stands first: what principle could cover? Since there is nothing to be covered, it too did not exist in its own form. In कुह (*kuha*), "in what place would it stand and cover?": the place that serves as support also did not exist. In कस्य शर्मन् (*kasya śarman*): for the happiness of which enjoyer, a soul, or while the realization of pleasure and pain was the occasion, would it cover? Creation is for the souls' enjoyment. Only if it existed would there be the covering of the egg of Brahmā by the elements; in dissolution the enjoying souls were merged through the dissolution of their limiting adjuncts, so no enjoyer of anything was possible, and the occasion for covering was absent, so that too is not tenable. By this it is said that the world of enjoyers, like the world of objects, did not exist then. {The text of this block breaks off at the end of the page and continues in the next.}

Even though the denial of the covering, the egg of Brahmā, has also removed the water within it, someone might suspect the existence of water because of the śruti *āpo vā idamagre salilamāsīt* (Tai. The śruti concerns the intermediate dissolution. (The remaining part of the block is grammatical: accent and the elision of the locative ending in शर्मन् (*śarman*).)

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- तदानीं (*tadānīṃ*)—in the state of dissolution, that is, before creation
- असत् (*asat*)—the asat, the cause of the world and the rest, which exists in unmanifest form, is not grasped by the senses, and cannot be called by any name
- न आसीत् (*na āsīt*)—was not
- सत् (*sat*)—the original thing called sat, which has manifest form, is accessible to the senses and is the basis of the world and the rest
- नो आसीत् (*no āsīt*)—was not
- रजः (*rajaḥ*)—the worlds
- न आसीत् (*na āsīt*)—were not
- व्योम (*vyoma*)—the atmosphere
- नो (*no*)—was not
- परः (*paraḥ*)—beyond that region of the atmosphere
- यत् (*yat*)—whatever worlds such as heaven exist
- नो (*no*)—were not (then)
- आवरीवः (*āvarīvaḥ*)—what covers, that is, what encloses all this
- किं (*kiṃ*)—was there any thing? (no)
- कुह (*kuha*)—in what place
- कस्य (*kasya*)—of what enjoyer
- शर्मन् (*śarman*)—were there things that give pleasure?
- गहनं (*gahanaṃ*)—impossible to enter
- गभीरं (*gabhīraṃ*)—unfathomable
- अंभः (*aṃbhaḥ*)—water
- किं आसीत् (*kiṃ āsīt*)—was there? (nothing was)

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

In the state of dissolution, that is, at the time before there was creation again after the world and the rest, created earlier, had been absorbed into the Supreme Self, there was neither the asat, which is the cause of the world and the rest, exists in unmanifest form, lies beyond the knowledge born of the senses and cannot be indicated by name and form, nor the sat, which is accessible to the senses, has manifest form and is the basis of the world and the rest. The worlds were not, the atmosphere was not. The heaven-worlds and the rest beyond the atmosphere were not. Then was there any thing that covered all this? Where were the means of pleasure for the enjoyer (for the multitude of souls or living beings)? Or was there water that cannot be entered and is unfathomable? (The meaning is that nothing existed.)

##### English translation
The non-existent was not, the existent was not ; then the world was not, nor the firmament, nor that which is above (the firmament.) How

### Printed p. 754
could there be any investing envelope, and where? Of what (could there be) felicity? How (could there be) the deep unfathomable water?

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

In the present Ṛk the state that existed before creation is described. It is said here that at that time none of these existed: worlds as they now are, the firmament, the worlds such as heaven, living beings, food and the like that are the means of their happiness, and the all-pervading water. Before saying this, the verse says that the non-existent (asat) and the existent (sat) were not. It is necessary to understand what asat is here and what sat is.

Asat, sat: Yāska in his Nirukta has listed the words sat, sarvam, idam, ṛtam, satyam, gahanam, gabhīram, vyoma and others among the 101 names of water (Ni. 2-24). How the meaning "water" of the word sat bears on this place we shall consider later. The word sat is formed from the root as — bhuvi (to exist). Therefore sat means a thing that exists, a thing visible to the eye. But here the word sat is used in a wider sense. Further, asat is not the mere negation of the word sat. Though the two are different things, they are not opposed to one another. They have opposite meanings only in the sense that asat is what is not accessible to the senses.

नासदासीन्नो सदासीत्तदानीं (*nāsadāsīnno sadāsīttadānīṃ*)—The fundamental things that are the cause of the many things in the world visible to our eyes are not of many kinds. However great the variety in the qualities and forms of things, the basic substance of all of them is one. For example, water, stone, gold, silver, earth and the like show many differences in quality and form, yet the origin of all these things is one substance. It may be called the paramāṇu (atom). Though *paramāṇu* does not describe this primal substance exactly, since Kannada has no other word that describes it exactly, it may be called by that name in the present context. In an ordinary object there are many crores of atoms. The arrangement of those countless atoms is not of one kind in all things; it differs in different things. Although the primal substance is one, because their inner arrangement differs, the things also appear different. The atoms in water and the atoms in stone are one in origin. Because those atoms are arranged in one way, the thing is water; because they are arranged in another way, the thing is stone, and so on.

### Printed p. 755
There was a time when it was believed that matter and energy are different. But scientists have recently discovered that the two are not fundamentally different things, and that one can be transformed into the other. Though this is new to modern science, it is nothing new to the Vedas, the Upaniṣads and the Vedānta treatises. Thousands of years ago this matter was firmly settled, admitting no doubt. It is thus: if one goes on dividing a particle of a thing, the extremely small part that cannot be divided further is called the paramāṇu. Even when a thing is divided down to the atom, the qualities of that thing are seen in that atom. Beyond that, though the atom cannot be divided in the ordinary way, it can be divided in a special way. That is, particles still more minute than the atom can exist. But those extremely minute particles lose the qualities of matter; they are transformed into energy. That is, the extremely subtle state of matter is itself energy. There is no difference between matter and energy; only the state is different. All things and energies seen in the world are produced from one primal substance. That primal substance is what is indicated here, that is, in the Vedas and Upaniṣads, by the word sat.

Asat does not mean "non-existent"; it means what is not perceptible to the senses. For example, we can see a tree or a man; it appears to our eyes. There are also many things that do not appear to the eye. The wind is not seen; so also the electric current flowing in wires is not seen. But can it be said that they do not exist? Because the eyes and other senses of man or of other beings are limited, subtle things such as energy cannot be seen. There are varieties among energies too: the radiant energy of the sun, the heat of fire, electricity, mental energy, vital energy, and so on. Therefore the most subtle energy of all, which is not perceptible to our eyes or senses, may be called (roughly) asat. There is no word in Kannada to describe it. It may be thought that this asat is the source of sat, that the Supreme Self is the cause of asat, or that the Supreme Self exists in that very form.

A doubt may arise here: the state of things perceptible to the senses, called sat, and the state of things beyond the senses, called asat, in whatever form they exist, are they not all inert things? It is not so. Together with things and energies in subtle form, the power of the Supreme Self called caitanya (consciousness) is also joined. There is no thing in the world without caitanya, the power of the Supreme Self. When we speak of sentient and insentient things, it is usual to regard living beings as sentient and other things as insentient

### Printed p. 756
but the reality is not so. The same kind of consciousness that lies hidden in living beings is present in other things too, but in greater or lesser measure. Because living beings have movement and the like, the consciousness in them is manifest. In plants and trees too consciousness is present, but not as much as in the animal class. In metals and the like it is present in a still smaller measure than in the plant class. In stones and similar substances that are not metals it is smaller still. In the five elements, earth and the rest, it is least of all. Whatever the measure, consciousness is present in everything; there is no thing without consciousness. This is what the Śruti sentence says: तत्सृष्टा तदेवानुप्राविशत् (*tatsṛṣṭā tadevānuprāviśat*)—having created all the things (living and non-living), the Supreme Self entered them in the form of consciousness. An example can be given: the power of conducting electricity is great in some things such as metals and so small in others as to be nothing; likewise is the range of this consciousness.

The power of consciousness in living beings becomes invisible as soon as they die. But the small measure of consciousness in the five elements that are the cause of the bodies of living beings does not go. For the consciousness of living beings departs with their vital energy. Since the five elements, mixed in a certain way in the body, become separate after death and return to their former state without undergoing any change, no loss occurs to the consciousness in them. Only at the time of their dissolution does everything perish.

From the explanation just given, asat has in a way been said to be the unmanifest form of the Supreme Self, endowed with sat (substance, existence) and cit (consciousness). When even the sages could not describe it fully, how can we describe it with our small intellect? We shall explain some Śruti sentences on this subject.

असद्वा इदमग्र आसीत् । ततो वै सदजायत । तदात्मानग्स् स्वयमकुरुत ॥ (*asadvā idamagra āsīt | tato vai sadajāyata | tadātmānags svayamakuruta ‖*) (Tai. U. 3-7)

In the beginning, that is, before creation, only asat, that is, the unmanifest thing beyond the senses (the Supreme Self), existed. From it arose sat, the thing perceptible to the senses; that is, it is said that asat itself was transformed into sat. There is a further point here. Did all of asat change into sat? Was everything now seen, the world and the rest, together in the unmanifest state called asat? Did nothing remain after it became sat? It is not so. Only some small part of asat was transformed into sat; the remaining great part stayed as asat. In another place of the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā—

### Printed p. 757
पादोऽस्य विश्वा भूतानि त्रिपादस्यामृतं दिवि ॥ (*pādo 'sya viśvā bhūtāni tripādasyāmṛtaṃ divi ‖*)
त्रिपादूर्ध्व उद्वैत्पुरुषः पादोऽस्येहाभवत्पुनः ॥ (*tripādūrdhva udvaitpuruṣaḥ pādo 'syehābhavatpunaḥ ‖*)
(Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-90-3, 4) (printed as मू (*mū*). सं (*saṃ*).)**NOTE**

When the Supreme Self (the unmanifest form called asat) created the world, only one pāda (a quarter) of its measure, that is, a very small part, was transformed into the world. The remaining three parts, that is, the greater part, remain just as they were, without any change (in the unmanifest form called asat). Both the sentences above say this in the same way. An example can be given. The water of the sea, heated by the sun's rays, becomes vapour, then through the clouds, that is, through rain, falls on the earth, flows as rivers and again joins the sea. The rivers arising from sea-water do not contain all the sea-water; that is, not all the water of the sea is transformed into rivers; only some part (a very small part) is drawn up as vapour, becomes clouds, then rivers, reservoirs and the like, stays for some time and finally joins the sea. In the same way only a very small part of the unmanifest form is transformed into this universe, the world and the rest, stays for some time and is again dissolved into the unmanifest. The greater part of the unmanifest (asat) always remains in the same state without any change. This is described in the Aitareya Upaniṣad thus: it has been said that the Self (asat, or the Supreme Self) existed before all. But who is this Self? By whose power do these senses engage in their respective functions? The Self is pure consciousness. Its name is prajñāna. The various activities in the mind and in the sentient being are only impulses of that pure consciousness. These external things also rest in this pure consciousness; that is, this consciousness is the shelter and support of all things. Without this consciousness no other thing exists in this universe; whatever exists must exist by its support. That pure consciousness is the origin of all things, the origin of the whole universe. By its own spontaneous impulse all the activities of this manifest universe go on. In another place in this same Upaniṣad—

कोऽयमात्मेति वयमुपास्महे कतरं स आत्मा येन वा पश्यति येन वा शृणोति येन वा गंधानाजिघ्रति येन वा वाचं व्याकरोति येन वा स्वादु चास्वादु च विजानाति ॥ १ ॥ यदेतद्धृदयं मनश्चैतत् । संज्ञानमाज्ञानं विज्ञानं प्रज्ञानं मेधा दृष्टिर्धृतिर्मतिर्मनीषा जूतिः स्मृतिः संकल्पः क्रतुरसुः कामो वश इति सर्वाण्ये वैतानि प्रज्ञानस्य नामधेयानि भवंति ॥ २ ॥ एष ब्रह्मैष इंद्र एष प्रजापतिरेते सर्वे देवा इमानि च पंचमहाभूतानि पृथिवी वायुराकाश आपो ज्योतींषीत्येतानीमानि च क्षुद्रमिश्राणीव ॥ बीजानीतराणि चेतराणि चांडजानि च जारुजानि ते स्वेदजानि चोद्भिज्ञानि चाश्वा गावः पुरुषा हस्तिनो यत्किंचेदं प्राणि जंगमं च पतत्रि च यच्च स्थावरं सर्वं तत्प्रज्ञानेत्रं प्रज्ञाने प्रतिष्ठितं प्रज्ञानेत्रो लोकः प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठा प्रज्ञानं ब्रह्म ॥ ३ ॥ (*ko 'yamātmeti vayamupāsmahe kataraṃ sa ātmā yena vā paśyati yena vā śṛṇoti yena vā gaṃdhānājighrati yena vā vācaṃ vyākaroti yena vā svādu cāsvādu ca vijānāti ‖ 1 ‖ yadetaddhṛdayaṃ manaścaitat | saṃjñānamājñānaṃ vijñānaṃ prajñānaṃ medhā dṛṣṭirdhṛtirmatirmanīṣā jūtiḥ smṛtiḥ saṃkalpaḥ kraturasuḥ kāmo vaśa iti sarvāṇye vaitāni prajñānasya nāmadheyāni bhavaṃti ‖ 2 ‖ eṣa brahmaiṣa iṃdra eṣa prajāpatirete sarve devā imāni ca paṃcamahābhūtāni pṛthivī vāyurākāśa āpo jyotīṃṣītyetānīmāni ca kṣudramiśrāṇīva ‖ bījānītarāṇi cetarāṇi cāṃḍajāni ca jārujāni te svedajāni codbhijñāni cāśvā gāvaḥ puruṣā hastino yatkiṃcedaṃ prāṇi jaṃgamaṃ ca patatri ca yacca sthāvaraṃ sarvaṃ tatprajñānetraṃ prajñāne pratiṣṭhitaṃ prajñānetro lokaḥ prajñā pratiṣṭhā prajñānaṃ brahma ‖ 3 ‖*) (the passage continues on the next page)

### Printed p. 758
स एतेन प्राज्ञेनात्मनात्मल्लोकादुत्क्रम्यामुष्मिन् स्वर्गे लोके सर्वान्कामानाप्त्वामृतः समभवत्समभवत् । इत्यों ॥ ४ ॥ (*sa etena prājñenātmanātmallokādutkramyāmuṣmin svarge loke sarvānkāmānāptvāmṛtaḥ samabhavatsamabhavat | ityoṃ ‖ 4 ‖*) (Ai. U. 3-5-1 ff.)

Who is this Self whom we worship? By whose help is a man able to see a thing, able to hear a sound, able to smell an odour, able to speak, able to know "this is tasty, this is not tasty"? Who is that Self? This heart, this mind, this consciousness, ignorance, knowledge, prajñāna, intellect, sight, firmness, thought, desire, distraction, memory, resolve, determination, breath, desire, longing: all these are only different names of prajñāna, that is, of pure consciousness. This Brahman, this Indra, this Prajāpati, all these gods, the five great elements — earth, air, space, water, and all the lights that shine in the sky (the stars) — small and great things, all grains, the many kinds of beings born from eggs, from the womb, from sweat, plants and creepers, horses, cows, men, elephants, all living creatures, birds, all immovable things (mountains and the like that cannot move): the impeller of all these is prajñāna itself. Prajñā is the eye of all these. All these are established in prajñāna. The origin of the universe too is from prajñāna. Prajñā is the eye of this world; prajñā is the foundation of knowledge and consciousness. Why more? Prajñāna is Brahman. He, going from this world with this Self made of knowledge, obtained all desires in that heavenly world and enjoyed (will enjoy) immortality, that is, eternal happiness: this is the main purport. Therefore asat, prajñāna-Brahman, Parabrahman, Ātman, Paramātman and the rest all indicate the unmanifest Parabrahman, who is of the nature of existence, consciousness and bliss.

नासीद्रजो नो व्योम परो यत् (*nāsīdrajo no vyoma paro yat*)—In the first pāda: before creation there were not the manifest and unmanifest forms called sat and asat. What then was there? None of the visible worlds was there. Here Yāska's explanation is that rajaḥ means world (Ni. 4-19). Although the singular rajaḥ is used here, taking the sense of a collection of worlds it has a plural meaning: the worlds. Which worlds? The worlds such as the earth, or, as described in the Purāṇas and elsewhere, the seven worlds from Pātāla to the earth. Vyoma means the firmament, or the world of the firmament

### Printed p. 759
Paraḥ yat: here the word paraḥ is to be understood as parastāt, "beyond that"; that is, the world that lies beyond the world of the firmament, namely the world of heaven; or, as in the Purāṇas and elsewhere, the seven worlds from heaven to Satyaloka. The purport is that at that time neither the three worlds of earth, firmament and heaven, nor the universe made of the seven lower worlds and seven upper worlds together, was there.

किमावरीवः कुह कस्य शर्मन् (*kimāvarīvaḥ kuha kasya śarman*)—Here āvarīvaḥ means envelope. The five elements beginning with space that envelop the worlds were also not there then. When there were no worlds, how could there be regions? When there was no region or ground, where were the living beings that live on it and the means of happiness such as food that bring them happiness? None of these was there.

अंभः किमासीद्गहनं गभीरं (*aṃbhaḥ kimāsīdgahanaṃ gabhīraṃ*)—When none of these was there, what else was there? Was there water, impenetrable and unfathomable, filling everywhere? Has it not been said before that nothing in the form of an envelope existed? Then how could the envelope called water have been there? In some Śruti sentences — आपो ना इदमग्रे सलिलमासीत् (*āpo nā idamagre salilamāsīt*) (Tai. Saṃ. 7-1-5-1) — it is said that before everything water alone covered everywhere. Is this not contrary to this? The answer: for that very reason it is said that even the water that covered everything was not there before that creation. Then what is the meaning of the sentence आपो ना इदमग्रे सलिलमासीत् (*āpo nā idamagre salilamāsīt*)? Was there only water before everything? Then that water itself would have to be the all-pervading Brahman. In one way this is quite consistent. Although the word āpaḥ means water, since this word is formed from the root āpḷ — vyāptau (to pervade, to cover), a consistent meaning of the word āpaḥ can be given as the all-pervading Brahman-substance. The Śruti sentence आपो ना इदग्ं सर्वं (*āpo nā idagṃ sarvaṃ*) and so on supports just this meaning. Or, if the word āpaḥ is taken to mean mere water, then it may be said that that water was not there before creation, that is, in the state of dissolution, that only the unmanifest form called asat existed, and that afterwards, at the time of the creation of the five elements, before the creation of the rest of the world, this water was created and spread everywhere, and from this water the later creation proceeded.

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Sāyaṇa raises an objection: the dissolution spoken of needs a dissolver, so Death (मृत्युः (*mṛtyuḥ*)) himself might be thought to exist. He answers with न मृत्युरासीदिति (*na mṛtyurāsīditi*), "Death was not." A further objection: if Death did not exist, the deathlessness (अमृतं (*amṛtaṃ*)) that follows from his absence, the continued life of beings, would hold at that time. He answers with अमृतं न तर्हि (*amṛtaṃ na tarhi*); तर्हि (*tarhi*) means at that time of dissolution. The sense is this. When the ripened action of all beings that causes enjoyment has been completely enjoyed, the world is purposeless for want of enjoyment, and the wish to withdraw it arises in the mind of the Supreme Lord. So Death withdraws the whole world; what need then of this Death as withdrawer, or how could deathlessness, which depends on his absence, exist? With this in view the Kaṭha text says: यस्य ब्रह्म च क्षत्रं चोभे भवत ओदनं । मृत्युर्यस्कोपसेचनं क इत्था वेद यत्र सः । (*yasya brahma ca kṣatraṃ cobhe bhavata odanaṃ | mṛtyuryaskopasecanaṃ ka itthā veda yatra saḥ |*) (Ka. U. 2-25).
Another objection: time, the substrate of all this, exists. He answers with न रात्रा (*na rātrā*). There was no knowledge of night or day, since the sun and moon that cause them did not exist. By this denial of day and night, all time in the form of month, season, year and so on is also excluded. How then does the word तदानीं (*tadānīṃ*) "then," which denotes time, occur in *no sadāsīttadānīṃ*? He says it is figurative. As the denial of what is "now" is delimited by time, so Māyā too is the cause of delimitation; through this similarity in delimiting, a time-denoting suffix is used even where there is no time.
He then shows the true being of Brahman, which he said he would state later: आनीत् (*ānīt*), "breathed." That Brahman-principle, known from all the Vedāntas, breathed, like a living being. Objection: then only Brahman that has become a living being, the one who breathes, would be real, not the Brahman without limiting conditions that is intended, since the text says अप्राणो ह्यमनाः शुद्ध (*aprāṇo hyamanāḥ śuddha*), Brahman is without breath and mind and pure, having no connection with breath. He answers with अवातं (*avātaṃ*). The intention: in आनीत् (*ānīt*) three meanings are understood: the action of the root, its agent, and the connection of the agent with past time. The whole is not enjoined, as in "an eight-potsherd cake for Agni," so that Brahman's existence would not follow. Rather, the agency is restated and the quality of existence in past time is enjoined, as in the injunction of the Agnihotra with curds, laid down through restatement of the Agnihotra enjoined by another sentence. Even there the existence of Brahman in an earlier time is not enjoined as qualified by agency, since the denial of it would then be inconsistent. Therefore

> कश्चिद्धोष इति । नन्नीदृशस्य ब्रह्मणो मायया सह संबंधासंभवात्सांख्याभिमता
> स्वतंत्रा सद्रूपा सत्त्वरजस्तमोगुणात्मिका मूलप्रकृतिरेवाभिमतेति कथं नो सदिति

> तृतीया सहशब्दयोगाभावेऽपि सहार्थयोगे भवति वृद्धो यूना ! पा. १-२-६५ ।
> इति निपातनाल्लिंगात् ॥ अत्र प्रकृतिप्रत्ययाभ्यां तस्याः स्वातंत्र्यं निर्वायते ।
> यद्यप्यसंगस्य ब्रह्मणस्तया सह संबंधो न संभवति तथापि तस्मिन्नविद्यया तत्त्वरूपमिव संबंधोऽप्यध्यस्यते यथा शुक्तिकायां रजतस्य । एतेन सद्रूपत्वमपि
> तस्याः प्रत्याख्यातं । ननु यदि माया ब्रह्मणा सहाविभागापन्ना तर्हि तस्या अनिर्वाच्यत्वाद्ब्रह्मणोऽपि तत्पसंग इति कथं तस्य सत्यमुक्तमानीदवातमिति । ब्रह्मणो
> ना सत्वात्तस्या अपि सत्यप्रसंग इति कथं नो सदासीदिति सत्यप्रतिषेधः । मैवं ।
> आयुक्तिदृष्टैक्यावभासेऽपि युक्ता विविच्य मायांशस्यानिर्वाच्यत्वं ब्रह्मणः सत्यं
> च प्रतिपादितं । ननु दृगृश्याविति द्वावेव पदार्थावानीदवातं स्वधयेति तौ चेदंगीक्रियेते तक्किमपरमवशिष्यते यन्नासीद्रज इत्यादिना प्रतिषिध्येत तत्राह तस्मादिति ।
> तस्माद्द तस्मात्पलु पूर्वोक्तान्मयासहिताद्ब्रह्मणोऽन्यक्तिं चन किमपि वस्तु भूतभौतिकात्मकं जगन्नास । न बभूव ॥ छंदस्युभयथेति लिटः सार्वधातुकत्वादस्तेर्भूभावाभावः ॥ ननु तदानीमन्यस्य सत्यनिषेधो न शंक्यः । असत्वे चाप्रसक्तत्वान्न
> निषेधोपयोग इत्यत आह पर इति । परः परस्तात्सृष्टेरूर्ध्वं वर्तमानमिदं
> जगत्तदानीं न बभूवेत्यर्थः । अन्यथोक्तरीत्या क्वचिदपि निषेधो न स्यादिति भावः ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

...through this agency, indicated by the present-time sense, the existence in past time is enjoined of the Supreme Brahman free of limiting conditions; so there is no fault.
Objection: such a Brahman cannot be connected with Māyā, so what is meant would be the independent, existent Primal Nature (मूलप्रकृति (*mūlaprakṛti*)) of the Sāṃkhyas, made of sattva, rajas and tamas; how then is existence denied in *no sat*? He answers with स्वधया (*svadhayā*). स्वधा (*svadhā*) is Māyā: what is held (ध्रियत (*dhriyata*)) in oneself, existing in dependence. By her that one Brahman existed undivided from her. The instrumental case is by सहयुक्तेऽप्रधाने (*sahayukte 'pradhāne*) (Pā. Sū. 2-3-19) even without the word सह (*saha*), through the sense of "with," just as the form in वृद्धो यूना (*vṛddho yūnā*) (Pā. Sū. 1-2-65) is by the stated indication. Here her dependence is denied by the base and the suffix. Though Brahman, being unattached, cannot be connected with her, a connection is nonetheless superimposed on it through ignorance, as silver is on mother-of-pearl. By this her being existent is also refuted.
Objection: if Māyā is undivided from Brahman, then, being indescribable, Brahman too would be affected; how then is its truth stated in *ānīdavātaṃ*? And since Brahman is real, Māyā too would be real, so how is truth denied in नो सदासीत् (*no sadāsīt*)? He replies: not so. Although unity appears to those who do not reason, one who reasons distinguishes and establishes the indescribability of the Māyā part and the truth of Brahman.
Objection: आनीत् अवातं स्वधया (*ānīt avātaṃ svadhayā*) give only two entities, the seer and the seen; if both are accepted, what other remains to be denied by *nāsīdrajaḥ* and the rest? He answers with तस्मात् (*tasmāt*): apart from that Brahman together with Māyā, nothing else, no world made of elements and their products, existed. The root is not replaced by भू (*bhū*), since the perfect, in the Veda, is treated as सार्वधातुक (*sārvadhātuka*). Objection: no existence of anything else is to be suspected then, and a denial of what was never in question is useless. He answers with परः (*paraḥ*): परः (*paraḥ*) means after, beyond creation; this world, existing afterwards, did not exist then. Otherwise a denial would be possible nowhere.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- मृत्युः (*mṛtyuḥ*)—death (before creation)
- न आसीत् (*na āsīt*)—was not
- तर्हि (*tarhi*)—then
- अमृतं (*amṛtaṃ*)—deathlessness also
- न (*na*)—was not (and then)
- रात्र्याः (*rātryāḥ*)—of night, and
- अह्नः (*ahnaḥ*)—of day
- प्रकेतः (*praketaḥ*)—knowledge
- न आसीत् (*na āsīt*)—was not
- तत् एकं (*tat ekaṃ*)—that Brahman-principle, known from all the Vedāntas and without a second
- स्वधया (*svadhayā*)—by its own power in the form of Māyā
- अवातं (*avātaṃ*)—the breathless, that is, the lifeless inert body
- आनीत् (*ānīt*)—made living with breath
- तस्मात् (*tasmāt*)—apart from that Brahman with that Māyā-endowed power
- अन्यत् किंचन (*anyat kiṃcana*)—any other thing made of elements and their products
- न आस (*na āsa*)—was not
- परः (*paraḥ*)—afterwards, this world that was created
- न आस (*na āsa*)—was not then

### Printed p. 762

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

In the state of dissolution before creation there was neither death nor deathlessness. There was no knowledge of which was night and which was day. The one Brahman-principle, famed in all the Vedāntas and without a second, alone existing, made the breathless, that is, the lifeless inert thing, animate by the excess of power called its Māyā. Apart from that Brahman-principle with that power, no other thing existed. This world, created afterwards, did not exist then.

##### English translation
Death was not nor at that period immortality, there was no indication of day or night; that one unbreathed upon breathed of his own strength, other than that thre was nothing else whatever.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

न मृत्युः आसीत् अमृतं न तर्हि (*na mṛtyuḥ āsīt amṛtaṃ na tarhi*): here it is said that at that time there was neither death nor freedom from death. Death is the separation of body from the living being that may occur after some time, the severance of the tie between body and breath. Or here मृत्यु (*mṛtyu*) may be taken as destruction, the destruction of the world and the rest. सर्वेषां प्राणिनां परिपक्वं भोगहेतुभूतं सर्वं कर्म यदोपभुक्तमासीत् तदा भोगाभावान्निष्ट्रयोजनमिदं जगदिति परमेश्वरस्य मनसि संजिहीर्षा जायते । तथैव स मृत्युः सर्वं जगत्संहरत इति किमनेन मृत्युना संहर्त्रा तदभावकृतं वा कथममरणं स्यादिति । (*sarveṣāṃ prāṇināṃ paripakvaṃ bhogahetubhūtaṃ sarvaṃ karma yadopabhuktamāsīt tadā bhogābhāvānniṣṭrayojanamidaṃ jagaditi parameśvarasya manasi saṃjihīrṣā jāyate | tathaiva sa mṛtyuḥ sarvaṃ jagatsaṃharata iti kimanena mṛtyunā saṃhartrā tadabhāvakṛtaṃ vā kathamamaraṇaṃ syāditi |*) The Supreme Lord created the world, created various beings in it, and made them experience their pleasure and pain. When they have fully experienced these, a disgust arises in the mind that the world is purposeless. Then the Lord himself destroys it in the form of Death (the destroyer). Such destruction may be called death. If such death did not then exist, does the world then remain deathless, everlasting, as if without destruction? It cannot be so either. When neither the world nor the beings in it exist, the question of death occurring to them does not arise. Likewise deathlessness, or freedom from death (destruction), does not exist. Is there not something there to be destroyed? When nothing exists, what is there to destroy? Nothing. So at that time there was no work for death or for deathlessness to do; there was no need of them. Hence the meaning is that they did not exist.

### Printed p. 763
न रात्र्याः अह्नः आसीत् प्रकेतः (*na rātryāḥ ahnaḥ āsīt praketaḥ*): प्रकेतः (*praketaḥ*) is understanding, knowledge. At that time there was no knowledge of which was night and which was day, or whether it was now night or day. Here it is necessary to understand what night and day are. By our worldly experience, the time from sunrise to sunset we know as day, and from sunset to the next sunrise as night. What is the need of night and day, and how do they arise? Beings in the daytime are engaged in various activities to obtain food and the like; at night they stop and take rest. Since beings need both activity and rest, both day and night are necessary. Day and night arise from the movements of the earth, produced by the Supreme Self's power and capacity. When the earth (or the part of it) faces the sun it is day, and when it turns away it is night. Since the earth's movements follow a fixed order and fixed time, the durations of day and night are roughly equal. Further, the earth revolves round the sun; the time of one revolution is called a year. Since time has no beginning or end and is endless, it is customary to take the year as a measuring rod for measuring some portion of it. Time can be measured as a year, the time the earth takes for one circuit, and as a number of such years. Likewise periods smaller than the year can be measured by divisions such as month, fortnight, day, daytime, night, muhūrta, kṣaṇa, kalā, kāṣṭhā. All this concerns the earth; it does not apply to other planets. Because their movements and their revolutions round the sun are various, the durations of their days, nights and years are, more or less than the earth's, various. In the present context, saying that there was then no room for knowledge of days and nights means there was no means of knowing divisions of time. With no sun or moon, no other planets or stars, and no movements of them, divisions of time could not be known. But was there no time at all? Time existed, always exists and is endless. It too is the very nature of the Supreme Self and not different; the Upaniṣads and other texts proclaim this. It is said in many places that the nature of the Supreme Self is to be endless in space, time and things.
आनीत् अवातं स्वधया तत् एकं (*ānīt avātaṃ svadhayā tat ekaṃ*): before explaining the meaning of this sentence, it is necessary to explain each word in it carefully. The word आनीत् (*ānīt*)

### Printed p. 764
is formed from the root अन (*ana*) "to breathe" and indicates past time. Yāska reads the word अनिति (*aniti*) (root) among words with the sense of going (Ni. 3-9). So this root means to move, to breathe. Since breathing and moving are the chief activity of beings, beings without them must be called lifeless and inert. So for beings to be known to have life or breath, they must breathe or show movement. This is the sign of having breath. Here the verb आनीत् (*ānīt*) has the meaning आनीदित्यत्र धात्वर्थक्रिया, तत्कर्ता तस्य च भूतकालसंबंध इति त्रयोऽर्थाः प्रतीयंते (*ānīdityatra dhātvarthakriyā, tatkartā tasya ca bhūtakālasaṃbaṃdha iti trayo 'rthāḥ pratīyaṃte*). That is, in that word three things are contained: the meaning of the root, the agent who does it, and the past time in which it was done. The chief sense of आनीत् (*ānīt*) is that the Supreme Brahman produced movement (breathing and the like). Now what is अवातं (*avātaṃ*)? वात (*vāta*) is wind. वातं (*vātaṃ*) here is the being that takes in air, that is, breathes. अवातं (*avātaṃ*) means the inert thing that does not breathe and has no power of movement.
स्वधया (*svadhayā*)—स्वस्मिन् धीयते ध्रियत आश्रित्य वर्तत इति स्वधा माया । तया तद्ब्रह्मकमविभागापन्नमासीत् ॥ (*svasmin dhīyate dhriyata āśritya vartata iti svadhā māyā | tayā tadbrahmakamavibhāgāpannamāsīt ‖*) The power and capacity that exists in oneself (the Supreme Self), dependent on oneself, is called स्वधा (*svadhā*). Some also call it Māyā. Was this power separate in Brahman? No. One cannot say Brahman is one thing and his power another. Everything is one in Brahman. The meaning of the word स्वधा (*svadhā*) is: by this extraordinary power of Brahman called Māyā. तत् (*tat*)—तत् (*tat*) means सकलवेदांतप्रसिद्धं ब्रह्मतत्त्वं (*sakalavedāṃtaprasiddhaṃ brahmatattvaṃ*): the thing called Brahman, set forth in all the Vedāntas and of unmanifest nature, is called by the word तत् (*tat*). It means the Supreme Brahman, in the sense of the word तत् (*tat*) in the sentence तत् त्वं असि (*tat tvaṃ asi*). एकं (*ekaṃ*) is अद्वितीयं एकमेव (*advitīyaṃ ekameva*): there is no other thing equal to or greater than Brahman, nor anything comparable; there are not two such things. It is always one. Having explained each word, let us now consider the meaning of the sentence. The meaning is that the Supreme Brahman, always without a second and alone, by its extraordinary Māyā-power filled the non-breathing inert thing with life so that it breathed, and made it a moving being. Had the Supreme Brahman not filled the world and other things he created with consciousness, his own portion, that is, had he not entered them as awareness, they would have remained inert and would have had no power to breathe or move. So the meaning is that the Supreme Brahman, first entering as inner self the things he had created, conducts all the activities of beings and of insentient things.

### Printed p. 765
तस्मात् ह अन्यत् न परः किं चन आस (*tasmāt ha anyat na paraḥ kiṃ cana āsa*): in the previous sentence the word एकं (*ekaṃ*) is used. एकं (*ekaṃ*) means without a second, one with nothing other than himself. This word means that apart from Brahman there is no other thing. That being so, is it not inconsistent to say that Brahman made the अवातं (*avātaṃ*), the unmoving inert thing, animate? If nothing but Brahman exists, whence came the inert thing? Did there not come to be two things, Brahman and the inert? Is this not a contradiction? The answer is given clearly in the sentence तस्माद्धान्यन्न परः किंच नास (*tasmāddhānyanna paraḥ kiṃca nāsa*). Before creation Brahman alone existed, and that too in an unmanifest (non-existent) form. There was no other thing. At the time of creation this Brahman itself, by its Māyā-power, was transformed into the world and the rest. So these transformed worlds and the rest are not different from Brahman. It is said that Brahman enters them as consciousness so that they may carry on their activities. It is not right to say on that account that Brahman is one thing and the world and the rest another, two separate things; they are two reflections of one thing. In the water filling many vessels the reflection of the sun appears like many suns, yet there is one sun, not many. Likewise, though the world and the rest appear in various ways, all of it is the nature of the one Supreme Self. Apart from that Supreme Self or Brahman-principle there is no other thing at all. Therefore the chief meaning of this sentence is that before creation this world and the rest, now seen, did not exist at all.

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> ननूक्तप्रकारेण यदि पूर्वमिदं जगन्नासीत्कथं तर्हि तस्य जन्म । जायमानस्य जनिक्रियायां कर्तृत्वेन कारकत्वात् कारकं च कारणावांतरविशेष इति कारकस्य

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Objection: if, as stated, this world did not exist before, how then was it born? What is born is the agent of the act of birth and so a factor (कारक (*kāraka*)), and a factor is a particular kind of cause, so for the factor.

> जगतः सर्गसमयेऽपि नोद्भवसंभव इत्यत आह तुच्छेनेति । आ समंताद्भवतीत्याभु तुच्छेन ॥ छांदसो यकारोपजनः ॥ तुच्छेन तुच्छकल्पनेन सदसद्विलक्षणेन.
> भावरूपाज्ञानेनापिहितं छादितमासीत् ॥ दधातेः कर्मणि निष्ठा । दधातेर्हि ।
> गतिरनंतर इति गतेः प्रकृतिस्वरत्वं ॥ एकमेकीभूतं कारणेन तमसाविभागतां
> प्राप्तमपि तत्कार्यजातं तपसः सृष्टव्यपर्यालोचनरूपस्य महिना माहात्म्येनाजायत । उत्पन्नं । तपसः सृष्टव्यपर्यालोचनरूपत्वं चान्यत्राम्नायते । यः
> सर्वज्ञः सर्वविद्यस्य ज्ञानमयं तपः । मुं. उ. १-१-९ । इति ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

(Continuation of the bhāṣya on Ṛk 3.) The objector says: if, as stated, this world did not exist before, how can it be born? A thing that is born is the agent of the act of birth, and an agent is a kind of causal factor, so it must necessarily exist at some definite moment before. To avoid this fault it is said that the world existed even before the act of birth. "How then is its birth?" He answers with तमसा गूढमग्र (*tamasā gūḍhamagra*). In the beginning, in the state of dissolution before creation, the whole world of elements and their products was covered by darkness, as nocturnal darkness covers every kind of object. Because it veils the truth of the Self, the positive ignorance called by the name māyā is here called "darkness". The world is hidden by it, enveloped and covered by it as its cause. When name and form later become manifest out of that covering darkness, that very manifestation is called the world's birth. By this the asadvādins, who hold that an effect that does not exist in the state of its cause comes to be, are refuted.

Objection: if the effect, the world, exists in the causal darkness, why does the denial "there was no space" and so on appear? He answers with तम आसीत् (*tama āsīt*): darkness, the positive ignorance, is the root cause; the world is of its nature, since the whole world was darkness before. Hence the denial. Further objection: the veiling darkness is the agent and the world, being veiled, is the object; how can agent and object be identical? He answers with अप्रकेतं (*apraketaṃ*), "not perceived". Though by reasoning there is a relation of object and agent between the world and the darkness, in that state it is not clearly known through name and form, as in ordinary dealings; hence the statement of identity. Hence also Manu recalls (Manu 1-5): आसीदिदं तमोभूतमप्रज्ञातमलक्षणं । अप्रतर्क्यमनिर्दॆश्यं प्रसुप्तमिव सर्वतः (*āsīdidaṃ tamobhūtamaprajñātamalakṣaṇaṃ | apratarkyamanirdèśyaṃ prasuptamiva sarvataḥ*).

Why is it not perceived? He answers: सलिलं (*salilaṃ*). All this visible world was "salila", joined with its cause and fallen into non-distinction. Or else सलिलमिति लुप्रोपमं (*salilamiti lupropamaṃ*): "like water". As water mixed with milk and become non-distinct is hard to know, so the world, become non-distinct with darkness, cannot be known.

Objection: how can a world of manifold, varied forms be overpowered by the utterly insignificant darkness, as water by milk? Answer: it is said that darkness too is strong like milk. Then, the world being weak, it could not emerge even at the time of creation; hence he says तुच्छेन (*tucchena*). "आभु (*ābhu*)" is that which becomes all around; "tuccha" is the insignificant, the positive ignorance, neither existent nor non-existent. What was covered by it was one, united with its cause, the darkness, in non-distinction; yet that whole effect was born through the greatness (mahinā) of tapas, which is the reflection on what is to be created. That tapas is of the nature of such reflection is taught elsewhere: यः सर्वज्ञः सर्वविद्यस्य ज्ञानमयं तपः (*yaḥ sarvajñaḥ sarvavidyasya jñānamayaṃ tapaḥ*) (मुं (*muṃ*). उ (*u*). 1-1-9)**NOTE**.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- अग्रे (*agre*)—before creation
- तमसा (*tamasā*)—by darkness
- गूळ्हं (*gūḷhaṃ*)—thickly covered
- अप्रकेतं (*apraketaṃ*)—in which nothing could be known
- तमः (*tamaḥ*)—darkness
- आसीत् (*āsīt*)—was
- इदं सर्वं (*idaṃ sarvaṃ*)—all this world that is now seen (at that time)
- सलिलं (*salilaṃ*)—consisting of water
- आः (*āḥ*)—was
- आभु (*ābhu*)—all around
- तुच्छेन (*tucchena*)—by the absence of anything, by nothingness
- यत् (*yat*)—which
- अपिहितं (*apihitaṃ*)—covered
- आसीत् (*āsīt*)—was
- एकं (*ekaṃ*)—that non-existent thing in which cause and effect were united as one
- तपसः (*tapasaḥ*)—of the nature of meditation on creating
- महिम्मा (*mahimmā*)—by the greatness
- तत् (*tat*)—as the world in the form of effect
- अजायत (*ajāyata*)—came into being

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

Before everything else, that is, at the beginning of creation, darkness, thickly covered by a darkness in which nothing could be known, spread everywhere. All the world now seen was not as it is now, but was altogether water; or it was covered by darkness as dense as water. The unmanifest form, which had no support and no covering and was one, without separate divisions called cause and effect, became the world as effect through the greatness of its meditation of the nature of the wish to create.

##### English translation
There was darkness covered by darkness in the beginning, all this (world) was undistinguishable water; that empty united (world) which was covered by a mere nothing, was produced through the power of austerity.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

It has been said that this world did not exist before. How then did the world arise? To make a thing one needs an agent who makes it, a raw material for it, and also a cause. For example, to make a pot there must be a potter who can make it; he is the agent. The raw material needed is clay, and a cause is needed. Such being so, who is the agent of the making of the world? The agent is Brahman, of unmanifest nature. What is the raw material of the world? The raw material is some other substance (raw material) that existed before the finished article. Here only the Supreme Brahman existed and there was no other thing; so with the help of what substance would Brahman, the agent, make the world? The answer is that Brahman has no need of raw material for creating the world.

### Printed p. 768

Nor does he need it. Brahman himself, being of unmanifest form, becomes of the nature of the existent, that is, the world and the rest. That is, Brahman is not different, and the existent world and the rest are not different. Therefore it should be understood that a small part of the non-existent became existent.

तम आसीत् तमसा गूढं अग्रे अप्रकेतं (*tama āsīt tamasā gūḍhaṃ agre apraketaṃ*)—Before creation there was none of the world and the rest. But the world's not existing does not mean that the existent (sat), its root cause, did not exist. The non-existent became existent and itself became the root cause of the world and the rest. Before this happened, in the state of dissolution, everything was full of darkness and nothing could be seen or known. As water spreads everywhere in the sea, everything was full of water, or was covered by darkness dense like water. This state is described in the Śruti and elsewhere by sentences such as आपो ना इदमग्रे सलिलमासीत् (*āpo nā idamagre salilamāsīt*). Here the bhāṣyakāra has given another meaning to the word tamas: आत्मतत्त्वस्यावरकत्वान्मायापरसंज्ञं भावरूपाज्ञानमत्र तम इत्युच्यते । तेन तमसा निगूढं संवृतं कारणभूतेन तेनाच्छादितं भवति । आच्छादकात् तस्मात्तमसो नामरूपाभ्यां यदाविर्भवनं तदेव तस्य जन्मेत्युच्यते। एतेन कारणावस्थायामसदेव कार्यमुत्पद्यते इत्यसद्वादिनोऽसत्कार्यवादिनो ये मन्यंते ते प्रत्याख्याताः । (*ātmatattvasyāvarakatvānmāyāparasaṃjñaṃ bhāvarūpājñānamatra tama ityucyate | tena tamasā nigūḍhaṃ saṃvṛtaṃ kāraṇabhūtena tenācchāditaṃ bhavati | ācchādakāt tasmāttamaso nāmarūpābhyāṃ yadāvirbhavanaṃ tadeva tasya janmetyucyate| etena kāraṇāvasthāyāmasadeva kāryamutpadyate ityasadvādino 'satkāryavādino ye manyaṃte te pratyākhyātāḥ |*) Here, that which covers the Self so that the true nature of Brahman, called the Ātma-tattva, is not known, is called māyā, that is, ignorance, the covering. That is, the covering called ignorance is the darkness. The thing endowed with name and form that emerges from that covering darkness of ignorance is called the origin of the world. That is the view of the asadvādins, that the non-existent in the state of cause itself takes on the form of effect. But this is contrary to Śruti sentences such as असद्वा इदमग्र आसीत् । ततो वै सदजायत (*asadvā idamagra āsīt | tato vai sadajāyata*), "at first only the non-existent was; afterwards it itself was born as the existent". Manu too describes the state of the non-existent (Manu 1-5): आसीदिदं तमोभूतमप्रज्ञानमलक्षणं । अप्रतर्क्यमनिर्देश्यं प्रसुप्तमिव सर्वतः (*āsīdidaṃ tamobhūtamaprajñānamalakṣaṇaṃ | apratarkyamanirdeśyaṃ prasuptamiva sarvataḥ*). It spreads everywhere like darkness. It cannot be known, examined, or described as being such and such. Without any movement or any activity, it is as a man in sleep lies sleeping without motion. The meaning is that it cannot be described in words.

सलिलं सर्वं आ इदं (*salilaṃ sarvaṃ ā idaṃ*)—Here the bhāṣyakāra has given the meaning of a lupta-upamā for this sentence. Salila means water. यथा क्षीरेणाविभागापन्नं नीरं दुर्विज्ञानं तथा तमसाविभागापन्नं जगन्न शक्यविज्ञानमित्यर्थः । (*yathā kṣīreṇāvibhāgāpannaṃ nīraṃ durvijñānaṃ tathā tamasāvibhāgāpannaṃ jaganna śakyavijñānamityarthaḥ |*) In water mixed with milk one cannot say separately which is milk and which is water;

### Printed p. 769

in the same way, in the darkness, that is, the darkness of unmanifest form, one cannot point out and say which is the world existing there as seed.

तुच्छेन आभु अपिहितं यत् आसीत् तपसः तत् महिना अजायात एकं (*tucchena ābhu apihitaṃ yat āsīt tapasaḥ tat mahinā ajāyāta ekaṃ*)—Here the word tuccha suggests the meaning "absence of anything" (nothing). The Brahman-substance alone existed, covered by such an absence (the absence of any thing), and nothing else existed. The meaning is that through the greatness, of the nature of meditation, of that one Supreme Brahman, the world, in the form of effect different from the cause, was created.

> 49

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Objection: if, as said, the Lord's reflection is the cause of the world's re-creation, what is the ground of that reflection? He answers with कामस्तदग्र इति (*kāmastadagra iti*). In the beginning, in the state before the creation of this whole product, desire arose well (samyak) in the mind of the Supreme Lord; the meaning is that the wish to create arose. Is the Lord's wish to create without a reason? He answers with मनस इति (*manasa iti*). It belongs to the mind, the inner organ; it remains as a residue of impressions, inhering in the inner organ dissolved in māyā. The singular is used with reference to the general: it inheres in the inner organs of all beings. By this the view that the Self is the support of qualities is refuted. Such a seed ("reto") of the coming world is the meritorious action done by beings in the previous (first) kalpa; because it was ripened and turned towards its fruit at the time of creation, it grew (bhūṣṇu, vardhiṣṭa). For that reason the wish to create arose in the mind of the Supreme Lord, the giver of fruit, witness of all, overseer of actions. When it has arisen, he reflects on what is to be created and then creates the whole world. So it is taught: सोऽकामयत बहुः स्यां प्रजायेयेति स तपोऽतप्यत स तपस्तप्तदं सर्वमसृजत यदिदं किं च। (*so 'kāmayata bahuḥ syāṃ prajāyeyeti sa tapo 'tapyata sa tapastaptadaṃ sarvamasṛjata yadidaṃ kiṃ ca|*) (Tai. Ā. 8-6).

> इति श्रुत्यात्मनेत्थमवगमितेऽर्थे विद्वदनुभवमप्यनुग्राहकत्वेन प्रमाणयति सत
> इति । सतः सत्येनेदानीमनुभूयमानस्य सर्वस्य जगतो बंधुं बंधकं हेतुभूतं कल्पांतरे प्राण्यनुष्ठितं कर्मसमूहं कवयः क्रांतदर्शना अतीतानागतवर्तमानाभिज्ञा योगिनो हृदि हृदये निरुद्धया मनीषा मनीषया बुद्ध्या ॥
> सुपां सुलुगिति तृतीयाया लुक् ॥ प्रतीष्य विचार्य ॥ अन्येषामपीति साहितिको
> दीर्घः ॥ असति सद्विलक्षणेऽव्याकृते कारणे निरविंदन् । निष्कृष्यालभंत । विविच्याजानन्नित्यर्थः ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Having thus understood the matter through the Śruti itself, he confirms it, as supporting it, by the experience of the learned, with सत इति (*sata iti*). The kavis, the sages of far-reaching vision who know past, future and present, the yogins, found in the heart, by the mind (manīṣā), that is, by understanding with restrained mind, the "bandhu" of the sat, of the whole world now experienced as real: the bandhu, the binding cause, is the mass of actions performed by beings in another kalpa. They did this by reflecting (pratīṣya, "having considered"). They found it "in the asat", that is, in the unmanifest cause, different from the existent; निरविंदन् (*niraviṃdan*) means that they drew it out and obtained it, that is, they distinguished it and knew it.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- मनसः (*manasaḥ*)—of the mind
- रेतः (*retaḥ*)—the seed of the creation of the world
- प्रथमं (*prathamaṃ*)—the action performed by beings in the former kalpa
- यत् (*yat*)—for which reason
- आसीत् (*āsīt*)—was
- तत् (*tat*)—for that reason
- अग्रे (*agre*)—before the creation of the world, in the mind of the Supreme Lord
- कामः (*kāmaḥ*)—the wish to create
- सं अधि अवर्तत (*saṃ adhi avartata*)—arose
- सतः (*sataḥ*)—of the entire world, a modification of the existent
- बंधुं (*baṃdhuṃ*)—the mass of actions of beings, which is kin or binding
- कवयः (*kavayaḥ*)—the seers of far-reaching vision
- हृदि (*hṛdi*)—in their hearts
- मनीषा (*manīṣā*)—by the understanding
- प्रतीष्य (*pratīṣya*)—having considered
- असति (*asati*)—that which is seed in the unmanifest form
- निरविंदन् (*niraviṃdan*)—found out

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

When the idea arose in the mind of the Supreme Lord that the actions, sin, merit and the rest, performed by beings in the former creation are the seed of the present creation, the wish to create the world arose in his mind before the creation of the world. The wise seers or yogins considered with their understanding in their minds, and understood, that the mass of actions of beings, which binds all the worlds that are modifications of the existent, abides as seed in the unmanifest form.

##### English translation
In the beginnig there was desire, which was the first seed of mind; sages having meditated in their hearts have discovered by their wisdom the connexion of the existent with the non-existent.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

In the present Ṛk it is explained that the wish to create, in the mind of the Supreme Brahman, became the cause of the creation of the world.

### Printed p. 771

कामः तत् अग्रे सं अवर्तत अधि (*kāmaḥ tat agre saṃ avartata adhi*)—Before the creation of the world, the wish to create the world first arose in the mind of the Supreme Lord. Why it arose is explained in the next pāda.

मनसः रेतः प्रथमं यत् आसीत् (*manasaḥ retaḥ prathamaṃ yat āsīt*)—The meaning of the words "मनसः रेतः (*manasaḥ retaḥ*)" here is that desire is born in the mind. When some work is to be done, the wish to do it first dawns, that is, arises, in the mind. As a seed is necessary for a plant to be born, so a cause, or seed, is necessary for a work to be accomplished. So, when the Supreme Self was to create, the wish to create arose first in his mind. That wish is the cause of the creation of the world. But why did that wish arise? प्रथमं यत् आसीत् (*prathamaṃ yat āsīt*): when the world was created in the previous kalpa, the beings in it could not fully experience the actions they had done, sin, merit and the rest, or their fruits, since the world was dissolved in the meantime; so those fruits of actions had to remain unexperienced. Therefore it is said here that the wish to create the world arose in the mind of the Supreme Self with the purpose that beings may experience them in this creation. This is supported by the Śruti sentence सोs कामयत ।बहु स्यां प्रजायेयेति । स तपोs तप्यत ।स तपस्तप्ता । इदग्० सर्वमसृजत । यदिदं किंच । (*sos kāmayata |bahu syāṃ prajāyeyeti | sa tapos tapyata |sa tapastaptā | idag0 sarvamasṛjata | yadidaṃ kiṃca |*) (Tai. Ā. 8-6).

सतः बंधुं असति निः अविंदन् हृदि प्रतीष्य कवयः मनीषा (*sataḥ baṃdhuṃ asati niḥ aviṃdan hṛdi pratīṣya kavayaḥ manīṣā*)—In the sentence above it was said that the mass of actions of the beings of the former kalpa is the cause of the creation of the world now made, was it not? How is that? In this sentence the manner in which this was known is explained. The yogins, sages and others, who can know matters of past, future and present, with their divine vision, that is, by meditation in the mind and by careful reflection, understood one important matter. That important matter is this: the existent worlds of the former kalpa, the beings in them, and their actions in the form of sin and merit, all these lie hidden as seed (in the form of cause) in the unmanifest non-existent (in Brahman); this they understood with their reflective understanding. That is, the cause that is the seed of the worlds lies dissolved in the non-existent of unmanifest form. Therefore a kind of binding relation came to exist between the existent world and the non-existent in unmanifest form. That is, since the existent comes into manifestation from the non-existent, the two are related to each other; this is explained here by the words "satah bandhuh asati".

> अयमेवार्थस्त्वितरीयके तत्सृष्ट्वा तदेवानुप्राविशत् । तै. आ. ८-६ । इत्यारभ्य

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Sāyaṇa says that avidyā, kāma and karman have so far been given as the causes of creation, and that he now shows how swiftly they produce their effect. The avidyā is the one taught in *nāsadāsīt*. The kāma is the one in कामस्तदग्र (*kāmastadagra*). The karman is the one in मनसो रेतः प्रथमं यदासीदिति (*manaso retaḥ prathamaṃ yadāsīditi*). For these creators of the elements (ether and the rest), the "ray" (रश्मि (*raśmi*)) is something like a ray. A sun-ray, once the sun has risen, pervades the whole world in the twinkling of an eye. In the same way the whole group of effects was spread out (विततः (*vitataḥ*), extended), pervading everything swiftly. The word स्विदासी३त् (*svidāsī3t*), which comes later, is connected here as well. He cites Pā. 8-2-97, according to which the syllable is pluta in the case of matters under deliberation, and the udātta is carried over from the previous sūtra. स्वित् (*svit*) means doubt. Was that group of effects at first lying across (तिरश्चीनः (*tiraścīnaḥ*)), that is, positioned in the middle? Or was it below? Or else was it above? He cites Pā. 8-2-102 for the anudātta pluta in दुपरि स्विदासी३त् (*dupari svidāsī3t*).

The fifth-case (ablative) śruti runs "From the Ātman ether arose, from ether wind, from wind fire" (Tai. A. 8-1) **NOTE**. It gives a sequence, like "then the Udgātṛ, then the Hotṛ". Even so, because creation spread as swiftly as a flash of lightning, that sequence is hard to make out. So it is asked in which of these three places the priority lay. The meaning is that creation was thus completed swiftly in all directions.

He then divides the matter. Among the created effects, some beings were रेतोधाः (*retodhāḥ*): the establishers of karma that is like seed, that is, agents and enjoyers, the living beings. Other beings were महिमानः (*mahimānaḥ*) (the affix is svārthika). These were the great objects of enjoyment, ether and the rest. Thus the Supreme Lord with māyā created the whole world and himself entered it. He made the division into enjoyer, enjoyed and so on. The same meaning is taught in the Taittirīya, beginning "Having created it, he entered into that very thing" (Tai. Ā. 8-6), and it continues on the next page.
