> प्रतिपाद्यते । तत्र च भोक्तृभोग्ययोर्मध्यॆ स्वधा । अन्ननामैतत् । भोग्यप्रपंचोऽवस्तादवरो निकृष्ट आसीत् । प्रयतिः प्रयतिता भोक्ता परस्तात्पर उत्कृष्ट
> आसीत् । भोग्यप्रपंचं भोक्तृप्रपंचस्य शेषभूतं कृतवानित्यर्थः ॥ विभाषा
> परावराभ्यां । पा. ५-३-२९ । इति प्रथमार्थेऽस्तातिः । अस्ताति च । पा. ५-३-४० ।
> इत्यवरशब्दस्यावादेशः । अवस्तादिति संहितायामिषा अक्षादित्वात्कृतिभावः ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

The Taittirīya passage teaches the same meaning. There, between the enjoyer and the enjoyed, स्वधा (*svadhā*) is a name for food. The world of the enjoyed was अवस्तात् (*avastāt*), below, low. प्रयतिः (*prayatiḥ*) is प्रयतिता (*prayatitā*), the enjoyer, who was परस्तात् (*parastāt*), higher, superior. The meaning is that he made the world of the enjoyed subordinate to the world of the enjoyers. The rest of the block gives the grammar of अवस्तात् (*avastāt*).

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- एषां (*eṣāṃ*)—for the carrying out of these creative works
- रश्मिः (*raśmiḥ*)—the ray in the form of readiness for action, or the beginning of the work that spreads very swiftly
- तिरश्चीनः (*tiraścīnaḥ*)—also across
- अधः स्वित् (*adhaḥ svit*)—also in the lower part
- उपरि स्वित् (*upari svit*)—also in the upper part
- विततः आसीत् (*vitataḥ āsīt*)—spread out widely (and)
- रेतोधाः (*retodhāḥ*)—the doers of seed-like actions and the living beings (creatures) who enjoy their fruits
- आसन् (*āsan*)—came into being
- महिमानः (*mahimānaḥ*)—the very great things, ether and the rest (the objects of the world), which are objects of enjoyment for creatures
- आसन् (*āsan*)—came into being (in these two kinds, the enjoyers and the enjoyed)
- स्वधा (*svadhā*)—the objects of enjoyment of the world, in the form of food
- अवस्तात् (*avastāt*)—lower than the enjoyers who enjoy them
- प्रयतिः (*prayatiḥ*)—the enjoyer
- परस्तात् (*parastāt*)—he became superior to the object of enjoyment

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

When Brahman became ready to act for the carrying out of these creative works, that beginning of action spread widely, like a sun-ray, at the speed of lightning: across, downward, upward, everywhere (in all places). That is, the beginning of the work of creation started to proceed in many places at once and very swiftly, like the speed of lightning. Among the things created in this way there were two main divisions. One division is the five elements, ether and the rest, the worlds and the many things in them. The other is the enjoyers who enjoy these things, that is, creatures and so on that have life and can experience pleasure, pain and the like. Of these two divisions, the class of creatures, enjoyers endowed with consciousness, is the superior. (Here "creatures" includes humans and the gods, all of them.) The objects of enjoyment, ether and the rest and the other things of the world, are inferior. The idea is that the object of enjoyment is lower than the enjoyer.

##### English translation
Their ray was stretched out, whether across, or below, or above; (some) were shedders of seed, (others) were mighty ; food was inferior, the eater was superior,

### Printed p. 774

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

Two matters are stated clearly in this Ṛk. In the first half comes the account of how creation took shape. In the second half it is taught that the created things are of two kinds, enjoyer and enjoyed, and that of these the enjoyer is superior to the objects of enjoyment.

तिरश्चीनः विततः रश्मिः एषां अधः स्वित् आसीत् (*tiraścīnaḥ vitataḥ raśmiḥ eṣāṃ adhaḥ svit āsīt*) उपरि स्वित् आसीत् (*upari svit āsīt*)—this sentence of the first half of the Ṛk describes how creation took place when it came into action. As soon as the wish to create arose in the Supreme Brahman, it came down into action. That action spread very quickly, as a sun-ray going out from the sun spreads very quickly all around. At one and the same time it spread below, above, in the middle and in the surrounding region, everywhere. That is, the work of creation did not proceed slowly, one region after another. The idea is that it went on in all places at once, and very swiftly.

रेतोधाः आसन् महिमानः आसन् (*retodhāḥ āsan mahimānaḥ āsan*) स्वधा अवस्तात् प्रयतिः परस्तात् (*svadhā avastāt prayatiḥ parastāt*)—in this sentence an explanation of some words is needed. For the word रेतोधाः (*retodhāḥ*) the gloss is रेतसो बीजभूतस्य कर्मणो विधातारः कर्तारो भोक्तारश्च जीवाः (*retaso bījabhūtasya karmaṇo vidhātāraḥ kartāro bhoktāraśca jīvāḥ*). That is, रेतः (*retaḥ*) is explained as seed, meaning seed-like karma. The meaning is the living beings who perform such karma and enjoy the fruits of that karma. "Living beings" means all creatures that have life: humans, gods, all of them. महिमानः (*mahimānaḥ*) is महंतो वियदादयो भोग्याः (*mahaṃto viyadādayo bhogyāḥ*), that is, the very great things, ether and the rest (the five elements, ether and so on), the worlds and the like that arose from their transformation, and the objects of enjoyment in them. Likewise स्वधा (*svadhā*) is food. A thing that is to be eaten is called food, so it is an object of enjoyment. स्वधा (*svadhā*) is the object of enjoyment that creatures experience. प्रयतिः (*prayatiḥ*) is प्रयतिता भोक्ता (*prayatitā bhoktā*), the one who strives, who obtains his food by effort, that is, the enjoyer who experiences the objects of enjoyment.

Next let us consider the sense of the sentence. It too has two divisions. The first is रेतोधा आसन् महिमान आसन् (*retodhā āsan mahimāna āsan*). At the time of creation, the created things fell into two main divisions. One is the agent or enjoyer, who performs actions and experiences their fruits. The other is the things the enjoyer is to experience. Which of them is higher and which lower is what the sentence स्वधा अवस्तात् प्रयतिः परस्तात् (*svadhā avastāt prayatiḥ parastāt*) tells. The greater importance belongs to the enjoyer. The object of enjoyment has no importance. It is inferior to the enjoyer. But the objects of enjoyment may be large in quantity and number, and the enjoyer may be very small.

### Printed p. 775
The objects of enjoyment, that is, the world and so on, are very large. The enjoyer who experiences the enjoyment in them (a human and the like) is of very small size. Yet the idea is that greater importance belongs to the enjoyer and less to the object of enjoyment.

On the matter of the Supreme Lord's creating the world and the rest, the Upaniṣads and similar texts describe how creation proceeded:

आत्मन आकाशः संभूतः । आकाशाद्वायुः । वायोरग्निः । अग्नेरापः । अद्भ्यः पृथिवी । पृथिव्या ओषधयः । ओषधीभ्योऽन्नं । अन्नात्पुरुषः ॥ (*ātmana ākāśaḥ saṃbhūtaḥ | ākāśādvāyuḥ | vāyoragniḥ | agnerāpaḥ | adbhyaḥ pṛthivī | pṛthivyā oṣadhayaḥ | oṣadhībhyo 'nnaṃ | annātpuruṣaḥ ‖*) (Tai. U. 2-1).

It says that at the time of creation ether first arose from the Ātman, or the Supreme Self existing in unmanifest form (asat). From that ether came wind, from wind fire, from fire water, from water earth, from earth the herbs and plants, from them the food that creatures need, and from that food creatures such as man. It is said that in creating, he first created the objects of enjoyment and afterwards the enjoyer. For as soon as the enjoyer is born he needs food and the like. So it is quite fitting that he first prepared food and the like and afterwards created the enjoyer who experiences them. But the objects of enjoyment have no importance merely because they were created first. It must be understood that superiority belongs to the enjoyer, who was created afterwards.

In this way it is said in many places in the Ṛk-saṃhitā itself that from the Ātman in unmanifest form the worlds and the rest, which are of the nature of sat, arose. After that the herbs and plants arose in those worlds, and after that gods, humans and the rest:

देवानां पूर्व्ये युगेऽसतः सदजायत (*devānāṃ pūrvye yuge 'sataḥ sadajāyata*) देवानां युगे ऽप्रथमे ऽसतः सदजायत । तदाशा अन्वजायंत तदुत्तानपदस्पॆरि ॥ (*devānāṃ yuge 'prathame 'sataḥ sadajāyata | tadāśā anvajāyaṃta taduttānapadaspèri ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-72-2, 3).

When the gods were being created, that is, at the beginning of creation, the worlds and the rest, of manifest form and called sat, came into being from the unmanifest called asat. After that the directions and the like arose, and after that trees and the like. Moreover:

या ओषधीः पूर्वा जाता देवेभ्यस्त्रियुगं पुरा (*yā oṣadhīḥ pūrvā jātā devebhyastriyugaṃ purā*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-97-1).

It is said that the herbs and plants arose three ages before the creation of the gods. Therefore it must be understood that the creation of the objects of enjoyment came first, and afterwards the creation of the enjoyer.

> सम्यक्को वेद को ना विस्तरेण वक्तुं शक्नुयादित्यर्थः । ननु देवा अजानंतः ।
> सर्वज्ञास्ते ज्ञास्यंति वक्तुं च शक्नुवंतीत्यत आह । अर्नागिति । देवाश्चास्य जगतो
> विसर्जनेन वियदादिभूतोत्पत्त्यनंतरं विविधं यद्भौतिकं सर्जनं सृष्टिस्तेनार्वागर्वाचीनाः कृताः । भूतसृष्टेः पश्चाज्जाता इत्यर्थः । तथाविधास्ते कथं स्वोत्पत्तेः
> पूर्वकालीनां सृष्टिं जानीयुः । अजानंतो वा कथं प्रब्रूयुः । उक्तं दुर्विज्ञानत्वं निर्गमयति । अधैवं सति देवा अपि न जानंति किल । तद्व्यतिरिक्तः को नाम
> मनुष्यादिर्वेद तज्ञगतारणं जानाति यतः कारणात्कृत्सं जगदाबभूव अजायत ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Sāyaṇa says that creation has thus been stated in brief in the form of enjoyer and enjoyed, as in "this is just food and the eater of food; Soma is the food, Agni the eater of food". Now, since that creation is hard to know, it has not been told at length, and so the Ṛk says को अद्धा (*ko addhā*). Which person truly (अद्धा (*addhā*), in reality) knows? Who in this world could declare it (प्र वोचत् (*pra vocat*), would speak forth)? This visible creation (विसृष्टिः (*visṛṣṭiḥ*)) is manifold, in the form of the elements, the things made of them, enjoyers, objects of enjoyment and so on. From what material cause, and from what efficient cause, was it born (आजाता (*ājātā*), fully born, come forth)? Who knows both of these properly? The meaning is that no one could tell it at length.

An objection: the gods, who are omniscient, will know it and be able to tell. He answers with अर्वाग् (*arvāg*). The gods too were made later (*arvācīnāḥ*) by the emission (विसर्जनेन (*visarjanena*)) of this world. That is, they were made by the varied elemental creation that came after the arising of the elements, ether and the rest. The meaning is that they were born after the creation of the elements. How could beings of that kind know the creation that preceded their own birth? Or, not knowing, how could they declare it? He then derives the stated difficulty of knowing **NOTE**. If so, even the gods do not know. Who else, a human or the like, knows the cause of the world, तज्ञगतारणं (*tajñagatāraṇaṃ*) **NOTE**, from which cause the whole world came to be (आबभूव (*ābabhūva*), arose)?

- इह (*iha*)—in this world

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

Which person can know this order of creation? Who in this world can know it and tell it? By whom and how did this manifold creation, made up of the various things we now see, come about? After creation began and some part of it, beginning with the five elements, ether and the rest, had advanced, the gods came into being. Therefore the gods too have not known it. Since things stand so, who is the person who can know by whom and how this creation of the world arose?

##### English translation
Who really knows ? who in this world may declarc it ? whence was
this creation. whence was it engendered ? The gods (were) subsequent to
the (world's) creation ; so who knows whence it arose ?

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

It was said earlier that creation came about in two main kinds, enjoyer and enjoyed. In this Ṛk and in the next, the seer describes, in the form of questions, how very hard it is to know this order of creation.

कः अद्धा वेद कः इह प्र वोचत् (*kaḥ addhā veda kaḥ iha pra vocat*)—who is the one who knows this order of creation as it truly was, or who is the person who, knowing it, says "it went on just so"? No one. No one has certain knowledge in this matter.

कुतः अजाता कुतः इयं विसृष्टिः (*kutaḥ ajātā kutaḥ iyaṃ visṛṣṭiḥ*)—from what substance did the creation of many kinds arise, the creation we now see, with the elements, the things made of them, enjoyers, objects of enjoyment and so on? That is, what is the original material needed to build it? Who is the agent (the person) who created it? None of this is known to anyone.

### Printed p. 778
ārvāk devāḥ asya visarjanena — The matter of this creation may be unknown to men such as ourselves. But is it therefore unknown to others, that is, to the gods, who have greater understanding than we? The answer: when creation began, the gods did not yet exist. The creation of the gods did not come first of all. Only after the creation of a part, that is, of the world beginning with the five great elements starting with space, did the creation of the gods take place. How then could gods born afterwards know a creation that had taken place before their own time? The meaning is that they too cannot know it.

atha kaḥ veda yataḥ abababhūva — Since matters stand thus, what person can know by whom and how this creation of the world came about? The meaning is that it cannot be known by anyone.

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Just as the creation of this world, as described, is hard to know, so the created world too is hard to sustain; this is what he says with इयमिति (*iyamiti*). The varied creation, in the form of mountains, rivers, oceans and so on, arose from the supreme Self as its material cause; whether he sustains it or not, who else could sustain it? If anyone sustains it, only Īśvara does, no other. By thus stating that the effect is sustained, Brahman's being the material cause is declared. The sūtra of Pārāśarya is cited: प्रकृतिश्च प्रतिज्ञादृष्टांतानुपरोधात् (*prakṛtiśca pratijñādṛṣṭāṃtānuparodhāt*) (Ve. Sū. 1-4-23 **NOTE**). Alternatively, this half-verse confirms the earlier statement that creation is hard to know; "who knows" is carried over. The discussion continues on the next page.

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

"Who knows" from whom, as the material cause, it came into being? No one. Many are deluded, thinking that the world has no birth and was never otherwise. The ablative ending (tasil) is explained by the rule जनिकर्तुः प्रकृतिः (*janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ*) (Pā. Sū. 1-4-30), the source being called apādāna. Who knows that supreme Self from whom it arose? No one; many are deluded that the world arises from primal matter or from atoms. Likewise that same Self, the material cause and himself also the efficient cause, "has set it in order", that is, created this world or did not create it. This is a doubtful statement about what is not doubtful, as when one says "if the scriptures are authority". Who knows him who ordained it? Many, ignorant of the ordainer, wrongly hold that this world arose by itself from insentient primal matter without a maker. Who knows that he is the material cause? No one; many hold that Īśvara, other than the material, stands apart and ordains. Where even the gods do not know, what hope have those who came later? If creation is so hard to know, does it rest on any means of knowledge? To meet that doubt, the Veda establishes its existence with यो अस्यॆति (*yo asyèti*): Īśvara, the overseer of this world of elements and their products, is in the highest व्योमन् (*vyoman*), which is real, pure like space, self-luminous. Or, with the root av in the sense of satisfying, vyoman is the one specially satisfied, of unsurpassed bliss. Or, with av in the sense of going: to be specially reached, unlimited by place, time and things. Or, with av in the sense of knowing: in the special knower, whose self is distinguished knowledge; he is established in such a self. The Chāndogya passage is cited: स भगवः कस्मिन्प्रतिष्ठित इति स्वे महिम्मि (*sa bhagavaḥ kasminpratiṣṭhita iti sve mahimmi*) (Chā. U. 7-24-1). Such is the supreme Lord; *aṅga* is an exclamation of familiarity. Does even he know, or not? Who else could know? Only the omniscient Īśvara could know that creation, no other.

- विसृष्टिः (*visṛṣṭiḥ*)—the wondrous creation made up of the various forms of rivers, mountains, oceans and so on
- आबभूव (*ābabhūva*)—arose (that very supreme Self)
- यदि वा दधे (*yadi vā dadhe*)—he upholds and nourishes this world
- यदि वा न (*yadi vā na*)—or he may not uphold it (in that case no one else can uphold and nourish it)
- अस्य (*asya*)—of this world
- अध्यक्षः (*adhyakṣaḥ*)—the lord
- यः (*yaḥ*)—which supreme Self
- परमे (*parame*)—in the excellent, or real

- व्योमन् (*vyoman*)—shines in his self-luminous nature, pure like space
- सः (*saḥ*)—that supreme Self alone
- वेद (*veda*)—can know this

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

The supreme Self from whom this wondrous creation, made up of the various forms of rivers, mountains, oceans and so on that we see, arose, that same supreme Self upholds and nourishes this world. Or, if he does not uphold it, no one else can uphold and nourish it. The supreme Self who is the lord of this world and shines in his own self-luminous nature, excellent, real and pure like space, he alone can know this for certain. If even he does not know, who else can know? No one can.

##### English translation
He from whom this creation arose, he may uphold it, or he may not (no one else can); he who is its superintendent in the highest heaven, he assuredly knows, or if he knows not (no one else does).

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

In the previous Ṛk it was said that no one, the gods and others included, knows the manner of this creation; in this Ṛk it is described still more fully.

इयं विसृष्टिः यतः आबभूव यदि वा दधे यदि वा न (*iyaṃ visṛṣṭiḥ yataḥ ābabhūva yadi vā dadhe yadi vā na*)—It is said that this wondrous creation, made up of mountains, rivers and oceans, arose from the supreme Self, the material cause. That is, from the manifest form of the real (sat), whose form was unmanifest, this world and the rest arose. Since the supreme Self is the one who exists in the form of the non-real (asat), that is, in unmanifest form, this whole world arose from him alone. But after the world was thus created, who upholds and nourishes it? On this each says something different. Some, deluded, say that this world has neither origin nor destruction, that it was so before and will be so hereafter. For if the world is said to have been created by the supreme Self, who knows that such a supreme Self exists? No one. So no one created the world and it has neither origin nor destruction; such is their argument. Others say that all things of the world are made of atoms, and that these atoms, according to their own nature, have been transformed into the various things and into the world.

### Printed p. 781
They say that no maker (the supreme Self) is needed to create it. Still other fools who know nothing say that the world is insentient matter, that no one made it and that it arose of itself in this manner. Still others say: let us grant that the world was made by the supreme Self whose form is the non-real, but why must the supreme Self himself uphold and nourish it? Some other, neutral person performs such work as upholding the world. All of these must be said to be deluded.

The supreme Self from whom this creation came is the one who upholds and nourishes this world. Or if he does not uphold it, no one else is able to do so. Creating is not the only work of the supreme Self; the one who upholds and nourishes it is also that same supreme Self. On this the Śruti passage तत्सृष्टा । तदेवानु प्राविशत् (*tatsṛṣṭā | tadevānu prāviśat*) supports this. It is said in many places that he enters as the inner self into the things he has created and upholds and nourishes them. So if there is anyone who upholds and nourishes this world, he is none other than the supreme Self. When the supreme Self is in unmanifest form he is in the form of the cause of the world and the rest; in manifest form he himself, transformed into the form of effect, exists as the world and the rest. So the supreme Self is both effect and cause of the world and the rest. He is the enjoyer and the means of enjoyment. He is the doer of all. The one who creates the world, upholds and nourishes it, and at the end destroys it and makes it dissolve in himself is that same supreme Self. This is said here in another way.

यः अस्य अध्यक्षः परमे व्योमन् सः अंग वेद यदि ना नवेद (*yaḥ asya adhyakṣaḥ parame vyoman saḥ aṃga veda yadi nā naveda*)—Here the commentator has explained the words परमे व्योमन् (*parame vyoman*) in various senses. परमे व्योमन् (*parame vyoman*) means in the excellent sky; or आकाशवन्निर्मले स्वप्रकाशे (*ākāśavannirmale svaprakāśe*), he who shines in his self-luminous nature, pure like space.

On this the commentator cites a passage of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: स भगवः कस्मिन् प्रतिष्ठित इति—स्वे महिम्मि (*sa bhagavaḥ kasmin pratiṣṭhita iti—sve mahimmi*) (Chā. U. 7-24-1). In the dialogue of Sanatkumāra and Nārada, Nārada asked Sanatkumāra: "Revered sir, in what is that Lord (the supreme Self) established?", that is, what is his support? Sanatkumāra answered the question: that supreme Self shines in his own self-luminous nature; he needs no support or basis from another; he is the support of all, all shines by him, and he shines in his own light and his own greatness.

अथवा अवतेस्तर्पणार्थात् (*athavā avatestarpaṇārthāt*)—If the word vyoman is taken to be formed from the root av, which means to satisfy, then the meaning is: he who is satisfied, whose desires are fulfilled, who shines in a nature of unsurpassed bliss.

### Printed p. 782
Or, if the root av is given the sense of going, then विशेषेण गते व्याप्ते! देशकालवस्तुभिरपरिच्छिन्न इत्यर्थः (*viśeṣeṇa gate vyāpte! deśakālavastubhiraparicchinna ityarthaḥ*): specially pervading, that is, he who pervades place, time and things without break and is not limited by them. Or अवतिर्ज्ञानार्थः । व्योमनि विशेषेण ज्ञातरि विशिष्टज्ञानात्मनि (*avatirjñānārthaḥ | vyomani viśeṣeṇa jñātari viśiṣṭajñānātmani*): if the root av is given the sense of knowledge, it means one whose self is distinguished knowledge, that is, the omniscient. The supreme Self who thus shines of himself in his own self-luminous nature and is the Lord of this world alone knows this matter of creation for certain. Except him there is no other who knows it. If even he did not know it, who could? No one else knows; such is the sense of the sentence.

## Sūkta 130 (Maṇḍala 10)
यो यज्ञ इति (*yo yajña iti*) the second sūkta, of seven Ṛks, has as its seer Yajña, son of Prajāpati. The first verse is in Jagatī, the rest in Triṣṭubh. Here too the creation of certain things, Yajña and others, is set forth. So the thing that is chiefly to be created is the deity; or the Prajāpati who makes it is the deity. So the Anukramaṇī says: यो यज्ञो यज्ञः प्राजापत्यो जगत्याद्येति (*yo yajño yajñaḥ prājāpatyo jagatyādyeti*). The viniyoga has already been given.

Anuvāda: The sūkta यो यज्ञः (*yo yajñaḥ*) is the second sūkta in the eleventh anuvāka. It has seven Ṛks. Its seer is Yajña, son of Prajāpati; the first Ṛk is in Jagatī metre and the remaining Ṛks in Triṣṭubh. In this sūkta too the order of creation of certain notions, Yajña and others, is described. Therefore whatever matter relating to creation is set forth in this sūkta is its deity; or Prajāpati, who created it, is the deity. In the Anukramaṇī it is said यो यज्ञो यज्ञः प्राजापत्यो जगत्याद्या (*yo yajño yajñaḥ prājāpatyo jagatyādyā*). The viniyoga has been given before.

Maṇḍala 10; Anuvāka 11; Sūkta 130. Aṣṭaka 8; Adhyāya 7; Varga 18. Number of Ṛks in the sūkta: 7. Ṛṣi: Yajña Prājāpatya. Devatā: Bhāvavṛtta. Chandas: 1 Jagatī; 2–7 Triṣṭubh.

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

The sacrifice (yajña) of the nature of creation, which is spread on every side by threads, that is, by the expanding elements beginning with space. *Ekaśata* is one and a hundred, that is, a hundred and one: because Brahmā lives for a hundred of his own years, it is called a hundred and one together with Prajāpati who lives them, as in शतायुर्नै पुरुषः शतवीर्य आत्मैकशत इति (*śatāyurnai puruṣaḥ śatavīrya ātmaikaśata iti*); the accusative expresses continuous connection. It is extended, lengthened, by acts done by enjoyers for the gods through Brahmā's hundred years, and lasts so long. The fathers, protectors, the world-creating gods who are Prajāpati's vital powers, weave, that is, fashion; the gods who "came" pervaded all that was to be created by weaving. And "pra vaya, apa vaya": pravāṇa is the creation of the excellent, conscious world of enjoyers; apavāna is the creation of the inferior, insentient world of things enjoyed. The root वेञ् (*veñ*) is in the sense of weaving threads; the imperative by समुच्चयेऽन्यतरस्यां (*samuccaye 'nyatarasyāṃ*) (Pā. 3-4-3). So, weaving, they make pravāṇa and apavāna. Being thus, those world-creators abide in the extended Satyaloka, worshipping Prajāpati in the form of the vital breath. Or else the sacrifice such as Jyotiṣṭoma is described under this figure as a loom: its threads are the forms such as Agniṣṭoma, or the seven metres. **NOTE**

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Sāyaṇa continues the explanation of the sacrifice as a woven cloth. The cloth is stretched out by the hundred and one divine rites, from the Gavāmayana to the Viśvasṛjām Ayana, which are of the nature of Ekāha and Sattra rites; this sacrificial cloth was created by Prajāpati. Our fathers, these Aṅgirases, weave it. They urge one another in turn: "Weave forth: make the stotras and śastras, which correspond to the lengthwise threads. Weave across: make the Yajus formulas, which correspond to the crosswise threads." The origin of the extended sacrifice from Prajāpati is set forth in the following verse.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- यः (*yaḥ*)—the creative sacrifice which
- यज्ञः (*yajñaḥ*)—sacrifice
- तंतुभिः (*taṃtubhiḥ*)—by threads in the form of ether and the other elements
- विश्वतः (*viśvataḥ*)—on all sides
- ततः (*tataḥ*)—is spread out
- देवकर्मेभिः (*devakarmebhiḥ*)—by the rites people perform for the gods
- एकशतं (*ekaśataṃ*)—for a hundred and one years
- आयतः (*āyataḥ*)—the sacrifice that is performed at length
- इमे (*ime*)—these
- पितरः (*pitaraḥ*)—the gods who are Prajāpati's vital breaths and who create the universe
- वयंति (*vayaṃti*)—weave and make
- ये देवाः (*ye devāḥ*)—which gods
- प्र वय (*pra vaya*)—the creation of the excellent, sentient enjoyer
- अप वय (*apa vaya*)—and the creation of the inferior, insentient world of objects of enjoyment
- आययुः (*āyayuḥ*)—pervaded through the work of creation
- तते (*tate*)—in the vast Satyaloka
- आसते (*āsate*)—worship Prajāpati in the form of vital breaths

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

The creative sacrifice is spread everywhere by threads that are the five elements beginning with ether, and is carried on for a hundred years by rites directed to the gods. The gods, who are Prajāpati's vital breaths and who carry creation forward, make this sacrifice as one weaves cloth. And those gods who create the excellent, sentient enjoyer and the inferior, insentient objects of enjoyment worship Prajāpati in the vast Satyaloka through meditation and the like.

##### English translation
The sacrifice which is extended on every side by the threads (of created things) spread out by the worship of the gods for a hundred and one (years), these our progeniotors, who have preceded us, weave it, weaving forwards, weaving backwards, rhey worship (Prajapati) when (the world) is woven.

### Printed p. 785

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

In this Ṛk the order of creation is described by comparison with a sacrifice and with cloth. Creating is itself a sacrifice. As cloth is woven from threads, the gods carry out creation through many kinds of sacrificial rites. Prajāpati first created this world, made of the five elements. Then he created the gods and made them carry forward the further creation still to be done. This is what is said here.

यः यज्ञः विश्वतः तंतुभिः ततः (*yaḥ yajñaḥ viśvataḥ taṃtubhiḥ tataḥ*)—Here creation is described as a sacrifice, and that sacrifice is compared to the making of cloth. The sacrifice that spread in all directions of the universe is like cloth woven of threads, which grows broader as it is woven: creation, composed of the five elements beginning with ether, spread everywhere. Here the five elements are the threads. As threads are necessary for making cloth and cloth is woven by joining them, so the creation of the world is made from the five elements.

एकशतं देवकर्मेभिः आयतः (*ekaśataṃ devakarmebhiḥ āyataḥ*)—Prajāpati's lifespan is here said to be a hundred and one years. That is, it is well known in the Purāṇas and elsewhere that the four-faced Brahmā lives a hundred years by his own (divine) reckoning. Instead of taking एकशतं (*ekaśataṃ*) to mean "for a hundred and one years", one may take it to mean Brahmā's span of life, or a very long time. In a sacrifice there are many subsidiary rites such as kindling the fire by friction, bringing the Soma, and invoking the deities. Likewise in the work of creation, once the world is made, plants, trees, sentient and insentient beings and so on must be created; as a sacrifice has its many rites directed to the gods, so creation has the creation of many kinds of things. The meaning is that creation, together with such subsidiary creations, is very extensive, that is, vast.

इमे वयंति पितरः (*ime vayaṃti pitaraḥ*)—Here the word पितरः (*pitaraḥ*) is explained as पालकाः प्रजापतेः प्राणभूताः विश्वसृजो देवाः (*pālakāḥ prajāpateḥ prāṇabhūtāḥ viśvasṛjo devāḥ*): the gods who are protectors and portions of Prajāpati. After Prajāpati has made the creation in the form of the world beginning with ether, the gods, as said above, make, that is, carry forward, the further creation.

ये आययुः प्र वय अप वय इति आसते ते (*ye āyayuḥ pra vaya apa vaya iti āsate te*)—Here प्रवय (*pravaya*) means प्रवाणं नाम प्रकृष्टस्य चेतनस्य भोक्तृप्रपंचस्य सर्जनं (*pravāṇaṃ nāma prakṛṣṭasya cetanasya bhoktṛprapaṃcasya sarjanaṃ*): the creation of the excellent, sentient enjoyer (the living being). Likewise अप वय (*apa vaya*) means अपवानं नाम अपकृष्णस्य 50 निकृष्टस्य अचेतनस्य भोग्यप्रपंचस्य सर्जनं (*apavānaṃ nāma apakṛṣṇasya 50 nikṛṣṭasya acetanasya bhogyaprapaṃcasya sarjanaṃ*)

### Printed p. 786
the creation of the other things, inferior and insentient, that serve as means of enjoyment. The commentator explains that the gods who make these two kinds of creation keep worshipping Brahmā in the vast Satyaloka.

The commentator gives another meaning for this Ṛk, comparing the sacrifice to the making of cloth: he explains the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices by comparison with the work of making cloth.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- यः यज्ञः (*yaḥ yajñaḥ*)—the cloth called the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices
- तंतुभिः (*taṃtubhiḥ*)—by threads in the form of the many varieties such as Agniṣṭoma and Atyagniṣṭoma, or by threads that are the seven metres
- विश्वतः ततः (*viśvataḥ tataḥ*)—is spread out, that is, woven
- एकशतं (*ekaśataṃ*)—beginning with the Agnicayana
- देवकर्मभिः (*devakarmabhiḥ*)—by the sacrifices from the Gavāmayana up to the Viśvasṛjām Ayana, or by the Ekāha and other Sattra sacrifices
- आयतः (*āyataḥ*)—this cloth called the sacrifice has been woven and made by Prajāpati (this cloth called the sacrifice)
- इमे पितरः (*ime pitaraḥ*)—the Aṅgiras sages, who are our fathers
- वयंति (*vayaṃti*)—weave (that is, perform the sacrifice)
- ये (*ye*)—which Aṅgiras sages
- आययुः (*āyayuḥ*)—performed the sacrifice; to that cloth in the form of the sacrifice
- प्र वय (*pra vaya*)—the long threads (the warp) that are the stotra and śastra mantras
- अप वय (*apa vaya*)—joining the crosswise threads (the weft) that are the Yajurveda mantras
- तते (*tate*)—so that it is extended
- आसते (*āsate*)—they weave (that is, they perform the sacrifice)

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

Here a likeness between the sacrifice and the making of cloth is stated. In making cloth, threads are used; in performing a sacrifice, many kinds of sacrifices such as Agniṣṭoma and Atyagniṣṭoma are performed. As threads are many, so are sacrifices and metres (mantras). As cloth is woven large, so the sacrifice is carried on for a long time. In weaving cloth the long and the crosswise threads, warp and weft, are used; in the sacrifice the Ṛgveda and Yajurveda mantras are used to accomplish the sacrifice. Weavers make the cloth; sages such as the Aṅgirases accomplish the sacrifice. In this way every part of cloth-making is explained and described by way of illustration of the various rites of the sacrifice. The main point is that creation was first compared to a sacrifice, and then that sacrifice was compared to the making of cloth. It should be understood that the seer describes the order of creation through these two illustrations.

> सेदुः । विश्वसर्जनहेतुभूतं विश्वसृजामयनाख्यं यज्ञं कर्तुमुपसीदंति ।
> उपसद्य च सामानि रथंतरादीन्वोतवे वयनाय यज्ञाख्यं वस्त्रमोतुं तसराणि
> तिर्यक्सराणि तिरश्चीनसूत्राणि चक्रुः ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

पुमान् (*pumān*) is the first person, Prajāpati; he spreads out, that is, has created, this sacrifice. The Brāhmaṇa says: स प्रजापतिर्यज्ञमतनुत तमाहरत्तेनायजतेति (*sa prajāpatiryajñamatanuta tamāharattenāyajateti*), and प्रजापतिर्यज्ञमसृजत यज्ञं सृष्टमनु ब्रह्मक्षत्रे असृज्येतामिति च (*prajāpatiryajñamasṛjata yajñaṃ sṛṣṭamanu brahmakṣatre asṛjyetāmiti ca*) (Ai. Brā. 5-32-7-19). The same person rolls up, that is, winds up, the created sacrifice; कृति (*kṛti*) is a root of the Rudhādi class meaning "to wind". The same Prajāpati spreads it out in this world, in नाके (*nāke*), the heaven-world, where there is no pain (अकं (*akaṃ*)). अधि (*adhi*) merely repeats the sense of the locative. मयूखाः (*mayūkhāḥ*) are rays, these gods, creators of the universe, who are Prajāpati's vital breaths. They approached the सदः (*sadaḥ*), the place of the divine sacrifice, in order to perform the sacrifice called Viśvasṛjām Ayana, the cause of the creation of the universe. Having approached it, they made the Sāmans, Rathantara and the rest, into तसराणि (*tasarāṇi*), crosswise threads, for weaving the cloth that is the sacrifice.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- पुमान् (*pumān*)—Prajāpati, the first person
- एनं (*enaṃ*)—this sacrifice
- तनुते (*tanute*)—has created (that same Prajāpati)
- उत्कृणत्ति (*utkṛṇatti*)—winds up that sacrifice (brings it to completion)
- पुमान् (*pumān*)—that Prajāpati
- अस्मिन् (*asmin*)—in this world of earth

### Printed p. 788
- अधि नाके (*adhi nāke*)—and in the world of heaven
- वि तत्ने (*vi tatne*)—spreads out (makes it flourish)
- इमे (*ime*)—these
- मयूखाः (*mayūkhāḥ*)—the gods, rays and vital breaths of Prajāpati, engaged in the creation of the universe
- सदः उ (*sadaḥ u*)—the sacrificial house that the gods worship
- उप सेदुः (*upa seduḥ*)—approached in order to perform the sacrifice called Viśvasṛjām Ayana, which is the creation of the universe, and sat down there (after sitting down)
- ओतवे (*otave*)—in order to weave the cloth that is the sacrifice
- सामानि (*sāmāni*)—the Sāma mantras, Rathantara and the rest
- तसराणि (*tasarāṇi*)—as the threads (weft) joined crosswise in weaving
- चक्रुः (*cakruḥ*)—made

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

पुमान् एनं तनुते उत् कृणत्ति (*pumān enaṃ tanute ut kṛṇatti*)—Here पुमान् (*pumān*) is Prajāpati, the first person; तनुते (*tanute*) means he extends, spreads; उत्कृणत्ति (*utkṛṇatti*) means he winds up or brings to completion. A weaver, when weaving cloth, spreads it broad and weaves by joining the long and crosswise threads, warp and weft. When the cloth is finished, he rolls it up and puts it away. In the same way Prajāpati first creates the sacrifice and makes it widely known so that everyone may perform it. After the sacrifice has been performed, he brings it to completion.

##### English translation
The first man spreads out this (web), the first man rolls it up, he spreads it above in this heaven; these his rays have sat down on the seat (of sacrifice), they have made the prayers serve as shuttles for weaving.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

पुमान् वि तत्ने अधि नाके अस्मिन् (*pumān vi tatne adhi nāke asmin*)—That Prajāpati makes it spread both on earth and in the world of heaven. On this point two Śruti sentences are cited as examples: स प्रजापतिर्यज्ञमतनुत तमाहरत्तेनायजत (*sa prajāpatiryajñamatanuta tamāharattenāyajata*) (Ai. Brā. 5-32) and प्रजापतिर्यज्ञमसृजत यज्ञं सृष्टमनु ब्रह्मक्षत्रे असृज्येतां (*prajāpatiryajñamasṛjata yajñaṃ sṛṣṭamanu brahmakṣatre asṛjyetāṃ*) (Ai. Brā. 7-19). That is, Prajāpati first created the sacrifice and then himself performed it; Prajāpati first created the sacrifice and then created Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas.

इमे मयूखा उप सेदुः सदः (*ime mayūkhā upa seduḥ sadaḥ*)—Here मयूखाः (*mayūkhāḥ*) means rays. Which rays? The gods created by Prajāpati, his vital breaths. As rays arise from the sun, so the gods, endowed with a part of his vitality, arise from Prajāpati.

### Printed p. 789
सदः (*sadaḥ*) means the sacrificial house. These gods, Prajāpati's vital breaths, engaged in the work of creation, came and sat down in the sacrificial house to perform the sacrifice of the creation of the universe.

सामानि चक्रुः तसराणि ओतवे (*sāmāni cakruḥ tasarāṇi otave*)—What did they do after coming and sitting in the sacrificial house? Cloth-weavers, in order to weave cloth, first spread the long threads evenly side by side; these are called warp threads. Then they weave by adding other threads crosswise, one by one, between those threads; these crosswise threads are called weft threads. In making cloth both warp and weft are necessary. Likewise, in carrying out the sacrifice, the gods recited the Sāma mantras, Rathantara and the rest, along with the Ṛk mantras. The Ṛk mantras became the warp threads; the Sāma mantras became the weft threads. The main point is that the five elements beginning with ether, and the world and the rest, first created by Prajāpati, became the warp threads; the other classes of things created by the gods became the weft threads. As both warp and weft are necessary for making cloth, so for the work of creation both Prajāpati's creations and those of the gods are necessary.

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

> क्थानि शस्त्राणि वा कान्न्यासन् । एतेषु प्रश्नॆषु त्रयाणामुत्तरं दृचेनाह ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Sāyaṇa continues the sentence begun on the previous page. The seers ask how the things that serve the sacrifice came to be, and he lists the questions. When all the Sādhya and other gods worshipped the god Prajāpati, what was the measure of that sacrifice, and of what kind was it? What was the pratimā, the deity, so called because it is "measured" or fashioned as the one who receives the oblation? What was the nidāna, the first cause, namely the fruit that impels one to undertake the sacrifice? What was the ghee (ājya), or the oblation marked by it? What was the paridhi? The paridhis are three enclosing sticks, a forearm in length, made from palāśa and similar trees and placed all around; the singular number is used with a general intent, so the question means "what were the paridhis?" What was the metre of that sacrifice, beginning with Gāyatrī? What was the pra-uga? This is only an indication: what were the ukthas, the pra-uga of the ājya and so on, or the śastras? Of these questions he says that the following Ṛk answers three.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- यत् (*yat*)—when
- विश्वे देवाः (*viśve devāḥ*)—the gods, the Sādhyas and others
- देवं (*devaṃ*)—Prajāpati
- अयजंत (*ayajaṃta*)—when they worshipped by performing the sacrifice, then (of this sacrifice)
- प्रमा (*pramā*)—the measure (in what manner and for how long it is to be done)
- का आसीत् (*kā āsīt*)—what was it? Or how was it?
- प्रतिमा (*pratimā*)—which was the deity
- निदानं (*nidānaṃ*)—the cause, that is, the fruit of performing the sacrifice
- किं आसीत् (*kiṃ āsīt*)—what was it
- आज्यं (*ājyaṃ*)—the ghee used for the oblation
- किं आसीत् (*kiṃ āsīt*)—what was it
- परिधिः (*paridhiḥ*)—the palāśa and other sticks placed on the four sides of the fire-pit to ward off the harm of rākṣasas
- किं आसीत् (*kiṃ āsīt*)—what was it
- छंदः (*chaṃdaḥ*)—the metres of the mantras
- किं आसीत् (*kiṃ āsīt*)—what was it
- प्रउगं उक्षं (*praugaṃ ukṣaṃ*)—the ukthas and śastra mantras, the pra-uga of the ājya and so on
- किं (*kiṃ*)—what

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

In the time of creation the Sādhyas and other gods performed a sacrifice addressed to Prajāpati in order to carry creation forward. Since the creation of the world was not yet complete, where were the materials of the sacrifice? Which were they? What was the limit of the sacrifice, that is, for how long and how was the sacrifice to be done? What was its deity? What was its fruit? What were the ājya and the sacrificial sticks called paridhis? What were the metres? What were the ukthas, beginning with the pra-uga, and the śastra mantras?

##### English translation
What was the authority (of the sacrifice), what was the limitation, what was the first cause, what was the clarified butter, what was the enclo-

### Printed p. 791

Sure, what was the metre, what was the pra-uga text, when the universal gods offered worship to the gods ?

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

It has been said before that Prajāpati first created the sacrifice, and that the gods performed the sacrifice created by Prajāpati in order to carry forward the work of creating the universe. At that time the creation of the world was not complete. Even so, how did the gods perform the sacrifice? What materials did they use for it? The seer asks this in this Ṛk and gives the answer in the next two Ṛks. Names of some things indispensable in the sacrifice, that is, of its materials, are mentioned here: the manner and time of performing the sacrifice, its fruit, the ājya (ghee) used for the homa, the paridhis placed on the four sides of the fire, the metres, and the śastra mantras such as the pra-uga and uktha. These are the materials of that sacrifice. This Ṛk sets out only the questions as to what materials were used in that sacrifice, performed by the gods in order to create, in place of these materials. The answer is given in the next two Ṛks.

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

The Gāyatrī, sayugvā, that is, joined with Agni as his helper, came into being: it was born from the mouth of Prajāpati, the one to be worshipped. Among the deities Agni and among the metres the Gāyatrī were both born. Accordingly the Taittirīya text says that Prajāpati desired to be born in offspring, and fashioned the Trivṛt from his mouth.

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

The Taittirīya text continues: Agni was created as deity, and the Gāyatrī as metre (Tai. Saṃ. 7-1-1-4). The god Savitṛ came into being together with the Uṣṇih metre; he too was born from Prajāpati. Soma, radiant, was born from that same Prajāpati together with the ukthas, that is, the praise-śastras, and with the Anuṣṭubh metre. The Bṛhatī metre took up, protected or went to the speech of the god Bṛhaspati; that is, Bṛhaspati too was born from Prajāpati together with Bṛhatī.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- बृहस्पतेः वाचं (*bṛhaspateḥ vācaṃ*)—the mantra that praises Bṛhaspati

- आवत् (*āvat*)—became

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

The Gāyatrī metre, that is, a mantra in the Gāyatrī metre, became a helper to Agni. The Uṣṇik metre became so to Savitṛ, ukthas and the Anuṣṭup metre to the radiant Soma, and the Bṛhatī metre to Bṛhaspati: mantras that help in praising them.

##### English translation
Gayatri became the associate of Agni, Savitri became combined with Ushnik, Soma radiant with sacred praises (was united) with Anushtubh, Brihati gave efficacy to the words of Brihaspathi.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

In the previous Ṛk the seer asked what the materials of the sacrifice were and what the gods used in performing it. In answer, in this Ṛk and the next he replies only to the question as to which metres were used. The ājya, paridhi and the other materials are not mentioned. This is because the metre is the essence of the sacrifice; so by describing the metres all the limbs of the sacrifice are as it were described, and the seer may have described only this with that thought. On the relation between sacrifice and metres the Taittirīya Saṃhitā says:

### Printed p. 793

प्रजापतिर्देवासुरानसृजत तदनु यज्ञोऽसृज्यत यज्ञं छंदाग्ंसि ते विष्टंचो व्यक्रामन्सोऽसुराननु यज्ञोपाक्रामद्यज्ञं छंदाग्ंसि ते देवा अमन्यंतामि वा इदमभूवन् यद्वयग्स्म इति ते प्रजापतिमुपधावन्सोऽब्रवीत्प्रजापतिश्चंदसां वीर्यमादाय तद्वः प्रदास्यामीति स छंदसां वीर्यमादाय तदेभ्यः प्रायच्छत्तदनु छंदाग्स्यपाक्राम ञ्छंदाग्ंसि यज्ञस्ततो देवा अभवनरासुरा य एवं छंदसां वीर्यं वेदा श्राव मास्तु शौषड्यज ये यजामहे वषट्कारो भवत्यात्मना परास्य भ्रातृव्यो भवति । (*prajāpatirdevāsurānasṛjata tadanu yajño 'sṛjyata yajñaṃ chaṃdāgṃsi te viṣṭaṃco vyakrāmanso 'surānanu yajñopākrāmadyajñaṃ chaṃdāgṃsi te devā amanyaṃtāmi vā idamabhūvan yadvayagsma iti te prajāpatimupadhāvanso 'bravītprajāpatiścaṃdasāṃ vīryamādāya tadvaḥ pradāsyāmīti sa chaṃdasāṃ vīryamādāya tadebhyaḥ prāyacchattadanu chaṃdāgsyapākrāma ñchaṃdāgṃsi yajñastato devā abhavanarāsurā ya evaṃ chaṃdasāṃ vīryaṃ vedā śrāva māstu śauṣaḍyaja ye yajāmahe vaṣaṭkāro bhavatyātmanā parāsya bhrātṛvyo bhavati |*) (Tai. Saṃ. 3-3-7-1, 2)

Formerly Prajāpati created the gods and the asuras. Afterwards he created the sacrifice, and after the sacrifice he created the metres. Then the gods and asuras came to Prajāpati. The sacrifice then left Prajāpati and went after the asuras. When the sacrifice had gone, the metres followed it and went also. Seeing this the gods thought: "The sacrifice has left us and joined the asuras, so henceforth in battles and the like the asuras will defeat us and be victorious; we shall have to be defeated." They ran to Prajāpati and told him. Prajāpati addressed the gods: "O gods, do not be afraid; I shall gather the vīrya, the essence, of those metres and give it to you; by it you may be victorious." He took the essence of the metres and gave it to the gods. Because Prajāpati had taken the essence of the metres, the metres became powerless and, unable to do anything, left the asuras and came back to the gods. The sacrifice too followed those metres and came to the gods. When the sacrifice had come to them, the gods performed it and defeated the asuras. The essence (vīrya) of the metres is: āśrāvaya, astu śrauṣaṭ, yaja, ye yajāmahe, vaṣaṭkāra; these are the mantras that are the essence of the metres. Prajāpati took these and gave them to the gods. Whoever knows this becomes victorious and his enemies are defeated. Thus the relation of the metres to the sacrifice is told.

अग्नेः गायत्री अभवत् सयुग्वा (*agneḥ gāyatrī abhavat sayugvā*)—Next it will be told which metres became dear to which deities, and with the mantras of which metre those deities are to be praised. As said above, mantras in the Gāyatrī metre are beneficial to Agni. For:

प्रजापतिरकामत प्रजायेयेति स मुखतस्त्रिवृतं निरमिमीत तमग्निर्देवता- (*prajāpatirakāmata prajāyeyeti sa mukhatastrivṛtaṃ niramimīta tamagnirdevatā-*)

### Printed p. 794

न्वसृज्यत गायत्रीछंदो रथंतरग्ं साम ब्राह्मणो मनुष्याणामजः पशूनां तस्मात्ते मुख्या मुखतोऽह्यसृज्यंत ॥ (*nvasṛjyata gāyatrīchaṃdo rathaṃtaragṃ sāma brāhmaṇo manuṣyāṇāmajaḥ paśūnāṃ tasmātte mukhyā mukhato 'hyasṛjyaṃta ‖*) (Tai. Saṃ. 7-1-1-4)

When Prajāpati created, he made from his mouth the Trivṛt stoma, Agni and the Gāyatrī metre. Therefore the Trivṛt stoma and the Gāyatrī metre are beneficial to Agni. Besides, because the Rathantara among the sāman mantras, the Brāhmaṇa among men and the goat among animals arose from Prajāpati's mouth, these have special pre-eminence. That is, in the sacrifice pre-eminence is stated for Agni, the Trivṛt stoma and the Gāyatrī metre.

उष्णिहा सविता संबभूव (*uṣṇihā savitā saṃbabhūva*)—Mantras in the Uṣṇik metre became dear to the god Savitṛ. Therefore Savitṛ is to be praised with mantras of that metre.

अनुष्टुभा सोमः उक्थैः महस्वान् (*anuṣṭubhā somaḥ ukthaiḥ mahasvān*)—The Anuṣṭup metre is dear to the radiant god Soma. Therefore Soma is praised at the midday pressing with mantras of that metre, and also with uktha mantras. The nature of the uktha mantras we have already explained at length (Part 8, p. 252).

बृहस्पतेः बृहती वाचं आवत् (*bṛhaspateḥ bṛhatī vācaṃ āvat*)—The Bṛhatī metre became dear to Bṛhaspati. Therefore Bṛhaspati is to be praised with mantras in the Bṛhatī metre.

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Moreover the Virāṭ metre was the abhiśrī, "resorted to", of the gods Mitra and Varuṇa. Mitra and Varuṇa too were born from Prajāpati together with Virāṭ.

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

In this sacrifice the "share of the day" is the portion of the day's three pressings, the midday pressing, and the Triṣṭup metre: both were to be resorted to by Indra. They, and Indra, were born from Prajāpati. The Taittirīya text says: from the chest and the arms he fashioned the Pañcadaśa; Indra was created as the deity, and therein the Triṣṭup metre and the Bṛhat sāman (Tai. Saṃ. 7-1-1-4). Likewise the Jagatī metre entered all the Viśve Devāḥ; the Viśve Devāḥ and Jagatī were born from Prajāpati. The Taittirīya text says: after him the Viśve Devāḥ were created as deities, the Jagatī metre and the Vairūpa sāman (Tai. Saṃ. 7-1 1-5). In the manner stated, the questions "what was the pratimā?", "what was the metre?", "what was the pra-uga?" and "what was the uktha?" are answered. For the questions "what was the ājya?" and "what was the paridhi?" the answer is to be seen in the Puruṣa Sūkta, where it is said: the gods spread the sacrifice; spring was its ghee, summer its fuel, autumn its oblation (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-90-6 **NOTE**); seven were its paridhis, thrice seven the sticks made (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-90-15). The meaning is: spring, producer of all saps, was the ājya of that sacrifice, the means of creating the world; spring was born together with saps such as ghee and curds. Summer, which dries all saps, was the fuel; it was born with dry sticks. Autumn, with the ripening rice, was the oblation of that sacrifice. The seven metres, made twenty-one-fold, thrice seven, were the eighteen (?) sticks and the paridhis. **NOTE**. To the questions "what was the measure?", "what was the pratimā?" and "what was the nidāna?" the answer is in the Taittirīya text (Tai. Brā. 3-12-9-2 to 8): the former Viśvasṛjs, the immortals, consecrated, sat in a sattra for a hundred thousand years; by this the Viśvasṛjs created this universe. So the measure of that sacrifice is a time of a thousand years; and the creation of the whole world is the first cause, the impelling fruit. What is meant is this: when the Viśvasṛj gods worshipped the god Prajāpati with the sacrifice called Viśvasṛjām Ayana, all the aids of the sacrifice were born from Prajāpati. Since the seven metres, the Gāyatrī and the rest, were born together with Agni and the other deities, those deities are the deities of those metres. The writer on metre also says in a sūtra: the deities are Agni, Savitṛ, Soma, Bṛhaspati, Mitra and Varuṇa, Indra, the Viśve Devāḥ (Pi. 3-63). **NOTE** Thus the sacrifice of Prajāpati was performed. By it the seers and men were "fashioned" (cākl̥pre), created. He explains the form cākl̥pre as: of kṛp in the passive, in the liṭ, ending re (the substitution of ire); the change of r to l (Pā. 8-2-18); lengthening of the reduplication through the tujādi rule. By that very sacrifice they created the whole world.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- मित्रावरुणयोः (*mitrāvaruṇayoḥ*)—for Mitra and Varuṇa
- विराट् (*virāṭ*)—the metre called Virāṭ
- अभिश्रीः (*abhiśrīḥ*)—was the resort
- इह (*iha*)—in this sacrifice
- त्रिष्टुप् (*triṣṭup*)—the Triṣṭup metre

### Printed p. 796

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- अह्नः (*ahnaḥ*)—of the day
- भागः (*bhāgaḥ*)—was the portion of the midday pressing
- जगती (*jagatī*)—the Jagatī metre
- विश्वान् देवान् (*viśvān devān*)—the Viśvedevas
- आ विवेश (*ā viveśa*)—entered and pervaded them
- तेन (*tena*)—by that sacrifice
- ऋषयः (*ṛṣayaḥ*)—the seers
- मनुष्याः (*manuṣyāḥ*)—and men
- चाप्लृप्रे (*cāplṛpre*)—were created

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

For Mitra and Varuṇa the Virāj metre became the support. The Triṣṭup metre was the portion of the Mādhyandina pressing, which takes place at midday in the sacrifice. The Jagatī metre entered the Viśvedevas. By that sacrifice, which the gods performed for the sake of creation, the seers and men came into being.

##### English translation
Viraj was the glory of Mitra and Varuna; Trishtubh was Indra's portion of the midday (oblation) at this (sacrifice). Jagati entered into the Viswedevas; by this (sacrifice) Rishis and men were created.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

विराट् मत्रावरुणयोः अभिश्रीः (*virāṭ matrāvaruṇayoḥ abhiśrīḥ*)—The Virāj metre was produced by Prajāpati together with Mitra and Varuṇa.

इंद्रस्य त्रिष्टुप् इह भागः अह्नः (*iṃdrasya triṣṭup iha bhāgaḥ ahnaḥ*)—At the Mādhyandina pressing Indra has the chief share. At this pressing the mantras in the Triṣṭup metre are to be recited. For the rule is that at the morning pressing mantras in the Gāyatrī metre are recited, at the midday pressing mantras in the Triṣṭup metre, and at the third pressing mantras in the Jagatī metre. The mantras to be recited at the three pressings and the rules governing them we have explained at length earlier (Part 26, p. 40). That the Mādhyandina pressing and the Triṣṭup metre were produced by Prajāpati is also stated in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā:

उरसो बाहुभ्यां पंचदशं निरमिमित तमिंद्रो देवतान्नसृज्यत त्रिष्टुप्छंदो बृहत्साम राजन्यो मनुष्याणामविः पशूनां तस्मात्ते वीर्यावंतो वीर्याद्भ्यसृज्यंत ॥ (*uraso bāhubhyāṃ paṃcadaśaṃ niramimita tamiṃdro devatānnasṛjyata triṣṭupchaṃdo bṛhatsāma rājanyo manuṣyāṇāmaviḥ paśūnāṃ tasmātte vīryāvaṃto vīryādbhyasṛjyaṃta ‖*) (Tai. Saṃ. 7-1-14)

Prajāpati fashioned the Pañcadaśa stoma from his chest and arms. Then he created Indra, the Triṣṭup metre and the Sāman mantra called Bṛhat. Therefore Indra, born from the arms of the mighty Prajāpati, became the most excellent of all. Therefore among men the kings became powerful, and among animals the sheep became fit for sacrifice.

### Printed p. 797

विश्वान् देवान् जगती आ विवेश (*viśvān devān jagatī ā viveśa*)—"The Jagatī metre entered the Viśvedevas" means that, since Prajāpati created the Viśvedevas and the Jagatī metre together, the Jagatī metre became dear to the Viśvedevas. On this point:

मध्यतः सप्तदशं निरमिमित तं विश्वे देवा देवता अन्वसृज्यंत जगतीछंदो वैरूपग्ं साम वैश्यो मनुष्याणां गावः पशूनां तस्मात्त आद्या अन्नधानाद्द्य सृज्यंत ॥ (*madhyataḥ saptadaśaṃ niramimita taṃ viśve devā devatā anvasṛjyaṃta jagatīchaṃdo vairūpagṃ sāma vaiśyo manuṣyāṇāṃ gāvaḥ paśūnāṃ tasmātta ādyā annadhānāddya sṛjyaṃta ‖*) (Tai. Saṃ. 7-1-1-5)

Prajāpati created the Saptadaśa stoma from his middle (abdominal) part. After that he created the Viśvedevas, the Jagatī metre and the Vairūpa Sāman mantra; likewise he created Vaiśyas and cows. Since these were born from Prajāpati's belly, the Vaiśyas were, among men, the best provided in anna-dhāna, that is, in food and the like, wealth and grain; and the cows were the best among the animals that produce milk for food.

In the Ṛk of this sūkta beginning कासीत्प्रमा प्रतिमा (*kāsītpramā pratimā*) several questions were asked about the materials of the sacrifice. Of these, three have now been answered here. That is: प्रतिमा कासीत् (*pratimā kāsīt*)—who is the deity? छंदः किमासीत् (*chaṃdaḥ kimāsīt*)—what is the metre? प्रउगं किमुक्थं (*praugaṃ kimukthaṃ*)—what are the Praüga and the Ukthya Śastra mantras? These three questions are answered in the previous Ṛk and in this one. The two further questions, आज्यं किमासीत् (*ājyaṃ kimāsīt*)—what was the ājya?—and परिधिः क असीत् (*paridhiḥ ka asīt*)—what was the paridhi?—are answered in the Puruṣa-sūkta (Ṛ. Saṃ. Maṇḍala 10, sūkta 90) as follows:

............ देवा यज्ञमतन्वत । वसंतो अस्यासीदाज्यं ग्रीष्म इद्मः शरद्धविः । सप्तास्यासन्परिधयस्त्रीसप्त समिधः कृताः ॥ (*devā yajñamatanvata | vasaṃto asyāsīdājyaṃ grīṣma idmaḥ śaraddhaviḥ | saptāsyāsanparidhayastrīsapta samidhaḥ kṛtāḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-90-6 and 15)

That is: spring, which makes all sap flow, that is, makes all trees and the like put forth shoots, became the ājya offered in the sacrifice that is the instrument of the world's creation. The meaning is that from that sacrifice spring arose, together with the saps (juices) such as ājya (ghee) and curds. In the summer season the heat is great, so it dries up all sap, that is, liquids such as water and also trees and the like. Therefore at that season dry wood and the like is found in abundance. For this reason summer became in that sacrifice the fuel-stick called idhma. That is, the intention is that from that sacrifice the summer season arose, together with dry wood.

### Printed p. 798

In the autumn season grains such as rice ripen well and become fit to eat; therefore autumn became the oblation of that sacrifice. That is, from that sacrifice the autumn season arose, rich in grain.

The seven metres became the paridhis. That is, त्रिः सप्त (*triḥ sapta*)—those same seven metres, repeated three times, made twenty-one. In that number of twenty-one, the three paridhis and eighteen fuel-sticks together made twenty-one.

Now, to the three questions कासीत्प्रमा प्रतिमा किं निदानं (*kāsītpramā pratimā kiṃ nidānaṃ*) an answer is to be given: what was the time-limit of the sacrifice? who were the deities? what was the fruit of the sacrifice? Since it is said

पूर्णे विश्वसृजोऽमृताः शतं वर्षसहस्राणि दीक्षिताः सत्रमासत ॥ (*pūrṇe viśvasṛjo 'mṛtāḥ śataṃ varṣasahasrāṇi dīkṣitāḥ satramāsata ‖*)

and also

एतेन वै विश्वसृज इदं विश्वमसृजंत (*etena vai viśvasṛja idaṃ viśvamasṛjaṃta*) (Tai. Brā. 3-12-9-2 and 8)

the gods, desiring in the beginning to create the world, performed the sacrifice for a thousand years. Therefore the time-limit of that sacrifice is a thousand years. The fruit of this sacrifice is the impulse to undertake the creation of the world. The main purport is this: when the gods, desiring to carry the work of creation forward, performed the sacrifice called Viśvasṛjām-ayana addressed to Prajāpati, all the implements of the sacrifice, that is, the materials of the sacrifice, were produced from Prajāpati himself. Then, since from Prajāpati's body the gods beginning with Agni arose together with the seven metres beginning with Gāyatrī, the deities of those metres are Agni and the others. In the work called Chandoviciti it is said: अग्निः सविता सोमो बृहस्पतिर्मित्रावरुणाविंद्रो विश्वे देवा देवताः ॥ (*agniḥ savitā somo bṛhaspatirmitrāvaruṇāviṃdro viśve devā devatāḥ ‖*)—Agni (Gāyatrī), Savitṛ (Uṣṇik), Soma (Anuṣṭup), Bṛhaspati (Bṛhatī), Mitra and Varuṇa (Virāj), Indra (Triṣṭup), the Viśvedevas (Jagatī): these deities are declared to be the deities of the respective metres. In this way the sacrifice called Prājāpatya (performed in honour of Prajāpati) was carried out, and it is explained here that from this sacrifice the whole world was created.

#### Ṛk 6

##### ॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)

> चा॒क्लृ॒प्रे तेन॒ ऋष॑यो मनु॒ष्या॑ य॒ज्ञे जा॒ते पि॒तरो॑ नः  ॒
> पुराणे ।  
> पश्य॑न्मन्ये॒ मन॑सा॒ चक्ष॑सा॒ तान्य इ॒मं य॒ज्ञ मय॑जंत॒ पूर्वे॑ ॥

### Printed p. 799

##### ॥ पदपाठः ॥ (Pada-pāṭha)

> चाक्लृप्रे । तेन । ऋषयः । मनुष्याः । यज्ञे । जाते । पितरः । नः । पुराणे ।  
> पश्यन् । मन्ये । मनसा । चक्षसा । तान् । ये । इमं । यज्ञं । अयजंत ।  
> पूर्णे ॥ ६ ॥

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> पुराणे चिरंतनेऽस्मिन्यज्ञे जाते विश्वसृड्भिर्देवैः सम्यगनुष्ठिते सति तेन
> यज्ञेनर्षयो मनुष्या नोऽस्माकं पितरः पूर्वपुरुषाश्च चाक्लप्रे । अकल्प्यंत ।
> असृज्यंत । इममीदृशं यज्ञं ये पूर्णे साध्या देवाः प्रजापतेः प्राणभूता
> अयजंत अन्वतिष्ठन् तान्देवान्त्राणात्मना सर्वत्र वर्तमानांश्चक्षसा दर्शनहेतुना
> मनसा पश्यज्ञानन्मन्ने । तानेव विश्वसृष्टान्देवान् सौमि । मन्यतिरर्चतिकर्मा ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

When this ancient, long-standing sacrifice had come to be, that is, had been duly performed by the world-creating gods, then by that sacrifice the seers, men and "our fathers", the forefathers, were fashioned and created (अकल्प्यंत (*akalpyaṃta*), असृज्यंत (*asṛjyaṃta*) are his glosses of चाक्लप्रे (*cāklapre*)). Those Sādhya gods of old, who are the vital breaths of Prajāpati and who performed this sacrifice, and who exist everywhere in the form of breath: those gods I perceive with the mind, which is the instrument of seeing. Those very gods, the creators of the world, I praise: मन्यतिरर्चतिकर्मा (*manyatirarcatikarmā*) (the root man here belongs to the verbs of worship). **NOTE**

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- पुराणे (*purāṇe*)—performed in extremely ancient times
- यज्ञे (*yajñe*)—this sacrifice
- जाते (सति) (*jāte (sati)*)—when it was performed by the gods desiring to create the world
- तेन (*tena*)—by that sacrifice
- ऋषयः (*ṛṣayaḥ*)—seers
- मनुष्याः (*manuṣyāḥ*)—men
- नः (*naḥ*)—our
- पितरः (*pitaraḥ*)—forefathers who are our fathers
- चाक्लप्रे (*cāklapre*)—were created
- इमं यज्ञं (*imaṃ yajñaṃ*)—this sacrifice
- ये पूर्णे (*ye pūrṇe*)—which gods of former time, the Sādhyas, who are the breaths of Prajāpati
- अयजंत (*ayajaṃta*)—performed
- तान् (*tān*)—those gods who exist everywhere in the form of breath
- चक्षसा (*cakṣasā*)—capable of seeing and understanding
- मनसा (*manasā*)—with the mind
- पश्यन् (*paśyan*)—having understood
- मन्ये (*manye*)—I praise those gods, the creators of the world

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

In extremely ancient times, when this sacrifice was performed by the gods desiring to create the world, by that sacrifice the seers, men and our forefathers the fathers were created. And those former gods called Sādhyas, who are the breaths of Prajāpati and who performed this sacrifice: those gods I understand, with a mind able to examine and perceive them, and I praise them.

##### English translation
When this ancient sacrifice was accomplished, by it Rishis, men, and our progenitors were created; beholding them with the eye of the mind, I glorify those who of old celebrated this sacrifice.

##### ॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)

> स॒हस्तो॑माः स॒हच्॑छंदस आ॒वृतः॑ स॒हप्र॑मा॒ ऋष॑यः स॒प्त  ॑
> दैव्याः ।
